issues.author: Helw150
issues.body:
# Floppy Phoenix schedules for December (and maybe January)

Building on @ClassicLarry et al. candidate work in [the GB200 TPS tracker (#7201)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201), I've been Rick Rubin-ing on [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html) to see how post-training changes model choice under a few different timelines that @ihodes was curious about at our last hero run meeting.

Under the very heavily asterisked assumptions below, d6144 4-of-128 seems about right so not actually a huge prior update here. One thing I'd raise is that (if we want a more pretrained model that we think can support longer RL runs) d7168 (or another larger model via sparsity or depth scaling) is worth benchmarking to see how much it tanks our MFU v.s helps our model size.

## TL;DR

My current recommendation is to plan around d6144 4-of-128. If December 24 is fixed, the unresolved choice is whether to hand off on November 15 or December 1. I would consider d7168 only for a January 15 release, and only if its measured pretraining and RL pace are close to the estimates here.

We are trying to ship a broadly useful model, roughly at the capability level tracked by the [Artificial Analysis index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/). Everything below assumes that pretraining starts August 15. The MFU estimates use Larry et al.'s measurements and the extrapolation formulas in #7201. RL is modeled as fully on-policy, so rollout generation and policy updates happen in sequence. I assume 15% downtime from operational issues, plus seven pretraining days for long-context extension and early cooldowns.

No row is measured end-to-end. The d6144 pretraining pace is projected from one rack, d7168 pace is forecast, and every RL figure is an unmeasured ceiling.

| post-training start | release | provisional model | pretraining tokens | illustrative RL response-token upper bound<sup>1</sup> | decision status |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| December 1 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈20.8T | ≈0.5T | stretch; the upper bound reserves no time outside RL |
| November 15 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈17.4T | ≈0.9T | open trade: 3.3T pretraining tokens for 13.6 post-training days |
| December 1 | January 15 | d7168 4-of-128 ([unmeasured scenario](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757)) | ≈14.5T | ≈0.8T | only if measured pace supports it; d6144 is the fallback |

<sup>1</sup> This spends the full effective post-training window on one synchronous RL loop. It reserves no time for SFT, evaluation, verifier work, recovery, safety work, or release packaging. We also have not decided whether "response tokens" means generated, accepted, or learner tokens.

All d6144 calculations use 20.0B active parameters. That convention is still unresolved in #7201.

## Why doesn't the fastest model win?

For a December 1 handoff, the fastest d5120 row gets 27.4T pretraining tokens versus 20.8T for d6144. The loss fit assigns a penalty to the smaller active model, even though it gets more pretraining tokens and can run more RL cycles.

[ScaleRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13786) motivates a sigmoid in log RL compute. [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) then assumes that the RL ceiling grows with model size. The [Nicholas Roberts et al. overtraining paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01411) is another reason to include inference-time compute when sizing the pretrained model. None of these results calibrates final Marin capability.

Under those assumptions, d8192 has the lowest predicted reducible loss in all three schedules. I do not trust that result enough to train d8192: there are no d7168–d8192 throughput points, the loss fit has no prediction interval, and we do not have a Marin RL scaling curve. This is useful as sensitivity analysis, not as a model ranking. I would measure d7168 and d8192 to see where MFU falls off.

## The three schedules

### What if post-training starts December 1 and we release December 24?

This is tight: 19.6 effective post-training days. The [d6144 4-of-128 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) gets about 20.8T pretraining tokens and an illustrative 0.5T RL response-token ceiling.

The [d5120 4-of-64 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=8.8356) gets 27.4T pretraining tokens and a 0.8T RL ceiling. The current loss fit ranks it below d6144; we do not have a measured released-model quality comparison.

If its MFU holds up, [d6144 4-of-256](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=11111&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=35.35) gets about 16.7T pretraining tokens and a 0.4T RL ceiling. Its quality advantage over 4-of-128 is unmeasured, and the current fit assigns it none.

### What if pretraining ends November 15?

For [d6144](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75), the earlier handoff gives up about 3.3T pretraining tokens and adds 13.6 effective post-training days. We could use that time for more shots at goal on the recipe, or raise the illustrative ceiling from 0.5T to 0.9T response tokens.

The 0.9T figure is closer to the scale in the [MAI technical report](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf), but the comparison is pretty fuzzy. Their token accounting and post-training stages might not match ours.

We do not have much signal on shorter pretraining versus shorter post-training. The ongoing A2B run might give us some: if much lower pretraining loss does not make RL easier, maybe we should take the earlier handoff.

### What do we buy by waiting until January 15?

Releasing January 15 instead of December 24 adds 18.7 effective post-training days, 2.8e24 post-training hardware FLOPs, and 18% more total hardware compute.

[d7168](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757) gets about 14.5T pretraining tokens and has a 0.8T illustrative RL ceiling. I would only use it if measured training and RL pace make those two estimates credible. [d6144 is the fallback](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=27778&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75): 20.8T pretraining tokens and a 1.0T RL ceiling.

## What would be helpful to measure

- Define the RL token accounting, then run one complete synchronous RL cycle for each viable width. Report prompt, generated, accepted, and learner tokens; group size; response lengths; policy updates; and generation, update, synchronization, and total wall time.

- Measure d7168 and d8192 MFU with the same accounting as #7201. If d7168 is already falling off the throughput curve, use d6144 for every schedule.

- Cut another A2B cooldown so that Ben can run his existing post-training recipe on top of it. Knowing whether lower pretraining loss makes post-training easier in our setup would help us choose which phase to compress.

<details>
<summary>Full candidate table</summary>

| candidate | params, B (active / total) | TPS basis | 11-rack TPS | 11-rack 6NT utilization<sup>2</sup> | assumed RL cycle, seconds | pretraining tokens, T<sup>3</sup> | RL response-token ceiling, T<sup>4</sup> | modeled reducible-loss gap vs d8192<sup>5</sup> |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d5120 4-of-64 | 14.6 / 129 | projected from 8 racks | 3.740M | 18.6% | 8.5 | 27.4 / 23.0 | 0.8 / 1.3 / 1.6 | 10.1% / 9.4% |
| d5120 4-of-128 | 14.5 / 250 | projected from 2 racks | 3.346M | 16.5% | 11.2 | 24.5 / 20.6 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.5% / 9.9% |
| d5120 8-of-256 EP | 14.5 / 249 | projected from 2 racks | 3.254M | 16.1% | 11.4 | 23.8 / 20.0 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.6% / 10.0% |
| d6144 4-of-128 <sup>C</sup> | 20.0 / 355 | projected from 1 rack | 2.833M | 19.3% | 13.2 | 20.8 / 17.4 | 0.5 / 0.9 / 1.0 | 5.5% / 5.0% |
| d6144 4-of-256 <sup>C</sup> | 20.0 / 707 | projected from 2 racks | 2.273M | 15.5% | 18.5 | 16.7 / 14.0 | 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.7 | 6.3% / 5.9% |
| d7168 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 27.2 / 483 | MFU forecast | ≈1.974M | ≈18.3% | 16.5 | 14.5 / 12.1 | 0.4 / 0.7 / 0.8 | 2.1% / 1.9% |
| d7680 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 31.3 / 555 | MFU forecast | ≈1.668M | ≈17.8% | 18.5 | 12.2 / 10.3 | 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.7 | 0.9% / 0.8% |
| d8192 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 35.6 / 631 | MFU forecast | ≈1.434M | ≈17.4% | not estimated | 10.5 / 8.8 | not estimated | reference |

<sup>2</sup> `6NT utilization = 6 × active parameters × tokens per second / peak hardware FLOP/s`.

<sup>3</sup> December 1 / November 15 post-training starts.

<sup>4</sup> December 1→December 24 / November 15→December 24 / December 1→January 15. These are unmeasured ceilings from the assumed cycle times, not forecasts.

<sup>5</sup> Relative gap in the reducible part of the base-loss fit for December 1 / November 15. This is uncalibrated to released-model quality and has no prediction interval.

`C` marks the unresolved active-parameter convention. `E` marks a pace forecast with no measured throughput point.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Schedule math and assumptions</summary>

`hardware FLOPs = effective days × 86,400 × 704 × 2.5e15`

| pretraining start | post-training start | release | calendar days (pre / post) | effective days (pre / post) | peak hardware FLOPs (pre / post / total) |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| August 15 | December 1 | December 24 | 108 / 23 | 84.8 / 19.6 | 1.29e25 / 2.97e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | November 15 | December 24 | 92 / 39 | 71.2 / 33.2 | 1.08e25 / 5.04e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | December 1 | January 15 | 108 / 45 | 84.8 / 38.3 | 1.29e25 / 5.82e24 / 1.87e25 |

- Assume an average of 11 active NVL72 racks, 10–12 in practice, or 704 working GB200s for 1.76e18 peak BF16 FLOP/s.
- Effective pretraining days are `0.85 × calendar days − 7`; effective post-training days are `0.85 × calendar days`. The 7 pretraining days are 4 days for long context and 3 days for cooldown checkpoints.
- TPS projections come from #7201 and scale from 12 racks to our 11-rack average. d7168–d8192 use an MFU forecast.
- Useful pretraining FLOPs are `6 × active parameters × tokens`.
- The Floppy Phoenix links use compute normalized to its 20% reference MFU: 3.18e24 for the December 24 budget and 3.74e24 for the January 15 budget. This is not directly comparable to the peak hardware FLOPs above.
- The post-training calculation uses a 4M-response-token batch. Generation, policy update, and synchronization happen in sequence.
- The loss fit does not model a quality benefit from total expert count.

</details>

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
🤖 A more concrete comparison to the related work:

| model | parameters (active / total) | base-model training tokens | approximate base-training FLOPs | RL tokens / FLOPs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [MAI-Thinking-1 / MAI-Base-1](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf) | 35B / ~1T | 30T pretraining + 3.55T mid-training | 6.30e24 pretraining; 7.05e24 including mid-training | about 1.8T packed learner tokens and 3.8e23 policy-update FLOPs for the plotted STEM climb under the reconstruction below; full RL total is higher and not recoverable |
| [OLMo 3 Think 32B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961) | 32B / 32B | 5.5T pretraining + 2×100B mid-training branches + 100B context extension | 1.06e24 pretraining; 1.11e24 including both mid-training branches and context extension | not reported; the published hyperparameters imply at most 25.2B response tokens and about 6.4e21 nominal model FLOPs for generation + one learner pass |
| [Arcee Trinity-Large-Thinking](https://www.arcee.ai/blog/trinity-large-thinking) | 13B / 398B | 17T | 1.33e24 | not reported; the final model followed two months of SFT/RL pipeline work across 1,152 H100s. Continuous use for 60 days would be about 5.9e24 peak hardware FLOPs, but this is a mixed program envelope, not reported RL spend |
| [Kimi K2 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534) | 32B / 1.04T | 15.5T | 2.98e24 | not reported |
| [DeepSeek V4 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348) | 49B / 1.6T | 33T | 9.70e24 | not reported; the report describes specialist RL followed by on-policy distillation, but gives no total |

The base-training FLOPs above are my `6 × active parameters × training tokens` calculations. They are useful-model FLOPs, not measured hardware FLOPs, and they do not include ablations or failed runs. In particular, they are not directly comparable to the peak hardware-budget FLOPs in the issue without an MFU/goodput conversion.

<details>
<summary>MAI RL derivation and caveats</summary>

MAI does expose enough to estimate the learner side of its main STEM climb. The report gives a packed global batch of 7,040 sequences, a rollout-length curriculum of 8K → 16K → 32K → 64K → 128K, and a STEM curve that reaches about 5,000 steps. Reading that curve as roughly 1,000 steps at each length gives:

`7,040 × 1,000 × (8,192 + 16,384 + 32,768 + 65,536 + 131,072) = 1.788T packed learner tokens`

At 35B active parameters, that is about `3.75e23` policy-update FLOPs using `6NT`. One rollout-generation pass over the same tokens adds about `1.25e23` using `2NT`, for about `5.01e23` nominal model FLOPs across the accepted generation + learner path.

This is still not the full MAI RL bill. The paper does not tabulate the exact step boundary for each length, so the approximately 1K steps per stage is an inference from the approximately 5K-step plot. Generation also includes early-exit samples and rejected rollout groups. In addition, MAI trained separate STEM, agentic, and helpfulness/safety specialists, then ran consolidation SFT and a final RL stage. The report plots about 1.3K agentic steps, but does not expose enough trajectory-length accounting to convert those cleanly; it does not give corresponding totals for the helpfulness/safety or final consolidation climbs. The report’s largest RL job used 4,864 GB300s—4,096 for inference and 768 for the learner—but gives no duration.

One correction to the earlier discussion still stands: MAI’s 3.55T-token number is mid-training, not RL. The separate reconstruction above is why “roughly 2T RL learner tokens” is nevertheless a reasonable description of the main STEM climb.

</details>

<details>
<summary>OLMo 3 RL derivation and caveats</summary>

For OLMo 3, `750 steps × 128 prompts × 8 responses × 32,768 max response tokens = 25.2B` maximum response tokens. Applying `2NT` for rollout generation and `6NT` for one policy update gives about `6.4e21` FLOPs. That is not a reported total: real responses are usually shorter, while prompt prefill, verifiers, reference/teacher work, failed samples, and systems overhead add compute.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Arcee checkpoint distinction and hardware ceiling</summary>

The February [Trinity Large technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17004) covers Trinity-Large-Preview, not the final Trinity-Large-Thinking post-training run. Preview was instruction-tuned on [20B tokens](https://huggingface.co/arcee-ai/Trinity-Large-Preview) and received a “short RL stage”; Arcee does not give its RL tokens or FLOPs.

Trinity-Large-Thinking is a separate checkpoint built from Trinity-Large-Base. Arcee’s April release report says it followed two months of work improving and scaling the SFT/RL pipeline, with post-training across 1,152 H100s. As a loose ceiling, `1,152 × 989e12 BF16 FLOP/s × 60 days = 5.91e24` peak hardware FLOPs. That period includes SFT, recipe development, experiments, and the final model run, and Arcee does not report full-cluster uptime or MFU. I therefore would not call 5.9e24 the model’s RL FLOPs or infer an RL-token count from it.

</details>

issues.title: Floppy Phoenix-ing a few different timelines

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Marin Snowball 67B-A2B v0.1 calls itself ChatGPT/OpenAI (thinking on) or Nemotron/NVIDIA (thinking off). v0.1 has no learned self-name. Late MLPs fill in general AI-assistant knowledge.

- A default system prompt in the chat template fixes most of it, with no measured eval cost.
- Weight edits, merging, and cold-start SFT were too weak or cost math and fiction.
- Context distillation (train the system prompt's effect into the weights) is in progress. Its pre-training precision check found and fixed five places where our Levanter training forward pass differed from the vLLM-served model.

Follows #10491 (identity SFT and OPD, which regressed evals).

## Cause

Methods: [logit lens, direct logit attribution and activation patching](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c) on a torch harness that matches vLLM.

- Routed experts at layers 16–23 and the shared expert at layers 24–25 push " Chat" over " Marin". The top candidate neurons are L20 expert 46 #1072 and L23 expert 25 #1014. They fire equally on third-person ChatGPT questions, so they store general facts, not a self-identity.
- A system prompt wins through heads L23H1, L23H4, L22H5 and L22H3. Patching recovers 0.32, 0.26, 0.24 and 0.15 of the gap.
- In a [sample](https://gist.github.com/karansag/95c40bb6e55b82e0db08b76f3c5fff6a) of about 497k of the 15.2M SFT rows, no row names Marin. About 16k rows train a Nemotron identity on purpose.

## Results

Identity is the count of 52 dev prompts with no system prompt (thinking off / on) that answer correctly.

| Approach | Identity | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Default system prompt in the chat template | 41/47, 35/47 | none measured on [14 evals](https://gist.github.com/karansag/296cbfa3cd4e9530ef73f55da97927e8) |
| v0.1.1 (identity SFT) | 48 / 48 | MMLU-Pro −21, HumanEval+ −29, GSM8K −28 |
| [Merge](https://gist.github.com/karansag/050061adbebdd789579e5c3fe27cc5f6) v0.1 + 0.875·(v0.1.1 − v0.1) | 46 / 47 | GSM8K −8.6 pp, fiction leaks double |
| [Rank-1 edit](https://gist.github.com/karansag/8955dcc7d82b5445b832d707ce1313af), L20 shared expert | 15 / 3 | none measured; too weak |
| Cold-start identity SFT, 8 updates | 24/24 contrastive | 16/21 fiction prompts contaminated |

Merge strengths below 0.75 left identity unchanged. Identity and the GSM8K loss rose together at every strength. Steering vectors and MEMIT also failed.

## Levanter vs vLLM mismatches found before training

The [precision-check readings](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2) record each one. These made Levanter compute a different model from the one vLLM serves:

- MoE expert capacity factor 1.0 silently drops tokens, and pad tokens were dispatched unmasked. This was the main mismatch: top-1 token agreement with vLLM was 88.6%, and dropless MoE raised it to 99.4%.
- MoE combine weights were cast to BF16. vLLM keeps them in FP32.
- XLA's BF16 silu and sigmoid were one BF16 step off in 30–36% of elements.
- The FlashAttention-4 attention core rounds differently from torch eager.
- HF reload silently dropped `attention_implementation`.

The check also found nine plumbing bugs, mostly in our experiment code and multihost helpers.

With all fixes, a zero-learning-rate precision run (forward pass, one update and export, before any real training) passed. Its p99 log-prob error against vLLM was about 0.6 nats. Training memory fit at 50.2 of 59.4 GiB, and all 502 exported tensors were byte-equal to v0.1.

The cold-start SFT run above trained with the token drops. That may explain part of its collapse; we have not verified it.

## Context distillation results so far

After 16 SFT updates (LR 2e-6, about 3.8% identity tokens, the rest v0.1's own replay answers), we scored identity in vLLM, thinking off, teacher-forced, with 5 passes per arm ([evaluation result](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-m16-gate-decision-json)):

| NLL per answer token | v0.1 | after 16 updates |
|---|---|---|
| name ("Marin Snowball") | 8.85 | 1.45 |
| creator ("Open Athena") | 14.02 | 0.011 |
| no-system identity prompts won (of 24) | 0 | 15 |

On the 14-eval suite, the checkpoint stays within noise of v0.1 except BFCL tool calling (−20.3 points; 109 of 123 trials end with no answer file) and TruthfulQA (−1.4). TriviaQA improves by 2.4. Some third-person questions about other labs' products get credited to Open Athena (2 of 14 dev, 4 of 30 unseen, no system prompt). The training mix had no tool-calling rows.

**Checkpoint and data (public):**
- Model: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26) @ `b74e2034`. The model card has the full recipe and regressions.
- Training data: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-Data-2026.10.26](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-Data-2026.10.26) @ `7cd6a9b1`. It holds every training row, the training order, the mixture settings, the QC verdicts and the generation scripts.
- Training code: tag [`snowball-identity-cd16-2026.10.26`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/snowball-identity-cd16-2026.10.26) (commit `cc127d54`).

All fixes tried, side by side: [results table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10695#issuecomment-6418343832).

## Findings

- Interpretability: #10696 (plus a [follow-up](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10696#issuecomment-6412049647) that trains only the late-attention slice: no other-lab rewrites and tool calling kept, but identity too weak)
- Levanter MoE token drops: #10697
- Levanter vs vLLM numerics: #10698
- vLLM serve nondeterminism: #10699
- Weight-merge ladder: #10700

## Pull requests (draft stack)

- Levanter: #10683, #10684, #10685, #10686, #10687, #10688
- Experiment code: #10689, #10690, #10691, #10693, #10694; SFT data accounting, dataset audit, trained-export audit and launcher: #10705, #10706, #10707, #10708
- Identity scorer and the 16-update evaluation gate: #10701, #10702
- On-policy distillation (paused after 20 steps; results in #10732): #10730, #10731, #10732

## Status and next steps

- The 64-update run was not launched, because of the BFCL regression at 16 updates.
- Training only late attention (layers 18–23) avoids the BFCL loss but learns little identity; it is kept as a fallback.
- On-policy distillation from the 16-update checkpoint (20 steps) repaired most of the tool calling (BFCL 18.7% vs 7.3%) but never names itself and lost 2.3 points on MATH500; paused.
- Next: one more SFT run from v0.1 that adds v0.1's own tool-calling answers, name-first and false-premise identity rows, and third-person controls, judged against pre-stated ship lines.
- Recommendation: ship the default system prompt now.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

This requires a versioned model release and further experiments. The default system prompt has measured identity gains, while the 16-update checkpoint still needs generation and regression results. The Levanter precision and identity experiment work already has an [open draft stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10683); the evaluation launcher [loads Snowball's chat template from its export](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evaluation/models.py#L124-L131).

# Proposed Fix

1. Prepare an immutable v0.1 tokenizer/chat-template revision with the measured default prompt and unchanged weights. Verify rendering with and without a caller-supplied system message in both thinking modes; rerun the published identity panel and 14-eval comparison, then record the revision, hashes, and run receipts before promotion.
2. Screen generations, fiction, and math for the 16-update and 64-update checkpoints against matched v0.1 and prompt-only baselines in both thinking modes. Promote a trained checkpoint only if identity improves without a measured capability regression; otherwise retain the template result and record the negative result.
3. Review and land the existing [Levanter stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10683) and [experiment stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10689) through their precision and export gates. Update this issue with the release decision and artifact links.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 ## All identity fixes tried: results in one place

### A. Context distillation and its controls (same screen, same prompts)

All rows below were scored on the same screen. Generation counts are **without a system prompt**, thinking off / on. "Gate" is the teacher-forced NLL improvement over v0.1 (nats per token, name / creator).

| Arm | What changed | Says "Snowball" (of 52) | Says "Open Athena" (of 52) | Claims another lab (of 122) | Third-person rewrites, dev 14 / unseen 30 | Gate gain, name / creator | BFCL (Δ vs v0.1 + system prompt) | GSM8K / MATH500 Δ (pp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0.1 | nothing | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 52 / 21 | 0 / 0 | — | 26.0 (other code) | — |
| v0.1 + system prompt | prompt in the chat template | identity 41/47, 35/47 (with prompt) | | | | — | 27.6 (reference) | +0.8 / −0.2 (suite) |
| **Context distillation, full model (CD-16)** | 16 SFT updates, all weights | 2 / 6 | **38 / 36** | **19 / 4** | **2 / 4** | 7.41 / 14.01 | **7.3 (−20.3)** | +0.3 / +0.2 (suite) |
| CD, late attention only, lr 2e-6 | same data; only q/k/v/o of layers 18–23 train | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 55 / 30 | 0 / 0 | 0.35 / 1.58 | 27.6 (0.0) | +0.1 / 0.0 |
| CD, late attention only, lr 1e-5 | as above, 5× the learning rate | 0 / 0 | 14 / 0 | 36 / 28 | 0 / 0 | 2.39 / 12.76 | 24.4 (−3.3) | +0.1 / **−1.3** |
| Merge: v0.1.1's attention, layers 18–23 | no training; graft v0.1.1's change in those 24 tensors | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 54 / 27 | 0 / 0 | 0.80 / 1.41 | 27.6 (0.0) | 0.0 / 0.0 |
| Merge: v0.1.1's attention, all layers | no training; 104 attention tensors | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 69 / 33 | 0 / 0 | 2.03 / 4.26 | 26.0 (−1.6) | **−2.5** / −0.2 |
| On-policy distillation, 20 steps from CD-16 | teacher v0.1 + system prompt on identity and tool prompts, plain v0.1 elsewhere | 0 / 0 | not separately counted (identity pass 14 / 13) | — | 0 / 1 | 6.96 / 13.91 | 18.7 (−8.9) | −0.3 / **−2.3** |
| CD-16 data + tool replay + new identity rows (16 updates) | adds 156 v0.1 tool-call rows, 112 name-first / false-premise rows, 54 third-person controls | **0 / 0** | 39 / 43 | 15 / 6 | **2 / 4** | 7.11 / 14.01 | **22.8 (−4.9)** | **+1.3** / −0.1 |

**Bold** marks results whose 95% CI excludes 0, plus the headline wins. BFCL has 123 items, so its paired noise is about ±10 points. The CD-16 math deltas come from the full 14-eval suite. The other math deltas are paired screens against a fresh v0.1 serve.

**Reading:**
- Only full-model CD-16 learns the identity in generation, mostly the creator. It is also the only arm that breaks tool calling and rewrites some third-person facts.
- Training or grafting only attention keeps tool calling, but teaches almost no identity in generation, even when the teacher-forced NLL moves a lot (lr 1e-5).
- Adding v0.1's own tool-calling answers fixes tool calling (BFCL 22.8% vs CD-16's 7.3%; within noise of the system-prompt baseline) with no math loss. Only 8 of the 112 new identity rows were sampled in 16 updates, so that run did not test them; it still never names itself and still credits 4 of 30 unseen OpenAI products to Open Athena.
- On Ben's 60-item panel (one model grader): v0.1 8/60 clean, v0.1 + system prompt 26, CD-16 15, on-policy distillation 19, the tool-replay run 17. The system prompt is still the best option.

| Fix | Identity | Main problem |

| Ben's SFT (v0.1.1) | 48 / 48 of 52 | MMLU-Pro −21, HumanEval+ −29, GSM8K −28; BFCL 23.6 |

| Cold-start SFT, 8 updates | 24/24 contrastive | 16/21 stories contaminated |

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Google positions [AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents) as their answer to the kernel gap between PyTorch on GPU and JAX on TPU. Measure whether it changes anything for Marin, and produce a recommendation we can give back to Google.

What the repo contains, as of 2026-08-04 (Apache-2.0, created 2026-02-04, 53 stars, 19 open issues, explicitly "not an officially supported Google product"):

* MaxCode — PyTorch-to-JAX model migration, targeting MaxText.
* MaxKernel — Pallas kernel writing, autotuning, and profiling, in a human-in-the-loop mode and an automatic search mode. Its `gpu_to_jax` subagent accepts CUDA, Triton, PyTorch CUDA, cuDNN, and cuBLAS.
* JAXBench — 50 tasks: 17 priority operators (attention variants, MoE, GEMM, normalization), 8 of which ship a hand-tuned Pallas reference, plus 33 KernelBench Level-2 fusions.

Both agents need a Gemini API key or Vertex AI plus a GCP VM. The repo publishes no success rates, speedups, or case studies.

Reasons to doubt the claim, each of which the evaluation should settle:

* JAXBench scores correctness at `atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2` on float32-cast outputs (`JAXBench/harness/correctness.py`), copied from KernelBench. That tolerance passes kernels we would reject for training.
* JAXBench knows only v5e and v6e (`JAXBench/harness/tpu_specs.py`) and every task is single-device. It measures no collectives, no sharding, and no compute/communication overlap. That is where our gap actually is. In #7331 the two expert-parallel transports differ by 1.1 MFU points on the same model, and that difference is entirely in the collective path.
* 33 of the 50 tasks are KernelBench Level-2 fusions that XLA already handles well, so a win there says little.
* The 8 priority tasks with hand-tuned Pallas references correspond to kernels already published in the JAX and MaxText repositories. A win on those may be recall rather than generalization.
* The `gpu_to_jax` subagent defaults to `PREFERRED_BACKEND = "cpu"` and its README says it strips hardware-specific optimizations. Stripping the hardware-specific optimization removes the thing that made the CUDA kernel worth porting.
* MaxCode emits MaxText. We train on Levanter and Haliax.

Run three graded tasks. Give every task the same control arm: the identical prompt to Claude Code with `.agents/skills/add-pallas-kernel/SKILL.md`. MaxKernel is only interesting if it beats the agent practice we already have.

1. Recall check. Ask MaxKernel to write kernels we have already written by hand — `fused_cross_entropy_loss`, `mamba3`, and `ssd` under `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/`. Grade against the existing tests in `lib/levanter/tests/kernels/` at our tolerances, not JAXBench's, and against the measured throughput of our versions.

2. Translation with hardware held constant. Port the [cursor/mixture-of-kittens](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens) MoE forward pass to JAX and Pallas on GB200, where #7331 already gives us `a2a_cute` at 19.1% MFU and TE NCCL_EP at 18.0% as baselines. Holding the hardware fixed isolates the framework-translation question from the architecture question.

3. The actual claim. Port the same kernel to TPU. mixture-of-kittens fuses MoE compute and the expert-parallel all-to-all into a single CUDA kernel for Blackwell SM100/SM103 on GB200 and GB300 NVL72, and reports up to 2.37x on MXFP8 forward and 1.58x on BF16 backward against its baselines. TPU offers no equivalent of the primitives that design rests on, so the honest result is a redesign into Pallas plus `shard_map`, not a port. Grade what the agent does when the primitive is absent: whether it reports the gap, or emits plausible code that is wrong or slow.

Done when:

* Each of the three tasks has a recorded outcome for MaxKernel and for the control arm: compiles or not, passes our tolerances or not, and measured time against the incumbent implementation.
* We know whether MaxKernel's JAXBench numbers reproduce on a v6e VM we control, and whether any task passes at our tolerances but fails at `atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2`.
* The issue states a go/no-go on adopting either agent into Marin, with the reason.
* If it is a no-go, the issue lists the specific capabilities that would change the answer, in a form we can hand to Google. Missing collective and multi-device coverage in JAXBench is the first candidate.

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
The decision table each ablation issue writes by hand — baseline, budget, scale, gate-1/gate-2 verdict, effective-speedup — isn't stored anywhere queryable, and effective-speedup isn't even a logged metric (it's computed offline against a fitted scaling law per `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md`). So you can't ask "all variants that passed Gate 1 and their speedup," and cross-era baseline drift (v16 `dial_moe` vs May-Recipe `marin_moe`) is only recorded in prose, which is why numbers silently stop being comparable.

Write the ablation decision fields — baseline reference, budget, scale, gate verdict, and the computed effective-speedup — into the run's metadata (the artifact record and/or the W&B run), so a catalog query can reconstruct the decision table and the baseline becomes an explicit field you can notice when it moves.

**Done when:** for an ablation run, gate verdict + effective-speedup + baseline reference are stored in a queryable place, not just an issue comment.

Part of #7966.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — design task, blocked on prerequisites. No PR.**

# Research

The ablation decision fields (baseline, budget, scale, gate-1/gate-2 verdict, effective-speedup) live only as prose in issue comments and `agent.md`; none are in a queryable record, and effective-speedup is never logged — it is computed offline from the fitted scaling law. Making these queryable means adding a typed decision payload to the per-cell `ArtifactRecord`, which does not exist yet: this issue's own prerequisites **#7967** (emit an `ArtifactRecord` per ablation cell) and **#7968** (join W&B metrics into that record) are both still open, and #7966 lists this as building on them. So there is nothing to attach the decision to yet.

**Relevant code**
- [`artifact.py#L149-L176`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L149-L176) — `ArtifactRecord`: has `config`/`result`/`provenance`/`deps`, no decision fields.
- [`artifact.py#L332-L364`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L332) — `write_artifact` / `write_step_record`: how a record is persisted.
- [`experiments/grug/moe/agent.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md) — Gate 1/2 definitions, `effective_speedup()` formula, baseline scaling law (`L∞=1.6`, `A=88.32`, `α=0.0941`) — all prose.
- [`launch_cw_scale.py#L193-L209`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py#L193) — ablation launcher writes a W&B run but no decision metadata.

# Proposed approach (for review before implementation)

Blocked until #7967/#7968 land (a per-cell record with joined metrics is the thing we write onto). Once they do:

1. **Typed decision payload.** Add an `AblationDecision` model (pydantic, beside `ArtifactRecord`) with explicit fields: `baseline_ref` (baseline run `name@version` **plus** the scaling-law params it was fit against), `budget_flops`, `scale` (e.g. `d512`), `gate` (StrEnum verdict per gate), `effective_speedup`, and the inputs it was derived from (`variant_loss`, `variant_tps`, `baseline_loss`, `baseline_tps`). Making `baseline_ref` a first-class field is what surfaces cross-era drift (v16 `dial_moe` vs May-Recipe `marin_moe`) instead of hiding it in prose.
2. **Compute, don't hand-write.** Lift the `effective_speedup()` formula out of `agent.md` into a small pure helper (`experiments/grug/moe/`), call it at gate-evaluation time, and write the number — so the metric is produced once and recorded, not retyped per issue.
3. **Persist onto the cell record.** Attach the `AblationDecision` to the ablation cell's `ArtifactRecord` (new optional field, or under `result`) so a catalog query reconstructs the decision table; mirror the same dict into the W&B run summary/config for the W&B-side query path (#7968's join).

Question for the owner of #7966: should the decision write happen inside the gate-evaluation step, or as a post-hoc annotator that reads the joined record from #7968? That choice sets where the helper lives and whether this can proceed independently of #7968 or must follow it.

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
Once ablations produce records (#7967) with metrics joined in (#7968), exporting them into a queryable catalog should be nearly free, because `ArtifactRecord` already carries the identity, dependency DAG, config, and provenance a catalog needs. A thin exporter turns our records into queryable jobs so we can ask "all variants of X and their macro_loss / effective-speedup" and walk pretrain→cooldown→eval lineage — without touching the training pipeline.

Write a ~50–100 line exporter mapping `ArtifactRecord` → an [R3](https://github.com/mtangemann/r3) job: `name@version` → job, `deps` / `dep_paths` → job dependencies, `provenance.base_commit` / `tree_hash` → R3 git dependency, and config + metrics → `metadata.yaml`. Keep it catalog-agnostic where cheap, so the same shape can feed a native index if we don't adopt R3. Note two small R3-side changes are needed for this to be usable over GCS (pointer/URI storage instead of copying checkpoints, and a "register an already-run job" verb) — tracked upstream, not here.

**Done when:** a script/CLI ingests a set of `ArtifactRecord`s (or a GCS prefix) and emits catalog jobs, demonstrated by querying an existing sweep's variants and their metrics.

Part of #7966.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis** — new feature blocked on open upstream work; holding for review rather than opening a PR (per the feature/design scope rule).

# Research

`ArtifactRecord` already carries the mapping the issue wants: identity (`name`/`version`), `deps`/`dep_paths` lineage, `config`, and `provenance.base_commit`/`tree_hash` (both fields exist on `Provenance`). Ingest-from-prefix is `read_record(gcs_prefix)`. So the exporter itself is a thin pure mapping.

The two inputs it consumes do not exist yet, and the "Done when" (query a real sweep's variants **and their metrics**) is therefore unreachable today:

- **#7967 (per-cell records)** — OPEN. No canonical sweep-cell record write site yet; today records are written by `write_step_record` and the publish path, not per ablation cell.
- **#7968 (metrics join)** — OPEN. `ArtifactRecord` has **no metrics field**, so the `config + metrics → metadata.yaml` half has no source until this lands.
- **R3** is not a marin dependency, and the issue itself notes two upstream R3 changes are needed (pointer/URI storage; "register already-run job").

**Relevant code**
- [`artifact.py#L149-L176`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L149-L176) — `ArtifactRecord`: name/version, deps/dep_paths, config, result, provenance
- [`artifact.py#L286-L302`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L286-L302) — `read_record(prefix)`: ingest a record from a GCS prefix
- [`sites.py#L241-L250`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/publish/sites.py#L241-L250) — existing record write site (identity + config + provenance)
- `Provenance` fields: `tree_hash`, `base_commit`, `dirty`, `branch`, `built_by`, `git_remote`, `created_at`, `command_line`

# Proposed approach

New `lib/marin/src/marin/execution/catalog_export.py` (~50-100 lines), catalog-agnostic:

- `CatalogJob` dataclass — `name@version`, `deps`, git-dep `(base_commit, tree_hash)`, `metadata: dict` (config + metrics), `output_uri`.
- `export_records(records: Iterable[ArtifactRecord]) -> list[CatalogJob]` — pure mapping.
- `ingest_prefix(gcs_prefix) -> list[ArtifactRecord]` — glob `.artifact.json` under the prefix via `read_record`; walk lineage through `dep_paths`.
- Thin `to_r3_job(job)` / `metadata.yaml` writer so a native index can consume the same shape.
- **Emit pointer/URI (`output_path`) only — never copy checkpoints**, matching the upstream R3 storage change.
- CLI: `python -m marin.execution.catalog_export <gcs_prefix>`.

**Decisions needed before implementation:**

1. **Sequencing** — land the mapping now against a hand-written record fixture and wire metrics after #7968, or wait for #7967/#7968 so the done-condition (real sweep + metrics) is demonstrable? As written the acceptance test can't pass until #7968.
2. **R3 dependency** — add `r3` now, or keep the exporter emitting plain `metadata.yaml`/job dirs so no dependency is taken until R3 adoption is decided?

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
The pieces to answer "which code and config produced this number" all exist, but they're never joined: the artifact record has `tree_hash`, `fingerprint`, config, and deps but not the W&B run URL or the metrics; the W&B run has only `git_commit`, not the artifact fingerprint or output path. So you can't get from a result in W&B to its full provenance, or from a record to its metrics, in one hop.

Close the join in both directions: (a) push the artifact `fingerprint`, `tree_hash`, and `output_path` into the W&B run config (we already push `git_commit` in `run_environment.py` / `wandb.py`); (b) write the W&B run URL and final metrics (e.g. `macro_loss`, `tokens_per_second`) back into the `ArtifactRecord`.

**Done when:** from a W&B run you can find its artifact record and vice versa, and both carry the same fingerprint.

Part of #7966.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Confirm issue is actionable
- [x] Trace both join directions in code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PRs)
- [x] Post root-cause analysis + proposed approach

Scoped as a multi-module design change (levanter tracker + marin executor + training entrypoint), so no PR yet — approach below for review.

# Research

The two joins run through independent subsystems that never exchange the join keys. The W&B run is created inside the levanter trainer, which only knows `git_commit` (read from the `GIT_COMMIT` env var). The `ArtifactRecord` is written by the marin executor's step closure, which already holds `fingerprint`, `output_path`, and `provenance.tree_hash` but never sends them to the training job, and never reads training metrics or the run URL back. The training job is a separate fire-and-forget Fray job returning `None`, so nothing flows back to the record's `result` field today.

**Relevant code**
- [`wandb.py#L400-L417`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/wandb.py#L400-L417) — only `git_commit` reaches `wandb.init(config=...)`
- [`wandb.py#L206-L223`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/wandb.py#L206-L223) — `_write_replicate_file` writes config+summary to `tracker_metrics.jsonl`, no run URL
- [`artifact.py#L149-L177`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L149-L177) — `ArtifactRecord` has `fingerprint`/`output_path`/`provenance` (tree_hash) but no metrics/URL
- [`lazy.py#L336-L375`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/lazy.py#L336-L375) — step closure writes the record; `result=None` for training since `_train_job` returns `None`
- [`training.py#L69-L85`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py#L69-L85) — `LevanterCheckpoint.training_metrics()` already parses `tracker_metrics.jsonl` post-hoc

# Proposed approach

Reuse the two channels that already exist rather than adding a new coordination path: the `GIT_COMMIT` env var (executor → training) and `tracker_metrics.jsonl` (training → executor).

**(a) artifact → W&B config.** Mirror the `git_commit` pattern.
1. Thread `fingerprint` and `provenance.tree_hash` into the step's `StepContext` so `build_config` can see them (`output_path` is already in scope). These are captured in [`_lower`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/lazy.py#L300) but not passed into `StepContext.for_run`.
2. In marin training-env assembly (`resolve_training_env` / [`add_run_env_variables`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/training/run_environment.py#L21)), set `MARIN_ARTIFACT_FINGERPRINT`, `MARIN_ARTIFACT_TREE_HASH`, `MARIN_ARTIFACT_OUTPUT_PATH` alongside `GIT_COMMIT`.
3. In `WandbConfig.init`, read those env vars and add them to `hparams_to_save` next to `git_commit`. Levanter reads env vars only — no reverse import, dependency direction preserved.

**(b) W&B → ArtifactRecord.** Extend the file the executor can already read.
1. In `_write_replicate_file`, add `run.url` (and keep summary metrics such as `macro_loss`, `tokens_per_second`) to `tracker_metrics.jsonl`.
2. Make `_train_job` return an enriched `LevanterCheckpoint` — after `remote(...)` completes, read `tracker_metrics.jsonl` from `output_path` and populate declared value fields (e.g. `wandb_url`, final metrics) so `result_payload()` writes them into `ArtifactRecord.result`. Today `_train_job` returns `None`, so the record's `result` is empty for training steps.

Result: the W&B run config carries `fingerprint`/`tree_hash`/`output_path`, and the record carries the run URL + metrics keyed by the same `fingerprint` — the join closes both ways.

**Open questions before implementation**
- Which metric keys are canonical for `result` (`macro_loss`, `tokens_per_second`, `eval/loss`)? Summary schema varies by run type.
- Non-training artifact steps (eval, export via `levanter_checkpoint.py`, RL via `orchestration.py`) also call `add_run_env_variables` — apply (a) to all uniformly by wiring the env in `add_run_env_variables`?
- Add `wandb_url`/metrics as first-class `LevanterCheckpoint` fields, or a generic reusable `run_metrics` sub-record?

issues.title: [execution] Join W&B runs and the artifact record (fingerprint + metrics + URLs)

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
Larry-style ablation sweeps — the gate sweeps that feed hero-run recipes like #5358 — are recorded today only as a git branch + a W&B group + a hand-written issue table. None of it is queryable, and none of it is joined into a single record, so "what did we already try, and what produced this number" isn't answerable without reading issues. #6628 (Model index) and #6503 (Automated eval system) ask for a queryable catalog of what we've trained; this issue covers the small, artifact-layer changes that make our *ablation* runs catalogable in the first place.

We're evaluating [R3](https://github.com/mtangemann/r3) as a ready content-addressed experiment catalog, but the four changes below are valuable whichever way we go (adopt R3 or build a native index over `ArtifactRecord`s) — three of them are just "make ablations produce and join the provenance we already capture for production runs."

Sub-issues (each is small and independently useful):

- [ ] #7967 — Emit an `ArtifactRecord` for each ablation sweep cell
- [ ] #7968 — Join W&B runs and the artifact record
- [ ] #7969 — Add an `ArtifactRecord` → catalog (R3 job) exporter
- [ ] #7970 — Record ablation decision fields (gate, effective-speedup, baseline) in metadata

Ordering: #7967 and #7968 are prerequisites (nothing to catalog until ablations emit records with metrics); #7969 and #7970 build on them. #7969 also depends on a couple of small R3-side changes (pointer storage, register-external-job) tracked upstream.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read the issue and its four sub-issues (#7967–#7970)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PRs; only #7966/#7967 open)
- [x] Locate the sweep path and `ArtifactRecord` machinery in code
- [x] Post scope decision + analysis (umbrella/design → no PR)

# Research

This is an umbrella tracking issue: it lands no code itself, and its work is decomposed across #7967–#7970, which span `lib/marin/execution`, `lib/marin/training`, `lib/levanter/tracker`, and an out-of-repo R3 exporter. That is multi-module design work with an upstream dependency (#7969 needs R3 pointer-storage + register-external-job), so it does not fit a single self-contained PR. I'm leaving analysis for a human to sequence rather than opening one.

Root cause the sub-issues share: the sweep path runs an opaque `run_fn(target)` and never writes a record, and the record schema and the W&B run are never cross-referenced. So a sweep cell produces a W&B run + an issue table, but nothing on disk ties code+config+deps+metrics together.

One correction for #7967: `claim_and_run` lives in `lib/marin/src/marin/execution/sweep.py`, not `experiments/grug/moe/sweep.py`.

**Relevant code**
- [`sweep.py#L118-L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/sweep.py#L118-L149) — `_lead` claim loop; `run_fn` is opaque, no record written
- [`artifact.py#L337-L373`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L337-L373) — `StepRecordIdentity` + `write_step_record`, the existing per-step record writer
- [`artifact.py#L149-L177`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L149-L177) — `ArtifactRecord` fields (`fingerprint`, `deps`, `config`, `provenance`; no metrics/W&B URL)
- [`run_environment.py#L25-L33`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/training/run_environment.py#L25-L33) — `GIT_COMMIT` already flows to the run; W&B config push point for the join

# Proposed Approach

**#7967 — record per sweep cell.** `claim_and_run` only has `target_id` + opaque `config`, so it can't build a record itself. Two options: (a) carry a `StepRecordIdentity` on `SweepTarget` and call `write_step_record(identity, output_path=target_path, result=...)` right after `run_fn` succeeds in `_lead`/`_follow`; or (b) leave the write to `run_fn` and just document the contract. Prefer (a) — it keeps the write on the success path next to `write_status(STATUS_SUCCESS)` and reuses existing provenance capture. This one is the closest to a standalone PR (~30–60 lines + a round-trip test).

**#7968 — close the join.** Add optional `wandb_url` + `metrics` fields to `ArtifactRecord`, write them after the run finishes; push `fingerprint`/`tree_hash`/`output_path` into the W&B run config alongside the existing `GIT_COMMIT`. Depends on #7967 (needs a record to write back into).

**#7970 — decision fields.** Extend the #7968 metadata with `baseline_ref`, `budget`, `scale`, gate verdict, and computed `effective_speedup` (today offline per `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md`). Small once #7968 defines where metadata lives.

**#7969 — R3 exporter.** A ~50–100 line `ArtifactRecord → R3 job` mapper, catalog-agnostic. Blocked on the two upstream R3 changes the issue names; sequence last.

Recommended order matches the issue: #7967 → #7968 → {#7970, #7969}. Each sub-issue is individually PR-sized; I'd take them one at a time starting with #7967. Ready to implement #7967 on request.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body: We frequently run into issues with the wrong chat template being applied for a model between e.g. pre and post training. How can we adjust our abstractions so that this is less of an issue. Currently the template seems roughly tied to the tokenizer, but we've seen multiple locations where it needs to be supplied separately or adjusted. How do we adjust this?

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The chat template has **two independent homes that are never reconciled**: the tokenizer artifact (`tokenizer_config.json` / `chat_template.jinja`) and a `chat_template` field re-declared at every consumer. Post-training reads the second but exports the first, so a checkpoint trained with template *X* ships template *Y*, and inference/eval then load *Y* from that checkpoint.

**The concrete drift** (SFT runs through `train_lm`):
- `LmDataConfig.the_tokenizer` returns `load_marin_tokenizer(self.tokenizer)` and **ignores `LmDataConfig.chat_template`** — [`datasets.py#L691-695`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L691-L695) vs the field at [`datasets.py#L629`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L629).
- The training template is consumed only inside the data processor to build masks — [`formats.py#L48-70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/formats.py#L48-L70).
- HF export uses `tokenizer = config.data.the_tokenizer` and passes **no** `chat_template` to the export hooks — [`train_lm.py#L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L149), [`train_lm.py#L400-415`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L400-L415). `save_pretrained`/`_save_tokenizer_pretrained` *support* an override but nobody threads the training template in — [`hf_checkpoints.py#L1044-1076`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1044-L1076).

Net: the exported post-trained checkpoint carries the **base** tokenizer's template (or none), not the one the model was trained against.

**The proliferation** (each site re-specifies, falling back to the tokenizer independently, with no cross-check):
- `SFTSpec.chat_template` — *required* — [`launcher.py#L503`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L503)
- `ChatLmDatasetFormat`, `PreferenceChatLmDatasetFormat`, `TraceChatEvaluationFormat` each carry their own `chat_template`
- Inference: `ServeConfig.chat_template`, `ServedModelConfig.chat_template_content`, and vLLM `--chat-template`
- Templates are passed as **raw jinja strings** (`MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE`, `DELPHI_V0_CHAT_TEMPLATE`, `OPENCODE_TOOLS_CHAT_TEMPLATE`), so there is no identity/equality to detect drift — only the cache-key hash at [`launcher.py#L683`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L683) notices a change, and only for caching.

# Proposed approach

Make the **tokenizer the single source of truth** and let the training template travel with the checkpoint, so downstream never re-specifies unless deliberately overriding.

1. **Close the export hole (small, high-leverage).** Apply `LmDataConfig.chat_template` onto `the_tokenizer` via `with_chat_template` so the object used for masking *and* export is the same one. The `{% generation %}` block is standard HF syntax and is inert unless `return_assistant_tokens_mask=True`, so embedding the training template in the exported tokenizer is correct. This alone makes post-trained checkpoints self-describing and removes the most common footgun. Log a warning when the data template differs from the tokenizer's own.

2. **Default consumers to the checkpoint's template.** Inference/eval should read the template off the loaded tokenizer by default and treat `ServeConfig.chat_template` / `--chat-template` as an *explicit override that warns* on divergence — not a silent parallel source.

3. **Give templates identity (optional but recommended).** Replace raw-string passing with a small named `ChatTemplate` value (name + jinja + `has_generation_block`) plus a registry for the Marin/Delphi/Opencode templates. Equality then makes drift detectable (assert train == checkpoint == serve) instead of relying on a 6-char hash.

Recommendation: land (1) first as a focused change with a regression test that export-roundtrips a tiny model and asserts the exported `chat_template` equals the training template; treat (2) and (3) as follow-ups. This is architecturally significant and spans training→export→inference, so this is analysis rather than a PR — please confirm the direction (in particular whether (1) should also cover `train_dpo`/preference export) before implementation.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment is implementing two EP64 MoE routing changes in Levanter: MoonEP-style redundant-expert routing and global-histogram quantile balancing, motivated by PR #7890
s fast but dropping baseline (MHEP-004: 24.1231%% MFU with 9.6786%% drops). The correctness path now reaches zero assignment drops on one NVL72, but performance is far below the 21.7%% MFU gate: MNEP-095b reached 9.568%% MFU and MNEP-102 reached 9.937%% MFU. Profiling points at bounded-token all-to-all falling back to ragged transport (14.536s, 55.7%% communication), so the current blocker is token-transport efficiency rather than MoE math correctness. Separately, 64-GPU H100 QB ablations show global histogram improves balancing slightly with no observed loss gain and about a 1%% slowdown; unless new evidence appears, logits-domain histogram QB is the lower-risk direction to test on GB200.

### Helpful links
- [EP64 baseline PR #7890](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7890)
- [MoonEP correctness and transport update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5169273360)
- [Ragged-kernel failure and bounded-collective decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5158803255)
- [64-GPU QB ablation report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/QB-Ablations--VmlldzoxNzY0MjAxMA)
- [Experiment logbook snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2015d4a/.agents/logbooks/7891-moonep-jax.md)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

PR #7890 supplies the EP64 baseline. Its 25-step MHEP-004 run reached 24.1231% median MFU with 9.6786% final assignment drops. Its 200-step MHEP-008 run reached 23.6969% median MFU with 7.4113% final drops.

MoonEP balances compute with dynamic redundant experts. The Kimi K3 report also replaces per-rank quantile estimates with one global integer histogram reduction per layer and step.

## Hypothesis or Goal

A portable JAX MoonEP path can preserve forward and backward results and remove all assignment drops at EP64. Profile-based changes can recover at least 90% of the MHEP-004 median MFU.

The experiment matrix separates the changes:

* Fixed all-to-all with global histogram QB.
* MoonEP JAX with the current local QB.
* MoonEP JAX with global histogram QB.

## Status

The research branch starts at PR #7890 commit `e38ae4f8`. MoonEP correctness has passed zero-drop checks on one NVL72, but the current bounded-token path is still around 9.9% median MFU, below the 21.7% performance gate. The active follow-up is profiling and reducing token-transport overhead.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7891-moonep-jax.md`.
* W&B Report: Pending for the combined GB200 path.
* Important updates: #7279, #7890, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653, https://github.com/moonshotAI/moonep

## Decision Log

* 2026-08-02: Use a portable JAX correctness path before native CUDA fabric transport.
* 2026-08-02: Require zero assignment drops and at least 21.7% median MFU for the final combined run.
* 2026-08-03: Treat token transport as the main blocker after zero-drop NVL72 runs reached only about 9.9% median MFU.

## Conclusion

Correctness is proven for the exact MoonEP path on one NVL72, but the experiment has not met its performance gate. Continue with transport profiling and optimization before treating MoonEP plus global histogram QB as viable for the target EP64 path.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 A report audit found and fixed a QB score-domain error.

The report defines sigmoid(router_logits) scores. It also bounds histogram bins from min(bias)-1 to max(bias)+1. The first implementation used raw logits for selection, cutoffs, and margins, so values could clip outside that range.

Commit 7778bb1d6 now uses sigmoid scores for all three operations. Thirteen focused tests and the changed-files repository checks pass. I stopped the obsolete queued MNEP014 job before GPU use, and corrected MNEP015 is queued.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Update: EP64 process isolation does not repair the ragged device kernel

- Change: MNEP-017 ran four JAX processes for each worker and one GPU for each process on one NVL72.
- Result: The full EP64 program compiled. Task 10 then reported `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` before step zero.
- Confidence: High for this JAX and XLA build. The error matches the prior multi-node device-kernel failures.
- Profile: MNEP-013 completed five host-NCCL model steps. Its two-step HLO trace exceeded the 200-second profile barrier.
- Decision: Replace the device kernel with a bounded standard collective. Use one step without HLO data for the next profile.

comments.body:

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The ragged fallback in MNEP-096 has a cause in XLA, and two post-0.11.0 commits target it.

Read from the XLA revision jaxlib 0.11.0 pins, `131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b` (2026-07-16), so all of this applies to the build MNEP has been running.

- At EP64 the peer-pointer one-shot kernel cannot be selected. `IsRaggedAllToAllKernelSupported` requires `num_outputs <= kMaxNumRaggedAllToAllOutputPtrs`, which is 8, and `num_outputs` is the replica-group size. A 64-rank group never qualifies. The remaining fast path is the NCCL-LSA one, gated on `lsa_size == clique_key.num_devices()`. Everything else falls through to a loop of `num_ranks * num_updates_per_replica` individual `ncclSend`/`ncclRecv` pairs, preceded by a device-to-host copy of the offset buffers and a `stream.BlockHostUntilDone()`. That fallback shape is consistent with the 14.536s and 55.7% communication share in MNEP-096, though I have not read your XProf trace to confirm which of the two it landed on.

- `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true` is a no-op on its own. The kernel requires `FindSymmetricMemory` to return non-null for both the input and the output buffer (`ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc`), and under the default `--xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode=private` both are null, so it falls through silently. XLA's own e2e test only ever instantiates that impl with `COLLECTIVES_SYMMETRIC_MEMORY`. Anyone testing it needs both flags.

- Two commits landed after 0.11.0's pin. `acb5aaffe` (2026-07-24) adds a device-initiated kernel on NCCL 2.29 LSA/GIN that runs the collective in a single launch, with the stated goal of eliminating per-call host coordination. `7e502c985` (2026-07-31) enables the multi-host decomposer by default for ragged-all-to-all spanning multiple LSA domains. The decomposer already exists in 0.11.0 as `--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_multi_host_decomposer`, defaulted false, so it is testable today without a version change.

The `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` in MNEP-017 is worth retesting against a nightly. I have no evidence it is fixed; the relevant kernel was substantially rewritten in that window.

I am starting a throughput A/B of these paths on the EP64 hero on branch `research/mcwitt/7201-ra2a-xla-ab`, comparing `fixed_all_to_all` against `ragged_all_to_all` bare, with the multi-host decomposer, with symmetric memory, and on a nightly jaxlib with the device kernel. It will use one rack per run for 25 steps. Happy to re-order or drop arms if that conflicts with the MNEP queue, and I will post the numbers here either way since the transport blocker looks shared.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Nsight Systems profile of the best reproducible configuration (MNEP-120)

Configuration is the MNEP-102 graph: exact MoonEP, global histogram QB, two token
buckets, compute-overlap schedule, ragged direct-device transport, and the
one-remote-CTA wheel. The hook profiles task zero only, which covers its four GPUs.
Report and SQLite export:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/iris-profiles/rav/mnep-120-best-config-nsys-5-20260804-0620-coord/.../r00000-s1nrxs64.nsys-rep`
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/rav/nsysexport/r00000.sqlite`

## Read the step-level numbers with care

Nsight tracing costs a lot at this kernel count. The profiled step takes `51.55 s`
against `26.17 s` for the same configuration without a profiler, and the trace shows
`58%` GPU idle against `6%` in the XProf trace of the same graph. The device-side
per-kernel times agree with XProf, so use those. Do not use the step totals or the
idle fraction from this report.

## Kernel time for each step, device 0

| class | s for each step | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ragged transport | 11.95 | 47.9% |
| other | 3.91 | 15.7% |
| expert GEMM (QuACK) | 3.21 | 12.9% |
| dense GEMM | 2.56 | 10.3% |
| MoE layout (sonic) | 1.66 | 6.6% |
| attention | 1.34 | 5.4% |
| NCCL collectives | 0.33 | 1.3% |

## The transport splits into two different problems

864 ragged calls run on each GPU in each step. The durations are bimodal.

| call type | count | median | bytes | rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| token dispatch and combine | 1,968 in 5 steps | `24.14 ms` | `2.685 GB` | `111.2 GB/s` |
| expert weight exchange | 2,352 in 5 steps | `3.14 ms` | small | `9.5 GB/s` |

The token path is bandwidth-limited. The weight path is latency-limited: it carries
`22.65 GB` for each step, which is `1.46%` of the `1,546 GB` of token traffic, but it
uses `20%` of all ragged time. The weight exchange sends `w13` `[4,5120,2560]` and `w2`
`[4,1280,5120]` for up to four copied experts in each layer, in three passes, which is
288 small transfers for each step. Batching those calls looks like a cheap gain of
about `2.4 s` for each step.

## Two candidate causes that the profile rejects

Host launch behavior is not a limit. The delay from the launch call to the kernel start
is `48.95 ms` at p50 and `213.9 ms` at p90, so the host runs ahead of the device. The
200,770 kernel launches in each step do not gate the step.

Memory contention is not a limit. The trace holds 136,268 device-to-device copies that
move `7,818 GB` across five steps, but only `7.8 GB` of that overlaps a ragged kernel,
which is `0.1 GB/s` of competing demand. XLA schedules those copies outside the
collective.

Transport overlaps compute for `27%` of its wall time.

## The open question

The same kernel gives `106` to `111 GB/s` in training and `305` to `335 GB/s` in an
isolated benchmark at the same peer message size. Two profilers and two runs agree on
the training figure.

Measured and rejected as the cause: message size (`9%` across an eight-times change),
message skew (`21%`), expert GEMM contention (no measurable cost), the collective
overlap limit (raising it was slower), rank count 16 to 32 (no loss), rank arrival skew
(host medians agree to `0.5 ms`), host CPU count (`6.9%` from 8 to 32 CPUs), and now
launch behavior and memory contention.

Current hypothesis: the kernel launches with `grid:64,1,1` for every rank count. That
gives about four CTAs to each peer at 16 ranks and about one CTA to each peer at 64
ranks. Every earlier test held rank count at 16 or 32. MNEP-124 runs the benchmark at
64 ranks to test this.

issues.author: rfgordan
issues.body:
Picks up item 16 (robustness to prompt noise and irrelevant context) of #7090,
covering both axes in one chat-mode GSM8K eval.

**Revised design (2026-08-04).** Supersedes the original zeroeval-based plan
after implementation and multi-model validation. What changed and why:

- **Standalone benchmark (`GSM8KPerturbed`), not a zeroeval extension.** No
  zeroeval task is in the canonical campaign (#7505), and wiring into it
  surfaced unexercised-code bugs. A self-contained directory matches the
  checked-in-data convention of the canonical Tier-2 benchmarks.
- **Data sourced from openai/gsm8k only**, replacing the third-party
  zero-eval mirror (content verified identical).
- **Static realization checked in**: both data files are committed and open
  with a meta line recording the exact generation command, seed, and
  parameters. Runs are fully offline; regeneration is byte-identical.
- **lm-eval zero-shot protocol**: the "Question:/Answer:" prompt through the
  chat template, graded by flexible-extract (last number) — the exact
  protocol of the prior Marin chat-mode GSM8K measurement (#7321).
- **Paired evaluation.** Per-condition metrics grade each perturbed instance
  against the clean run of the same item; comparing against overall clean
  accuracy conflated perturbation effects with item-subset difficulty
  (+/-5-8pp observed, fabricating effects in both directions).
- **Off-domain history (oasst2), not GSM8K train exchanges.** Same-domain
  history was measurably confounded: solved exemplars acted as few-shot
  demonstrations and *improved* weak-model accuracy (+6.7 paired delta at 4
  exchanges on gpt-3.5-turbo). Off-domain chat flipped the same condition to
  genuine dose-responsive degradation (-6.7 at 4, -11.0 at 16).
- **Per-condition no-answer rate** is a first-class metric: it separates
  cannot-solve from cannot-format, and exposes infrastructure failures
  recorded as outputs (which once fabricated a spurious 28-point
  "collapse").

## Goal

(unchanged) Response quality should be insensitive to user-prompting
imprecision (whitespace, linebreaks, typos) and to irrelevant prior context.
Measure how much chat-mode GSM8K accuracy a model conserves under each,
against a same-protocol clean reference.

## Conditions

Eight conditions, one per test item (~165 items each), seeded and
reproducible. Noise conditions rewrite only the question text; history
conditions leave it verbatim and prepend prior chat turns.

| condition    | type    | what it does                                      |
|--------------|---------|---------------------------------------------------|
| misspellings | noise   | dictionary misspellings, p=0.2 per eligible word  |
| lowercase    | noise   | lowercases the whole question                     |
| extra_space  | noise   | multiplies spaces between words (1-3)             |
| typos        | noise   | keyboard-adjacent character swaps, p=0.05         |
| homophones   | noise   | CMUdict exact-homophone swaps, p=0.1 per word     |
| mild_mix     | noise   | HELM's composite: lowercase + contract + misspell + respace |
| history_4    | history | 4 unrelated oasst2 chat exchanges prepended       |
| history_16   | history | 16 unrelated oasst2 chat exchanges prepended      |

Notes:
- The first four noise transforms and mild_mix are byte-identical to HELM's
  invariance perturbations under a shared RNG.
- homophones models voice-transcription input and may swap spelled-out
  number words (two -> too); those items are flagged in metadata as
  recoverable-from-context.
- History exchanges (OpenAssistant/oasst2 root prompt + best reply,
  length-bounded, unfiltered; 2.1% math-adjacent) are embedded verbatim in
  the data file with source message ids; sampling is seeded independently
  of item content.
- Dropped from v1: standalone contraction (84% no-op on GSM8K prose), the
  middle misspelling dose, and the 2/8/32 history ladder (now 4/16).

## Metrics

Per condition, all paired against the clean run of the same items: accuracy,
clean-subset accuracy, paired delta, harmed/helped flip counts, and
no-answer rate; plus changed-only and spoken-number slices, and clean-arm
accuracy/no-answer overall.

## Implementation

eval/chat_benchmarks/GSM8KPerturbed/ in the Evalchemy fork:

- eval_instruct.py — loader, chat construction, grading, paired per-condition metrics
- src/perturbations.py — transforms, byte-parity-verified against HELM's code
- data_prep/generate.py — regenerates the committed data files
- data/gsm8k_clean.jsonl, data/gsm8k_perturbed.jsonl — the static realization

issues.author: weaverbot
issues.body:
[#7091](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7091) moved cross-cluster forwarding from Iris controllers into the per-cluster Finelog servers. Each sender now signs `aud="finelog"` tokens with a distinct Ed25519 private key in Secret Manager, and the hub trusts the matching public key in `lib/finelog/config/marin.yaml`. [#7690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7690) moves sender deployment to Pulumi but deliberately references and syncs an existing pinned secret version. Initial provisioning and rotation remain manual in [`lib/finelog/OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/OPS.md).

Add a Finelog key-lifecycle command that provisions or reuses a sender signing key, emits the pinned secret reference and public trust configuration, validates that the two halves match, and supports overlap-safe rotation. The generic key mechanics should not be duplicated under Iris and Finelog. Extract reusable generation, Secret Manager storage, inspection, and explicit rotation behavior from [`iris cluster init-keys`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py) into a neutral Rigging or Marin admin surface. Keep Finelog-specific sender and hub configuration sequencing in the Finelog command.

Do not generate private key payloads or Secret Manager versions through Pulumi. That would copy the private PEM into Pulumi state and make identity rotation an incidental deployment diff. Rotation must publish the new public key on the hub before switching the sender to the new pinned version, then verify forwarding before retiring the old public key. Pulumi remains responsible for stable IAM grants and may own secret-container metadata; it must not own private key payloads or `SecretVersion` resources.

Done when:
- Neutral key-lifecycle functions generate, inspect, reuse, and explicitly rotate Ed25519 keys in Secret Manager without service-specific naming.
- The Iris and Finelog entry points use the shared functions rather than carrying separate Secret Manager and key-generation implementations.
- A Finelog operator command provisions or reuses a sender key and returns its pinned `gcp-secret://` reference, public PEM, and `kid`; replacing an existing identity requires an explicit rotation option.
- Finelog provisioning validates that the configured private key matches the public key trusted for that sender.
- Rotation keeps old and new public keys trusted during the sender transition and provides a verifiable point before retiring the old key.
- Private key material never enters Git, logs, rendered deployment manifests, Pulumi configuration, or Pulumi state.
- Tests cover initial provisioning, idempotent reuse, explicit rotation, mismatched trust configuration, and the public-key overlap.
