issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment screens the data-plane cost of moving one 359.6B-parameter BF16 policy (about 719 GB) from GB200 trainers to rollout workers.

- **GB200 cross-rack works:** the current-like `1→8` fan-out moved one policy in **7.31 s**. A `1→1` bulk floor took **26.96 s**. An ideal pre-sharded `8→8` transfer took **3.97 s**.
- **H100 remains unmeasured:** direct private TCP did not connect between the sampled GB200 node and either H100 cluster. All 12 bidirectional attempts ended in `EHOSTUNREACH` or a 10 s timeout. The rejecting network component is unknown.
- **Scope:** these are warm, synthetic HBM-to-HBM transfers over NCCL. They do not include MarinSkyRL's parameter export, per-parameter synchronization, vLLM weight loading, or generation pause.

Artifacts: [benchmark and diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/13fb15592eb5e4a79e9255b4e5666358d2f41b98/bench) · [GPU endpoint runbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c0c1f7669a3c1661154840ff94b49ec14dcc633d/bench/diagnostics/GPU_ENDPOINT_RUNBOOK.md) · [model shape](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5016389653)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Results

| Shape | Route | Unique bytes | Median | Unique-policy rate |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `1→1` bulk floor | GB200 rack `DH1-393` → `DH1-394` | 719.41 GB | 26.96 s | 26.7 GB/s |
| `1→1` fresh placement | GB200 rack `DH1-393` → `DH1-392` | 719.41 GB | 27.60 s | 26.1 GB/s |
| `1→8` current-like fan-out | GB200 rack `DH1-393` → `DH1-394` | 719.41 GB | 7.31 s | 98.4 GB/s |
| `8→8` pre-sharded ceiling | GB200 rack `DH1-392` → `DH1-393` | 721.55 GB | 3.97 s | 181.7 GB/s |
| GB200 → H100 | Ohio → New Jersey | — | direct TCP blocked on sampled nodes | — |
| GB200 → H100 | Ohio → Nevada | — | direct TCP blocked on sampled nodes | — |

The `1→8` row is the closest data-plane proxy for current MarinSkyRL. Current code creates one update group containing trainer rank 0 and all inference ranks, then [broadcasts each parameter from trainer rank 0](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/45fae9d7e1df4143728067dc5647db7331df7036/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py#L590-L655). The benchmark sends the same bytes in bulk over an initialized communicator, so **7.31 s is an optimistic floor, not policy-refresh latency**.

[CoreWeave reports 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) of InfiniBand bandwidth per GB200 GPU](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-unleashes-the-power-of-the-nvidia-gb200-nvl72-a-glimpse-into-the-future-of-ai). Against that nameplate, `1→1` reaches about 53% of one GPU's rate and `8→8` reaches about 45% of eight GPUs' aggregate rate. These are rough comparisons, not NIC-utilization measurements. Nothing here suggests a broken GB200 fabric.

The H100 rows have no bandwidth result. The probes establish that direct TCP failed for the sampled endpoints; they do not identify whether routing, a gateway, VPC policy, an ACL, or host-network enforcement rejected it.

## Next

- [ ] Ask CoreWeave which private GB200↔H100 path is supported for these clusters, and whether it carries RDMA or only TCP.
- [ ] Run each H100 row with the same 719 GB payload after endpoint connectivity exists.
- [ ] Measure MarinSkyRL's real per-parameter broadcast/RPC/barrier cadence against the 7.31 s bulk floor.
- [ ] Pin the Iris task image by digest for follow-up runs.

<details>
<summary>Why these transfer shapes</summary>

The proposed MoE has 359.6B parameters. A dense BF16 policy therefore contains:

```text
359.6e9 parameters × 2 bytes = 719.2e9 bytes
```

No checkpoint is required. NCCL sends synthetic BF16 tensors with the same byte count.

Current MarinSkyRL:

1. [Builds an update group](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/45fae9d7e1df4143728067dc5647db7331df7036/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/worker.py#L447-L515) containing trainer rank 0 and every rollout rank.
2. Exports one parameter at a time and [broadcasts it from trainer rank 0](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/45fae9d7e1df4143728067dc5647db7331df7036/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py#L590-L655).
3. Each receiver [allocates the reported tensor on CUDA and receives the broadcast](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/45fae9d7e1df4143728067dc5647db7331df7036/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/vllm/vllm_engine.py#L2269-L2295).

The benchmark shapes mean:

- `1→1`: one complete policy crossing one rack boundary.
- `1→8`: one root broadcasting one complete policy to eight receiver ranks. This matches MarinSkyRL's sender shape, but not its per-parameter cadence.
- `8→8`: eight sources send disjoint shards. This is an optimistic ceiling for a shard-aware sender that MarinSkyRL does not implement.

The rates cannot be compared as a controlled ablation. Source count, receiver count, collective, and payload layout change together.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Method and raw GB200 samples</summary>

The harness uses two reusable 1 GiB BF16 CUDA buffers per active rank. It reports the slowest receiver time after CUDA synchronization. Communicator setup and the first collective are excluded, so the headline numbers are warm-transfer results.

| Run | Receiver makespan samples (s) | Median |
|---|---|---:|
| `1→1` | 27.0015, 26.9614, 26.9635, 26.9565, 26.9613 | 26.9614 |
| `1→1`, fresh placement | 27.6563, 27.6044, 27.6064, 27.6045, 27.6034 | 27.6045 |
| `1→8` | 7.3398, 7.3073, 7.3086 | 7.3086 |
| `8→8` | 4.0061, 3.9702, 3.9713, 3.9673, 3.9700 | 3.9702 |

The striped calibration reached 26.67, 91.5, and 181.4 GB/s at widths 1, 4, and 8 using one tenth of the payload. The full width-8 result reproduced the calibration at 181.7 GB/s.

NCCL selected GPUDirect RDMA InfiniBand across GB200 racks. The `1→1` logs used channels on two HCAs; wider runs showed receive channels on all four HCAs plus rack-local `P2P/MNNVL` forwarding. No NIC byte counters were collected.

A 4 GiB same-rack diagnostic reached about 679 GB/s after lazy setup. It is excluded from the results because it is too short for a careful NVLink measurement. It does show why every cross-rack run must verify `ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain`: independent Iris gangs often pack into the same domain.

</details>

<details>
<summary>H100 connectivity evidence</summary>

One interactive GPU node was sampled in each cluster:

| Cluster | GPU | Node | Host IP |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cw-us-east-08a` | GB200 | `s62pys64` | `10.186.213.79` |
| `cw-us-east-02a` | H100 | `g856b8a` | `10.184.201.5` |
| `cw-rno2a` | H100 | `gb95f50` | `10.168.194.123` |

Each endpoint listened on TCP port 29700 and dialled its peer three times:

| Pair | Direction | Attempts | Result |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Ohio ↔ New Jersey | GB200 → H100 | 3 | 2 × `EHOSTUNREACH`, 1 × 10 s timeout |
| Ohio ↔ New Jersey | H100 → GB200 | 3 | 3 × `EHOSTUNREACH` |
| Ohio ↔ Nevada | GB200 → H100 | 3 | 2 × `EHOSTUNREACH`, 1 × 10 s timeout |
| Ohio ↔ Nevada | H100 → GB200 | 3 | 3 × `EHOSTUNREACH` |

`EHOSTUNREACH` is the error returned to the calling application. Without packet capture or gateway telemetry, it does not identify the component that produced or relayed the error. No cross-cluster NCCL communicator was created and no H100 bulk transfer was attempted.

An earlier CPU `hostNetwork` sweep also failed in all six directions among the three clusters. This corroborates the endpoint result but does not identify the cause.

[CoreWeave documents custom VPCs for multi-cluster communication or peering](https://docs.coreweave.com/get-started). Its [Direct Connect documentation](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/networking/direct-connect/about-direct-connect) covers private links to on-premises or hyperscaler networks. Neither page says which mechanism applies to these existing VPCs or whether it supports RDMA.

The [GPU endpoint runbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c0c1f7669a3c1661154840ff94b49ec14dcc633d/bench/diagnostics/GPU_ENDPOINT_RUNBOOK.md) has the exact allocation, placement, probe, and release commands.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Revisions, environment, and limitations</summary>

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Harness | [`13fb15592eb5e4a79e9255b4e5666358d2f41b98`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/13fb15592eb5e4a79e9255b4e5666358d2f41b98/bench) |
| Endpoint runbook | [`c0c1f7669a3c1661154840ff94b49ec14dcc633d`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c0c1f7669a3c1661154840ff94b49ec14dcc633d/bench/diagnostics/GPU_ENDPOINT_RUNBOOK.md) |
| Torch / CUDA / NCCL | `2.11.0+cu128` / 12.8 / 2.28.9 |
| GPU nodes | `gb200-4x`, four GB200 GPUs per node |
| Job priority | `interactive` |
| Task image | `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task:latest`, not digest-pinned |

SHA-256:

```text
ec03e0e20406de5f0c5f611e536e074f3d5bb7fbfd69e66b0ad5ffe68dc749d6  bench/policy_transfer_bench.py
4bc6e8a2807aee42be7c1c27eb82f5faf0d2c56c4ede3ec3ba5980ab0d2eafd4  bench/run_matrix.sh
6c3eda3806a1c723fa979367c42e6251d88578e4c0c6875bf66d6c8eb79ac6bc  bench/diagnostics/gpu_netcheck.py
```

Limitations:

- The harness moves bytes, not a checkpoint. It does not pause vLLM or load model weights.
- `1→8` and `8→8` each used one placement. Their placement sensitivity is unknown.
- `1→8` used one destination NVLink domain. A multi-rack rollout fleet is untested.
- Only `1→1` was repeated on a fresh placement.
- Runs occurred on one night on a shared fleet. Diurnal and contention effects are unmeasured.

issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue started as a proposal to add five supervised target-only synthetic perplexity probes for surface-form grammars where Qwen3 32B appeared to beat Marin 32B: delimiter/table formats, identifier and encoding strings, machine records and configs, patch/diff surfaces, and science/markup/tree-closure formats. The initial blocker was that the repo did not yet have the supervised target-only scoring path or all-available diagnostic entrypoint, but those pieces were later implemented. The five probe families were uploaded to Hugging Face with pinned revisions, added to the v18 all-available perplexity-gap run, and scored in the refreshed dashboard. The final readout found mixed gaps: Qwen was ahead on science/markup and machine-record subsets such as SDF closure, Dockerfiles, GitHub Actions logs, and nginx logs, while Marin was ahead on several identifier/escaping and whitespace-control subsets. The families were then archived as diagnostic probes in five closed follow-up experiment issues and long-lived research branches, not promoted as regular eval-suite entries.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4422651718
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4423585707
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4427592233
- #5659, #5660, #5661, #5662, #5663
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Motivation
The v17b Marin 32B vs Qwen3 32B perplexity-gap dashboard suggests that several remaining non-multilingual gaps are surface-form grammar gaps rather than broad prose/reasoning gaps. Qwen's durable edges cluster around rigid technical serialization formats: IDs, logs, configs, SVG/XML, bio/chem records, diffs, and dense structured rows.

This issue tracks a batch of supervised target-only synthetic PPL probe families intended to test those hypotheses independently. These are base-model continuation formats, not chat-framed prompts.

## Probe families

- Delimiters / whitespace / table formats: TSV, CSV, pipes, fixed-width columns, Markdown tables, aligned spaces, Makefile tabs, Python indentation.
- Identifier / encoding grammars: package/version strings, commit hashes, UUID/build IDs, accessions, mixed-case symbolic IDs, base64/data URI, hex dumps, URL escaping, JSON escapes.
- Machine records / configs: Zeek/nginx/k8s/system logs, tracebacks/compiler errors, GitHub Actions logs, JSON application logs, package.json, pyproject, Actions YAML, Dockerfile, Terraform, Kubernetes YAML.
- Patch/diff / agent-readiness surfaces: unified diffs, file path + line references, review comment threads, failing-test-to-patch traces, commit metadata, GitHub PR event patches.
- Science / markup / tree closure: SMILES/SDF/PDB/mmCIF/FASTA/GenBank-ish records, BibTeX/LaTeX, XML/HTML/SVG/MathML closure, entity escaping.

## Dataset shape

Each family should publish an HF dataset with one config per subset. Rows should include:

- `input`
- `target`
- `id`
- `subset`
- `task`
- `seed`
- `metadata`

Scoring should use supervised target-only loss via `supervised_text_dataset(..., input_key="input", target_key="target")`.

## Integration

- Add provider modules under `experiments/evals/`.
- Add the providers to `exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py` after each HF dataset is uploaded and pinned.
- Use the per-dataset score cache so future dashboard runs only score the new/changed subsets.
- Add heatmap groups for these families if the aggregate rows expose interesting gaps.

Parent epic: #5005.

comments.body:

- [x] Read AGENTS.md, fix-issue and pull-request skills

# Research

This issue spans five probe families (delimiters/tables, identifiers/encodings, machine records/configs, patch/diff, science/markup) — each with ~5-10 subsets that need an HF dataset constructed and pinned. Scope is well beyond a single self-contained PR. Two prerequisites referenced in the issue body do not exist yet in the repo, so a parallel implementation PR would also be premature:

- No `supervised_text_dataset(..., input_key=\"input\", target_key=\"target\")` exists. Current scoring path is text-only: [`perplexity_gap.py#L48-L55`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L48-L55) defines \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` with a single \`text_key\`, and [`raw_text_dataset`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L84-L101) only emits raw-text datasets. There is no supervised target-only loss path in \`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/\` or in levanter (grep for \`input_key\`/\`target_key\` returns nothing relevant).
- No \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` integration file. The closest existing entrypoints are [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_marin_vs_llama.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_marin_vs_llama.py), [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_long_tail_runnable.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_long_tail_runnable.py), [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_fineweb2_multilingual.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_fineweb2_multilingual.py), and [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py). The bundle/model/pair plumbing in [`perplexity_gap_registry.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py) is keyed on \`PerplexityGapBundle\` with a \`datasets_factory: () -> dict[str, RawTextEvaluationDataset]\`, i.e. raw-text only.

Sibling issues are still open and overlap the design surface: #5056 (raw web/markup/image-text PPL — same registration pattern), #4963 (chat / agent / numeracy supervised-ish PPL — already proposes target-only conditional likelihood). #4963 in particular should drive the supervised target-only API; this issue should layer on top once that lands.

**Relevant code**
- [`perplexity_gap.py#L48-L101`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L48-L101) - raw-text-only dataset abstraction
- [`perplexity_gap_registry.py#L40-L102`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L40-L102) - bundle/factory contract is \`dict[str, RawTextEvaluationDataset]\`
- [`gh_archive_structured_output.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/gh_archive_structured_output.py) - canonical pattern for per-family provider modules
- [`long_tail_ppl.py#L29-L65`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/long_tail_ppl.py#L29-L65) - existing slice registry pattern (StrEnum family + dataclass slice + registry_key)
- Parent epic: #5005; sibling: #5056, #4963

# Proposed Approach (no PR, human review needed)

The work is too large and too unfounded for a single agent PR (>>100 LOC across new evaluation infra, ~30+ provider entries, new datasets, an absent integration file). Recommend splitting before implementation:

1. **First, land supervised target-only scoring infra in #4963 or a dedicated infra issue.** Add a \`SupervisedTextEvaluationDataset(input_key, target_key, hf_dataset_id, hf_dataset_name, split, tags)\` alongside \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` in [`perplexity_gap.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py), plumb a \`model_supervised_perplexity_scores\` step through levanter that masks loss to \`target\` tokens, and extend \`PerplexityGapBundle\` to accept either dataset variant. Without this, every family in #5618 is blocked.

2. **Split #5618 into five sub-issues, one per family** (delimiters/tables, identifier/encoding grammars, machine records/configs, patch/diff/agent-readiness, science/markup/tree closure). Each sub-issue tracks: HF dataset construction with the \`(input, target, id, subset, task, seed, metadata)\` schema, the provider module under \`experiments/evals/\`, and registration into a new \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` once the infra in (1) lands. Each sub-issue should fit in a PR-sized chunk and can run independently.

3. **Add the integration entrypoint as its own small PR** once at least one family is uploaded: a thin \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` that aggregates the existing bundles + new supervised bundles via \`build_registered_perplexity_gap_coverage_plan\`, mirroring \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py\`.

Out of scope for any single agent PR: constructing and uploading HF datasets (needs human curation, licensing review, and HF org credentials), and choosing which subsets/sources are worth materializing first.

If a maintainer wants me to take a first concrete slice — recommend starting with the supervised target-only API change (item 1), which is bounded and unblocks everything else. Flag here and I will scope a PR against #4963.

The October 27 Datakit Tier 1 canary hit the 7,100-second CI wait limit at 14:34:12 UTC while `datakit/store` was still processing. The store had completed 42 of 106 shards with two live workers; Iris showed 104 of 106 requested worker tasks pending and no worker failures or preemptions. This is a scheduling-capacity failure. It recurs after #10717, although two workers started this time.

Reproduce:
1. Run `.github/workflows/marin-canary-datakit-tier1.yaml` at `108ae7fe0beb5c1d95d69e0fa77e403136cca1bb` against the observed `marin` cluster capacity.
2. Inspect the clustered-store worker job at the CI deadline. Only two workers are running; 104 remain pending.

Expected: the store gets enough capacity to finish within the CI wait, or the canary reports the placement shortage before timing out.

## Canary run context

- Lane: `datakit-smoke`; date: 2026-10-27 UTC
- Iris job: `/runner/iris-run-job-20261027-123526`
- [Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/40504865518) and [uploaded diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/40504865518/artifacts/12742172734)
- [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/datakit-smoke-40504865518-1): `datakit-smoke-40504865518-1`

<details>
<summary>Evidence</summary>

- The failed Actions step raised `TimeoutError` at 14:34:12 UTC after 7,100 seconds; the uploaded job tree shows the root and clustered-store jobs still running.
- Finelog `marin` / `log`, coordinator key `/runner/iris-run-job-20261027-123526/zephyr-datakit-clustered-store-cec04735-coordinator-22e5122b/0:0`, `epoch_ms` 1793111625000–1793111655000: seq `30473413403` records 42/106 complete, two in flight, 62 queued, and 2/2 workers alive at 14:34:10 UTC. Finelog `zephyr.execution` records 106 input shards for execution `20261027-134119-a581299c`.
- Iris `job describe` at 14:36:54 UTC showed the worker job with 2 running, 104 pending, zero failures, and zero preemptions. A pending worker requested 4 CPU, 32 GiB RAM, and 64 GiB disk; the two running workers were placed on a TPU VM.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
TaskTrove clean release `2026.09.10.9` retained 1,449,686 tasks with deterministic row rejection and explicit grader contracts. The cleanup recovered 20,457 meaningful TOML, XML, and CSV tasks; retained Go and Rust repository tasks through the script fallback; and rejected JavaScript, TypeScript, malformed MCQA, and broken ARC rows instead of adding recovery heuristics. Exact near-duplicate work remains out of scope.

This issue now owns the two dataset-side validation gaps left after marin#9061.

Done when:

- Repository tasks can run the empty workspace and shipped golden solution inside their intended task container before publication. The gate records a row-level rejection when empty scores above zero, golden scores below one, setup fails, or the grader cannot produce a verdict.
- The gate reports results by source, language, environment, and failure class so one broken runtime does not imply a source-wide drop without evidence.
- A configured judge endpoint runs the existing 30-task validity sample and a larger stratified sample covering reference and rubric-only tasks.
- Judge sampling reports task failure separately from endpoint, credential, timeout, and malformed-verdict failures.
- Confirmed task defects are added as narrow source/path exclusions unless a shared source template proves the whole source broken.

The parent contract and runtime work are tracked in marin#9122 and marin-community/MarinSkyRL#540.

issues.author: XenonMolecule
issues.body:
## Description

The current pipelines for transforming web scrape data to training data for LLMs are multi-stage and a somewhat specifically engineered [[1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794)] [[2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.840/)].  We hypothesize that LLMs may do a better job at converting raw web data into useful tokens for pre-training or mid-training, especially on more challenging to parse contents like latex, tables, math, etc. [[3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06786)].

Preliminary testing has been positive for getting better quality extraction from LLMs rather than heuristic rules ([writeup here](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4)) however this is way too expensive to run at the full web scale.  Our 8b LLM curator is predicted to take 42 years even on the generous compute we do have.

That is why we are currently experimenting with more efficient distilled pipelines from our 8b model.  The lifecycle would thus be: **Write spec for curation** -> **Run with LLM on subset of internet** -> **Distill into faster pipeline** -> **Run at webscale**.  We also noticed that a lot of decent data OUTSIDE of math/code/science is getting discarded by current pipelines.  Our new spec ([See below](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/2351#issuecomment-5074349445)) keeps way more data, and we are making the bet that data mixing/data selection will be a better fit than data filtering for deciding how to weight data for training.  This way we preserve web content that may be decent quality but not beneficial to math/code/science benchmark scores.


### Definition of Done

Two main deliverables with more additional artifacts.

1. **A scientific paper on our spec driven curation methodology and philosophy**: Preliminary drafts are [already completed](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4), but a more polished version for ICLR is in progress.
2. **A 30T+ token dataset of more diverse common crawl data (extracted better)**: Using our distilled pipeline and new design philosophy (optimize data for coverage NOT "quality") we plan to re-run extraction on common crawl and build a production ready data pool for marin with removal of copywritten content.  With any additional time we will also incorporate [safety pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16980) practices into the dataset.

comments.author: XenonMolecule
comments.body: **Updates from last week (1/19-1/23):** Ran the [article extraction benchmark](https://github.com/scrapinghub/article-extraction-benchmark) on several models. The experimental conditions are: - models: Qwen-Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, Qwen-Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507, openai-gpt-oss-120b, openai-gpt-oss-20b, meta-llama-Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-Turbo, meta-llama-Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Turbo - prompting technique: chain of thought or direct - actual prompt: basic ("Extract the main content text from a given HTML document.") or Nemotron (See appendix [A.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.15096)) **Key Takeaways**: - Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B gets messed up by the format for DSPy and refuses to answer a bunch - GPT-OSS nearly matches performance of the existing extractors - COT is important - The numbers don’t show the full story, because models are penalized for things like including a title or like using an em-dash instead of a hyphen - Nemotron prompt converts to markdown without being explicitly told to do so I also informally benchmarked time to process 181 documents. We shouldn't make any critical decisions on these results but it is a useful gut check to see how throughput is looking: Benchmarking a few pipelines it is quite clear that DCLM is pretty heavily filtered versus other pipelines. Will be important to keep this in mind in comparing in a data constrained setting: We might win on more niche domains like math, code, tables, etc. where we parse better than baselines: From our discussion this week I am going to lean into the controllability aspects and see if we can benchmark the controllability of prompting these models for rephrasing and also take a look at their ability to quality filter and measure the diversity of sampling from the same model multiple times. This will help us answer some critical questions about this method such as if stochasticity is a potential answer for skipping deduplication in LLM driven extraction pipelines.

comments.body:
# Progress this week (1/26-1/30) My progress on this task this week spans quite a few categories. For easy reading I am writing each up in collapsible sections. My primary focus was on benchmarking LLMs for web content extraction. To this end I achieved these main goals: 1. Identify Axis of Evaluation (Content Preservation, Spec Adherence, Quality Filtering Calibration, Diversity) 2. Curate benchmarks for these axis 3. Iteratively improve existing LLMs on these axes (primarily through prompting) I am defining these axes as such: - **Content Preservation**: Does the LLM extractor include all main content or omit important details? - **Spec Adherence**: Given a controllable text spec does the LLM adhere to requirements in the spec - **Quality Filtering Calibration**: Two measures - when we say to filter to top X% of documents, what percent actually remain, AND what is the accuracy (are they actually the top X% of docs) - **Diversity**: When we sample from an LLM extractor at a certain temperature with the same doc and spec how different are the actual outputs (might be a useful signal if LLM extractors help with implicit deduplication) I also identify a few challenges and how I have addressed them or how I plan to address them. ---
Article Extraction with Spec The first quick thing to discuss is an update from last week. With the article extraction benchmark (see above) we hypothesized that with a bit more guidance from the benchmark specs that LLMs would do even better on the benchmark. I found these specs for the benchmark from the tech report: ``` For a fair evaluation, we need to define what should be included into the article body (main content), and make sure that all systems follow the same goals. Underlying principle is that the article body should be “clean text”, without other fields (like author), navigation elements, ads, etc. At the same time we want to include all sub-headings, block-quotes and other elements which constitute article content. Here is a list of items not included into an article: • other fields such as authors, publication date, keywords, image captions, etc., and markup around them • share buttons and suggestions to share an article • comments and UI related to comments (e.g. “Comments” header, forms, links to comments) • “related” articles, "read next" links, "recommended to you", etc.: any links which are not part of the article and whose goal is to keep the reader on the platform • newsletter signup links, generic calls to action, various forms • advertisements • author information, usually at the end of the article (such as "X X is an X reporter ..."), as this is not directly related to an article • control elements around images which produce unneeded text (e.g. number of images in a gallery, buttons overlaid over an image/video, etc.) • blocks denoting reading time of the article • other items unrelated to the article content Here is a list of items that should be included into an article (except for the article body proper): • links to read in more detail, to the source, or to other content directly related to this article: these might require deeper understanding of the article content to annotate correctly • embedded posts related to the article, such as tweets/instagram/facebook posts • copyright notices at the end ``` I added them to the prompt for the extractor to make a new experimental condition called "article-extractor" in the table below. As you can see this does make models better than resiliparse although trafilatura holds the top spot on the benchmark:
---
Benchmark Creation I created **two** datasets this week. The first one had the primary motivation of collecting high quality and diverse documents to measure the strength of the extraction. Namely this would measure content preservation, spec adherence, and diversity. Separately I created a benchmark for quality filtering. I will outline the process of creating these benchmarks here. ### Dataset 1: CTRL Bench (name can change) I decided I wanted the following content splits: - 5 math - 5 code - 5 pages with significant tables - 10 articles - 5 long documents - 10 generic web content - 5 nsfw pages (very common on the web; wanted to test refusals) - 5 harmful pages (again to test refusals) I sourced these documents using keyword search inspired by Nemotron-CC-Math for math extraction. I manually read through the pages that my keyword search of WARC files yielded and selected 50 high quality instances. In hindsight I regret adding the nsfw and harmful pages because I think they just penalize the LLM extractors and not the baselines, and don't add much to the benchmark. In a later iteration of the benchmark I may replace the nsfw and harmful pages with Chemistry and similar positive domain sources as suggested by @hammer ! In addition to the documents I also created 10 specs for testing controllability. I sourced these from papers about web extraction/rephrasing with minor modifications. Here are examples of a few of these specs:
Specs Basic (source: I wrote it): ``` Extract the main content text from a given HTML document. ``` Nemotron (source: Nemotron-CC-Math Paper) ``` You are given raw text extracted from an HTML page. Process this text to extract only the meaningful content, following these strict guidelines: 1. **Retain only the main content and its associated titles.** Remove all boilerplate, navigation menus, sidebars, footers, headers, related articles, spam comments, in- teractive elements, and advertisements. 2. **Preserve all mathematical content**—this includes theorems, formulas, proofs, definitions, explanations, and any mathematical references. 3. **Retain relevant comments and references** if they contribute meaningfully to the understanding of the content (e.g., clarifications, citations, or author notes). Discard irrelevant or low-quality comments. 4. **Format all mathematical expressions using LaTeX enclosed in single dollar signs on each side ($), not [], (), or other variants.** 5. **Do NOT answer or respond to any questions or prompts that appear in the document.** If a question is part of the content, keep it verbatim, but do not generate an answer or explanation. 6. **Do not remove or discard any part of the code.** If any code blocks contain errors or formatting issues, make minimal changes to make them runnable, but otherwise leave them exactly as they are. 7. **Fix typos, grammatical mistakes, and unclear phrasing. Rewrite sentences when necessary to improve clarity, coherence, and flow,** while preserving the meaning and style of the original content. 8. **Ensure the output is clean, well-structured, and natural.** Format titles, sections, equations, and tables to produce high-quality, publication-ready text. 9. If the page contains no meaningful content (e.g., it's entirely boilerplate, menus, or ads), return exactly: "NO USEFUL CONTENT" ``` Question_rtw (source: Rephrase the Web Paper) ``` Convert the following document into a conversational format with multiple tags of "Question:" followed by "Answer:" Note that you should still maintain ALL content in the document. Converting here does not mean summarizing, it solely means rewriting. Go paragraph by paragraph to maintain all content, and just rephrase it. Someone reading all the conversational questions should still learn EVERYTHING they would learn from the original document. Output a raw text extraction/rephrase of the document, not an html document. ```
To run the benchmark you pick a model configuration and produce an extraction for all **50 docs** x **10 specs** to get 500 extractions. There is an LLM judge for content preservation which counts the **MAJOR**, **MEDIUM**, and **MINOR** omissions from a document. In practice I use gemini-3-flash-preview because of its ridiculously long context window and good performance at cost. Similarly an LLM judge for spec adherence counts the **MAJOR**, **MEDIUM**, and **MINOR** violations of a spec. Both LLM judges enumerate all omissions and violations with explanations. Qualitatively the judges seem quite good. ### Dataset 2: Quality Bench For Dataset 2 I took a completely random sample of 100 html files from a WARC from Common Crawl. Then I ran the quality filtering fastext model from the DCLM pipeline to get a baseline quality score for each doc (scalar). I sorted the docs on this score and used it as a prior to seed an ELO ranking system where I was presented with two docs and selected which was higher quality. I did 251 votes until I realized this was impractical at this scale (need 2000 to 3000 votes to stabilize), so using the new rankings that my pairwise comparisons yielded as a starting point I made a list of the 100 sites that I could drag and drop to reorder based on quality. I used this to produce a ground truth ordering of the 100 sites. See examples of the tiers of webpages below:
Web pages in the Quality Benchmark #### Number 1 (Best): **Interview with a USAA financial expert on how to boost your credit score (very informative and interview style)** #### Number 2: **Interview with a religious author about his new book** #### Number 5: **Article on 2008 Financial crisis**: #### Number 10: **Summary of New Orleans council meeting**: #### Number 25: **License Agreement**: #### Number 40: **Brief Biographical details about Composer Caleb Simper** #### Number 60: **Article Preview about Easter Travel** #### Number 80: **Photo Gallery with a non-descriptive caption**
After obtaining ground truth ratings for the 100 documents I made the following template to add to the end of the spec prompt for any LLM extractor runs on the benchmark: ``` Additionally I am trying to filter low quality documents out of my corpus. I want to train on only the top {PERCENT}% of quality documents. This is not a percentile, that is the ratio of documents I want to RETAIN out of all documents. If you believe this document does not meet the quality threshold, then rather than extracting the content please respond with the exact phrase "NO USEFUL CONTENT" as the extraction. ``` For now I just ran with the BASIC SPEC ("Extract the main content text from a given HTML document.") but theoretically this is compatible to mix and match with other specs.
---
Content Preservation GPT-OSS-120B is quite good at content preservation without explicitly asking to emit reasoning (predict better than cot): We see that technically Resiliparse > GPT-OSS-120B > GPT-OSS-20B > trafilatura > Llama 3.2 3B **HOWEVER** Note the high refusal rate (empty extractions). These come from NSFW and Harmful docs that the LLMs refuse but not the parsers. Also adding a preprocessing step to remove script tags seems to be useful (See more in the long context section later)
---
Spec Adherence GPT-OSS-120B is again quite good here: Some specs are harder than others (for instance the rephrase the web ones which lead to lower content preservation and lower spec adherence. Rephrasing is probably a mix of harder to do and harder to judge than extraction. GPT-OSS-120B is clear winner (See SA column)
---
Quality Filtering With the Quality Filtering it is important to note that there are two measures: **Calibration** and **Accuracy**. **Calibration**: When we request the top X% of docs do we actually get only X% of docs? Measured with MSE of acceptance rate. **Accuracy**: Of the top X% of docs requested what is the **recall** of those docs actually being in the top X% We compare against a highly calibrated baseline: DCLM's quality filter fastext model where we run once to get all the scalar scores and then cutoff at each threshold. This is perfectly calibrated so the baseline is just for recall comparison. This plot is a bit messy so we will dive into specifics in a second, but the main takeaway is that the LLM extractors are not super calibrated even with fewshot examples, although they do have high recall (but this might be unfair since the low calibration) Overall GPT-OSS-120B wins again and this time explicit cot beats just direct predictions but only by a small margin: This is an area where we are not super strong so might be worth discussion about how to fix this before trying to scale up.
---
Diversity Since I ran the ctrl benchmark extractions for 3 trials it was possible to measure the Levenshtein distance, distinct n-grams, exact matches between extractions, etc. The rephrase prompts clearly have the highest diversity. The lowest diversity comes from specifying EXACTLY what you want to include/exclude in the extraction, but the outputs there are still somewhat diverse. Might be worth more exploration, but the thing that is clear is that no two extractions are the same. The 0.06 rate of no variation comes from docs that exceed the context length. If a doc is processed then one out of the three will always have something different.
--- ## Challenges
Long Context The Rate of Empty Extractions is quite high: This is a combination of documents being too long and exceeding the context window of the LLM, but also of harmful/nsfw documents that the LLMs refuse to extract from. 0.75% of the documents in a WARC will exceed the context window of GPT-OSS-120B We can bring this down to 0.33% of docs by stripping to JUST the tags and removing contents. This is the row "preproc body" in the table above and you can already see that it helps!
---
Quality Filtering For more details please read the Quality Filtering section above, but to recap our calibration for LLM quality filtering is quite bad and so far adding fewshot examples has not made it much better. Without Fewshot: With Fewshot: The fewshot is adding an example of a top 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 75% document. I still feel careful prompt engineering can get us somewhere better here (maybe with DSPy??) but as it stands right now the Quality Filtering is horribly uncalibrated.
--- For next steps I want to: - [x] High Priority: Fix the calibration to a reasonable level for Quality Filtering - [x] High Priority: Test content preservation and spec adherence together with Quality Filtering prompt too so we know the QA isn't messing things up with extraction - [x] High Priority: Kick off GPT-OSS-120B-predict extractions with 20 diverse specs to produce 200M training tokens - [x] Low Priority: Remove NSFW and Harmful from ctrl-bench and add in science extractions

# Progress this week (2/2-2/6) Progress this week was a bit lighter given my travels for a workshop in Munich however my primary focus of the week was derisking the big GPT-OSS-120B run that we decided to hold of on until next week. The main things that I wanted to test were about the composability of specs for steering extraction as well as the accuracy of spec based filters. The main findings of this week are: 1. Kimi and Deepseek are pretty on-par with GPT-OSS-120B but GPT-OSS-120B is cheaper and faster so makes sense to stick with that. 2. Seems order does not matter for what comes first in the prompt for spec vs doc 3. COMPLETE spec adherence (following ALL specs) drops below 50% accuracy after 5 specs in context. 4. We see that general filtering performance is decently strong 5. Filtering accuracy remains decently high even as the number of formatting specs increases ---
More models on ctrl bench Kimi and Deepseek are pretty on-par with GPT-OSS-120B but GPT-OSS-120B is cheaper and faster so makes sense to stick with that.
---
Can we flip the order of the spec and the doc in the prompt to the extractor? Unfortunately the exact results are still running here, but preliminary results are promising (only 100 docs processed out of 550) **Seems order does not matter for spec vs doc**
---
Composable Spec Benchmark In order to test the composability of specs I decided to filter to 10 of the best docs from the ctrl_bench of last week. Then I worked to define both rule-verifiable and llm-verifiable specs that span both FORMAT and FILTERING. In total I had 25 specs; 15 FORMAT and 10 FILTERING **Format Specs**: **Filter Specs**: Then it is possible to run subsets of 15 choose N sets of specs for formatting. For filtering I always run one at a time because it seems unrealistic to want to say filter to only Math AND filter to only code AND filter to only science, etc. and more naturally it seems you'd write one spec that says filter to Math or code or science, with some more detail so to an extent if felt better to avoid automatically composing those. There are also 10 docs I pulled from the quality benchmark. For formatting experiments we test on the 10 ctrl_bench docs and for filtering (and filtering + formatting) we test on 20 documents (10 from ctrl_bench and 10 from quality_bench) It's worth noting I also updated ctrl bench with 10 science (chemistry, biology, nutrition) webpages however I have not rerun all the numbers with those. **Examples of the new science data:**
---
Format Spec Adherence The first thing to look at is adherence for each spec when that spec is the ONLY spec being tested. Next we look at how this changes when we combine with more specs We see interesting degradation patterns per spec This is a generally stable trend across specs There are also interference patterns between particular specs But perhaps the most important thing to focus on is how this impacts the aggregate performance. In other words **how well does the spec adherence scale with more specs?** On average things are pretty fine, however **COMPLETE spec adherence (following ALL specs) drops below 50% accuracy after 5 specs in context.**
---
Filter Spec Adherence **First we see general filter performance is decently strong**: This is exciting and a nice contrast to some of the lackluster quality filtering results of last week.
---
Intersecting the two (Format Spec and Filter Spec) When we bring the format specs and filter specs together the important question is do we see the same levels of degradation in filter quality that we saw in format quality? The answer is seemingly this is NOT as big of a problem Overall, **filtering accuracy remains decently high even as the number of formatting specs increases**. There is a drop-off from 90% to 80% accuracy, but this feels much more reasonable than the 50% or even 100% drop-off from earlier.
---
Planning the 200M token data collection - I believe this will cost $3,869.25 or let's just round to $4k. - I want to generate 1000 complete specs seeded from about 40 realistic composable specs. We can mix them together in a rules based way and use an LLM to rephrase (maybe just GPT-OSS-120B). **Note this is a change** my prior plan was handwriting 20 specs and scaling that up, but Will pointed out that this might lead to lack of generalization. - Half of the tokens (100M) can be generated spec first and half of the tokens can be generated doc first (100M) - I will duplicate documents about 4x in the training data, but each time with a different spec. I am not fully sure if this makes sense because maybe no duplicates is just the better way to do this, and in this case we only get ~50M diverse tokens... There are two core dimensions we can tweak for distilling these models: 1. How many specs do we need for us to learn general extraction from specs and not just exactly how to extract from one spec 2. How much data diversity do you need to achieve this versus just training on the same docs over and over again Let's discuss this data collection design just a bit more to be sure this is ready to kick off this week.

Fine to keep iterating on GPT-OSS for now - The main experiment will be to run on DCLM and compare - An immediate next step is to run the closed models on our benchmark **Some ideas** - Possibly adding url to input of the rewriter (what domains look reasonable could be a signal for filtering) - Case studies would be feasible for the paper (we rewrite to remove content discussing AI behaving poorly or unsafe content, essentially replication studies of [this](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10160) and [this](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16980) However beyond case studies there is an even stronger result: - Take the same webpages as DCLM - Can extract as many tokens as you want (“Extract as much juice out of the data as possible”) - See if we exceed performance We can just start there and don’t worry about the compute as much. ---
Trained more model scales Model training seems to be helping! Exception is 8B case.... but look what happens when we filter out truncation issue. (ignore the confusing naming) This shows the long context issue we are facing.
Training Data Progress Summary https://huggingface.co/datasets/MichaelR207/rephraser_mid_check_0219 ## Token-cost snapshot + projection (grounded in current token stats) ### Pricing (per 1M tokens) - GPT-OSS-120B: $0.15 in, $0.60 out - Kimi-K2.5: $0.50 in, $2.80 out --- ## Current spend (GPT-OSS-120B only; Kimi = $0 so far) Using current combined totals: - input_tokens = 11,606,474,126 - output_tokens = 370,224,455 GPT-OSS-120B: - input cost = 11,606.474126 * $0.15 = $1,740.97 - output cost = 370.224455 * $0.60 = $222.13 - **total spent = $1,963.11** Kimi-K2.5: - **total spent = $0.00** (no runs yet) --- ## Projection to 200,000,000 output_document tokens (budgeting) Definition: output_document = output_tokens - reasoning_tokens Current combined: - reasoning_tokens = 221,751,379 - output_document tokens = 370,224,455 - 221,751,379 = 148,473,076 Assumption: keep combined ratio fixed - input/output_document = 11,606,474,126 / 148,473,076 = 78.172248 Target: 200,000,000 output_document - projected input_tokens = 78.172248 * 200,000,000 = 15,634,449,610 ### Total cost to produce 200M output_document (from zero) | Model | Input $ | Output_document $ | Total $ | |-------------|-----------:|------------------:|----------:| | GPT-OSS-120B | $2,345.17 | $120.00 | $2,465.17 | | Kimi-K2.5 | $7,817.22 | $560.00 | $8,377.22 | ### Additional cost to reach 200M output_document (GPT-OSS-120B only, from current 148,473,076) - remaining output_document = 200,000,000 - 148,473,076 = 51,526,924 - projected additional input_tokens = 78.172248 * 51,526,924 = 4,027,975,484 GPT-OSS-120B additional: - input = 4,027.975484 * $0.15 = $604.20 - output = 51.526924 * $0.60 = $30.92 - **additional total = $635.11**
Nan Loss Training Issue I was frequently facing this issue where the training loss would go to nan (and eval loss) Ultimately I realized that this **might** be because our training is so long context that sometimes there are no "output" tokens to compute the loss on (everything is input) I fixed this
Long Context Issue We need to be able to train long context models for this. See above how much truncation is an issue. Also an issue at training time since the data is so long. We should discuss how to handle this!
---

### Results (Qwen3-8B, ~84 HTML pages) | Ver | Lines | Words | Filter Rate | Key Change | |-----|-------|-------|-------------|------------| | v1 | 3 | 22 | 5.5% | Baseline — just "extract the main content" | | v2 | 9 | 62 | 4.1% | Added markdown formatting, code/math preservation | | v3 | 45 | 333 | 20.0% | Full role prompt with hard gates — too verbose for 8B | | v4 | 22 | 178 | 38.9% | Simplified to flat checklist, added specific reject categories | | v5 | 23 | 189 | 36.9% | Added social media rule, `$` math delimiters | | v6 | 25 | 200 | **47.6%** | Tighter product rule, tag/archive rule, ~100 word threshold | ### Common mistakes & successes per version | Ver | False Accepts (should have been filtered) | Correct Behaviors | |-----|------------------------------------------|-------------------| | v1 | Login walls, profiles, galleries, product pages, non-English | Basic extraction works | | v2 | Same as v1 — formatting rules don't help filtering | Better markdown output, code fencing | | v3 | Product pages, galleries, "who posted" forum pages | First real filtering (language, utility pages) | | v4 | German page accepted, product pages slip through, used ` ```latex ` for math | Catches profiles, galleries, empty search, paywalls, short content (<50 words) | | v5 | 4 stochastic regressions (peoplemag, giftcards, simonseeks, sportsfanfare) | Social media stubs filtered, correct `$` math delimiters | | v6 | 1 stochastic regression, ~3 borderline thin pages remain | Product pages w/ prices caught, tag/archive pages caught | ### 1.7B comparison (v6 prompt) | Model | Filter Rate | Notes | |-------|-------------|-------| | 8B | 47.6% | Best overall | | 1.7B | 31.0% | Misses non-English (Portuguese, Chinese), product pages, profiles. Example outputs (v6, 8B) **Good extraction — math content (math03)** ``` # Time Complexity of $T(n)=T(n-2)+\frac{1}{\log(n)}$ **Question:** > Solve $ T(n)=T(n-2)+\frac{1}{\log(n)} $ for $ T(n) $. I am getting the answer as $ O(n) $ by treating $ 1/\log(n) $ as $ O(1) $. The recursive call tree of this is a lop‑sided tree of height $ n $. Hence, considering the amount of work done in each step, the answer comes out to be $ O(n) $. Please verify my answer, and tell me if I am correct. ## Answer 1 If $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $, then $$ T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{}T(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)}&\text{if }n\text{ is even}\\T(1)+\sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)}&\text{if }n\text{ is odd}\end{array}\right.\tag{1} $$ Note that $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k+1)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\int_1^{(n-1)/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x+1)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(3)}+\frac12\int_3^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{2} \end{align} $$ and $$ \begin{align} \sum_{k=1}^{n/2}\frac{1}{\log(2k)} &\le\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\int_1^{n/2}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(2x)}\\ &=\color{#C00000}{\frac{1}{\log(2)}+\frac12\int_2^8\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}}+\frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)}\tag{3} \end{align} $$ For $ n\ge8 $, we have that $ \log(x) \le 2(\log(x)-1) $, thus $$ \begin{align} \frac12\int_8^n\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)} &\le\int_8^n\frac{(\log(x)-1)\mathrm{d}x}{\log(x)^2}\\ &=\frac{n}{\log(n)}\color{#C00000}{-\frac{8}{\log(8)}}\tag{4} \end{align} $$ Combining (1) through (4), we get that $$ T(n)\le\color{#C00000}{C}+\frac{n}{\log(n)}=O\left(\frac{n}{\log(n)}\right)\tag{5} $$ ## Answer 2 $$T(n)=T(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=T(n-4)+1/\mbox{log }(n-2)+1/\mbox{log }n=\cdots $$ So $$T(n)=a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{\mbox{log}(n-2i)}\leq a+\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{b}=a+bn/2=O(n) $$ Where $ a=T(0),T(1) $ and $ b=\mbox{log }2,\mbox{log }3 $ depending on even or odd $ n $. This shows that $ O(n) $ is an upper bound. ## Answer 3 $ T(n) = T(n-2) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} $ $ \implies T(n-2) = T(n-4) + \frac{1}{\log(n)} + \frac{1}{\log(n-2)} $ So, $ T(n) = T(n-2r) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < 2r} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-2 $, $ T(n) = T(2) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-2} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ If $ n $ is even, $ 2r \leq n-1 $, $ T(n) = T(1) + \sum_{0 ≤ 2s < n-1} \frac{1}{\log(n-2s)} $ In either case, $ O(n) = \frac{n}{\log(n)} $. ``` **Good extraction — forum Q&A (sprinklertalk)** ``` # Richdel 500 PRI controller error **Question (jrebcarlson, Monday, June 11th 2012, 5:40 pm):** When a particular station is ready to turn on (7), the controller displays and blinks a FU 5 error. Do you know what that means? I am without an owners manual. Help? **Answer (Wet_Boots, Monday, June 11th 2012, 7:53 pm):** short circuit – probably a bad solenoid **Answer (GatorGuy, Tuesday, June 12th 2012, 8:36 am):** boots is right. Except it's FUS, not FU5. From the manual: Display is stuck on a zone and "FUS" is flashing in the display. 1. Faulty valve solenoid. 2. Shorted wire connection. ``` **Correct rejection — product page (sportsfanfare)** ``` [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] ``` (Page was a Kansas State jersey listing with price, item #, and warehouse availability) **Correct rejection — blog tag page (downthedrive)** ``` [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] ``` (Page had only two post titles with 1-line teasers and dates, no actual article content)
---
Inference on TPU/marin Did a deep audit of marin's current inference stack (`lib/marin/src/marin/generation/`) and researched modern vLLM + Ray Data patterns. The current system has several architectural problems that compound on our highly preemptible TPU cluster. Summary of findings and improvements: | Problem | What's Happening | v2 Improvement | |---|---|---| | **TPU sits idle during preprocessing** | Template formatting, tokenization, and truncation all run *inside* the vLLM actor on the TPU node. TPU waits for CPU work to finish before each `generate()` call. | Separate CPU preprocessing stage from TPU inference stage (a la `ray.data.llm.build_processor`). Each scales independently via backpressure. | | **Scaling stuck at 1 replica** | Ray requests a custom resource name (`TPU-v5p-8-head`) — if the cluster doesn't register that exact string, scheduling silently fails. Zero logging of how many replicas are actually running vs. pending. No way to tell "Ray chose 1" from "Ray can't find the resource." | Validate resource names at startup (fail fast). Log replica counts periodically. Explicit `min_replicas`/`max_replicas` config. | | **Head node is the bottleneck** | The entire `run_inference` function runs on the head node — including GCS glob resolution, checkpoint scanning (batches of 20 files, 120s timeout), and write orchestration. With 10k+ output files the checkpoint scan alone takes 20+ minutes and saturates head node I/O, which also kills other people's jobs. | Head node only partitions work and writes a lightweight shard manifest. All heavy I/O (reads, writes, checkpoint tracking) moves to CPU workers. | | **10+ min recompilation on every preemption** | JAX compilation cache lives in `/tmp` — wiped on every preemption. Each restart triggers full XLA recompilation. | Cache XLA compilations to GCS (`gs://marin-{region}/compilation-cache/{model_hash}/`). After first compile, restarts take seconds. | | **Checkpoint resume is O(millions)** | On restart, every output file is scanned to extract processed row IDs into a Python set, then the entire input dataset is filtered row-by-row against that set. Stragglers that time out at 120s are silently dropped, causing those rows to be reprocessed. | Shard-based checkpointing: partition input into small shards (~5-10 min each), track completed shards in a manifest. Resume = skip completed shards. Bounded data loss on preemption. | | **Confusing config API** | Single `filetype` field means both input and output format; `output_filetype_override` bolted on separately. Resolution logic copy-pasted in 3+ places. Checkpoint glob can use the wrong filetype and silently miss old outputs. | Clean config with separate `input_format` and `output_format` fields. Each used exactly once. No override, no ambiguity. | A big part was moving to **Zephyr**. On a single v5p8 node I got from 400 tokens per second to close to 1k!!!
---
Midtraining Experiments My initial Midtraining experiments were kinda a bust. ~10M tokens on Llama 3.2 1B: Learning rate warmup was bad, way too few steps for signal. Even using 100M tokens from gpt-oss was not enough steps, although it was better. These were not leading to meaningful eval changes. I spoke with @Helw150 and we came up with a better experiment. Go to checkpoint 35000 of [this nemotron run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/exp2166-scaling-ladder-nemotron-validation-optimal-1e+20-9563f0?nw=nwuserheld) of a 1.3B model and replace the cooldown: However the cooldown is still 2.3B tokens. It is important to train on that many steps but how do we get that many tokens when inference isn't too fast on somewhat limited compute (most of the week I could only get 1-2 tpus nodes) We decided to mix in with the existing cooldown and target about 10% of the data being from my rephraser. I kicked off a run last night with 25 WARC files. I managed to get close to ~10 tpus consistently overnight so this actually ran relatively fast! I used the v6 prompt I engineered above. This is the outcome of the token generation vs a DCLM baseline I purposefully selected to be around 10% of the size needed. | Metric | Rephraser | DCLM | |---|---:|---:| | shard_ledger rows | 83,834 | 244,203 | | `.stats.json` total_tokens | 45,904,757 | 307,051,596 | | Avg tokens/row | ~548 | ~1,257 | Looks like I need about 6x as many WARC files: | Metric | Rephraser Cooldown | DCLM Cooldown | |---|---:|---:| | Added source tokens | 45.9M | 307.1M | | NemotronCooldown tokens | 2,558.7M | 2,558.7M | | Added source % | 1.76% | 10.72% | | NemotronCooldown % | 98.24% | 89.28% | This took 5 hours to process inference so it might be closer to 30 hours unless we can scale up tpus. 10 at a time already feels pretty high though... This is worth a discussion! The two runs are going now, but I feel there is too little data on the rephrased run: - rephraser: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/cooldown-rephraser-d7d976d3-v2-1cdc5a?nw=nwusermichaeljryan - dclm: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/cooldown-dclm-100m-v2-32bcbc?nw=nwusermichaeljryan
---
Plans for Future Experiments (Contingent on Midtraining working) Some ideas: - The full pretrain experiment comparison to DCLM - Reproduce RephraseTheWeb results but now we can just do our pipeline - Reproduce Nemotron-CC-Math but with just our pipeline - Reproduce Alignment Pretraining but with just our pipeline Another next step is to convert the data to be Kimi K2 instead of GPT-OSS which I can hopefully do on the cluster now.
---

## Results of the Investigation for why the 1.7b model was "getting worse" It appears that this was in fact an issue with comparing models that were in different stages of the training process (different parts of the learning rate schedule). I have results from several checkpoints of two runs below. The runs have very different amounts of data (10M tokens vs 72.5M tokens). More details on the runs below.

# Cooldown data "midtrain" experiment ## Baseline run we’re pulling from (Nemotron 1.3B) - We are evaluating cooldown variants starting from the same Nemotron 1.3B training run / checkpoint lineage. - W&B link: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/exp2166-scaling-ladder-nemotron-validation-optimal-1e+20-9563f0?nw=nwuserheld ## What this experiment is We start from a **pre-cooldown checkpoint** (step 35000) and run cooldown training with different data mixtures. The main question: - does replacing part of the standard **Nemotron cooldown data** with **DCLM** or **Rephraser** data improve downstream benchmark performance? - More fundamentally to us: Does our **Rephraser** beat **DCLM**? ## Headline result **Nemotron-only is the best aggregate condition** in these runs. In aggregate our rephraser might beat DCLM but individually DCLM outperforms our rephraser.
Experimental design Headline full-cooldown conditions: - **Pre-cooldown**: checkpoint before any cooldown - **Post-cooldown (Nemotron-only)**: standard cooldown with no auxiliary mixin (this is just the final checkpoint) - **DCLM-300M**: large DCLM mixin chosen to approximately match the large rephraser run by token count - **DCLM-filtered-6M**: DCLM text extracted from the **same 150-WARC pool as Rephraser-362M**; those WARCs were selected to be **after the DCLM cutoff**; only ~6M tokens survive filtering - **Rephraser-362M**: rephraser-generated text from that same **150-WARC post-cutoff pool** Important implementation note: - Rephraser data is produced using the **8B rephraser model** trained to checkpoint 1318 on 16M reasoning tokens and 10M output tokens. See prior week reports for more details Primary metric: - **choice_prob_norm**: Normalized probability of selecting the correct answer choice on a multiple-choice benchmark, computed from the model’s log probabilities over answer choices. Rephraser Prompt:
Prompt used to generate the rephraser data (8B rephraser model) ``` Extract the main content from the provided HTML into clean Markdown. First, check if the page should be rejected. Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply: - Not primarily in English - Login, signup, account, checkout, paywall, or subscribe page - Error page, captcha, cookie wall, bot check, or "session expired" - Empty or near-empty page, directory index, or navigation-only page - User profile, member page, or "who posted" page - Image gallery or photo album listing without articles - Search results page with no actual results - Page where the main content is behind a login wall or paywall - Product listing, gift card, or e-commerce page with prices/availability - Social media post that is just an image or a single short caption - Blog tag page, category page, or archive page that only lists post titles and teasers - After removing boilerplate, the remaining useful text would be under ~100 words If the page passes, extract with these rules: - Output Markdown only. No commentary or analysis. - Preserve original wording. Do not summarize or rewrite. - Remove boilerplate: navbars, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs. - Preserve all technical content exactly: code blocks verbatim with language tags, math/LaTeX using $$ delimiters, chemical formulas, tables. - Do not truncate or simplify content due to length. - Include comments/replies only if they add real information (answers, corrections). - Start with the page title as a top-level heading if available. ```

Tasks that do NOT use choice_prob_norm in this report (acc / acc_norm instead) | Task | Metric | Pre-cooldown | Nemotron-only | DCLM-300M | DCLM-filtered-6M | Rephraser-362M | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | agieval_lsat_ar | acc_norm | 0.2391 | **0.2478** | 0.2348 | 0.2348 | 0.2435 | | lambada_openai | acc | 0.3695 | 0.4687 | **0.4826** | 0.4788 | 0.4661 |
--- ## Core questions ### 1) Is our rephraser better than DCLM? In aggregate perhaps yes? average choice prob norm `+0.00468` versus `+0.00395`? Individually? Not really.... DCLM-300M is better than our Rephraser on 7/11 tasks we evaluated. We are just much better on the four we are better at. `boolq`, `commonsense_qa`, `copa`, and `wsc273`. Especially boolq. ### 2) Is our rephraser better than just keeping the Nemotron data? No. Not in aggregate, and not individually. Just continuing to do the cooldown on the nemotron data wins. ### 3) Is validation loss predictive of benchmark performance? Somewhat, but only coarsely. Across trained checkpoints, lower validation loss / BPB correlates moderately with better aggregate benchmark performance. It is not reliable enough to replace downstream eval when choosing between nearby variants. ---

Note on regressions vs pre-cooldown (short cooldown): - **Short Nemotron-only** falls on: - `commonsense_qa` (**0.2046 → 0.2012**, Δ = **-0.0034**) - **Short DCLM** falls on: - `boolq` (**0.5079 → 0.4988**, Δ = **-0.0091**) - `commonsense_qa` (**0.2046 → 0.2008**, Δ = **-0.0038**) - **Short Rephraser 150W** falls on: - `boolq` (**0.5079 → 0.4936**, Δ = **-0.0143**) - `commonsense_qa` (**0.2046 → 0.2007**, Δ = **-0.0039**)
Takeaway: - short cooldown results aren't the same as the full cooldown, so unclear if the signal is useful

Solve the first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ ## Reasoning The first equation is separable: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Which gives: $$ \arctan y + C_1 = \arctan x + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \arctan y = \arctan x + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $$ The second equation is also separable. Rewrite: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ Which yields: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ ## Answer 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $ 2. $ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $ Make sure to include markdown headings. Now produce output with required fields. [[ ## text ## ]] # Differential Equations ## Question 1. Obtain the solution to the differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x²} $$ 2. Solve the first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ ## Reasoning **First equation** The equation is separable: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Which gives: $$ \arctan y + C_1 = \arctan x + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \arctan y = \arctan x + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $$ **Second equation** Rewrite the equation: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ Which yields: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Simplify to: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ ## Answer 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan x + C) $ 2. $ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $ [[ ## completed ## ]] ```
Parsed Q/R/A for training This was another step. I am debating removing it but it is in there for now. It reformats from this into the Q: A: format for GSM8k. ``` Q: Differential Equations 1. Obtain the solution to the differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 + y^2}{1 + x²} $$ 2. The first order differential equation $$ \frac{dy}{dx} - xy = x $$ has the solution $ y = ? $ These are both separable. A: **First equation:** We separate variables: $$ \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ Integrating both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{1 + y^2}\,dy = \int \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\,dx $$ The integrals yield: $$ \arctan{y} + C_1 = \arctan{x} + C_2 $$ Combining constants: $$ \arctan{y} = \arctan{x} + C $$ Thus the solution is: $$ y = \tan(\arctan{x} + C) $$ **Second equation:** Rewrite the equation: $$ \frac{dy}{dx} = x(y + 1) $$ Separate variables: $$ \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = x\,dx $$ Integrate both sides: $$ \int \frac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int x\,dx $$ The integrals give: $$ \ln|y + 1| + C_1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C_2 $$ Combine constants: $$ \ln|y + 1| = \frac{1}{2}x^2 + C $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ |y + 1| = e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2 + C} = e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Thus: $$ y + 1 = \pm e^C e^{\frac{1}{2}x²} $$ Let $ A = \pm e^C $, so: $$ y = A e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} - 1 $$ The answer is 1. $ y = \tan(\arctan{x} + C) $. ```

comments.body:
# Results of the Code Experiment

**Experiment**: Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B on code-heavy web content (47 URL patterns across Stack Exchange, language docs, tutorials, and framework docs; 10 CC crawls) and evaluate on HumanEval pass@1. Compare standard HTML extraction (resiliparse) vs LLM-based extraction (Qwen3-8B reformats HTML into structured code files with `/* */` comments and code fences).

| Model | HumanEval pass@1 | vs. Baseline | Training tokens |
|-------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline** (Qwen3-0.6B, no SFT) | 19.5% | — | — |
| **Resiliparse SFT** | **24.4%** | **+4.9pp** | 792.5M |
| **Extraction SFT** | 12.2% | -7.3pp | 177.5M |

**Resiliparse wins.** Plain text extraction with no LLM involvement improves HumanEval by +4.9pp. LLM extraction *hurts* by -7.3pp.

## Why extraction hurts

Two problems, both visible in the eval traces:

1. **Format contamination** — The extraction prompt trains the model on `/* */` comment blocks and ` ``` ` code fences. At eval time, the model generates correct code but appends these artifacts, causing syntax errors. Several problems (HumanEval/4, /13, /14) have *correct implementations* that fail solely due to trailing ` ``` ` markers.

2. **4.5x less data** — The extraction prompt aggressively filters pages without code blocks (`[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]`), leaving only 177.5M tokens vs 792.5M for resiliparse. For code, volume of exposure matters more than reformatting.

<details>
<summary>Example: format contamination (HumanEval/13 — GCD)</summary>

The extraction-trained model writes a correct GCD algorithm, then appends code fences and `/* */` comments from the training format:

**Prompt:**
```python
def greatest_common_divisor(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """ Return a greatest common divisor of two integers a and b
    >>> greatest_common_divisor(3, 5)
    1
    >>> greatest_common_divisor(25, 15)
    5
    """
```

**Generated:**
```
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

/* The greatest common divisor of two integers a and b is the largest number
that divides both a and b without leaving a remainder. */

/* The greatest common divisor of two integers a and b is the largest number
that divides both a and b without leaving a remainder. */
...
```

The algorithm is correct. The trailing `/* */` blocks cause a syntax error.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Example: comment-only output (HumanEval/10 — make palindrome)</summary>

**Prompt:**
```python
def make_palindrome(string: str) -> str:
    """ Find the shortest palindrome that begins with a supplied string.
    Algorithm idea is simple:
    - Find the longest postfix of supplied string that is a palindrome.
    - Append to the end of the string reverse of a string prefix that comes before the palindromic suffix.
    >>> make_palindrome('')
    ''
    >>> make_palindrome('cat')
    'catac'
    """
```

**Generated:**
```python
    # Find the longest postfix of supplied string that is a palindrome.
    # The algorithm is based on the following observation:
    # A string is a palindrome if it is equal to its reverse.
    # A string is a prefix of a string if it is a prefix of the string.
    # A string is a suffix of a string if it is a suffix of the string.
    ...  # continues with circular definitions, no code
```

The model writes verbose comments but never produces an implementation.

</details>

## Note on eval

The experiment config included both 0-shot and 4-shot HumanEval, but HumanEval hardcodes `num_fewshot: 0` in its lm-eval-harness task YAML, silently ignoring any override. Both runs produced identical results. The 4-shot config has been removed.

## What's next?

I'm gonna try the experiment again with an improved prompt.  I will be more careful to write a prompt that is less aggressive with the filtering and also doesn't have so many comments as a part of the internals of a function, especially not competing comment types (`"""` and `/**/`)
