# Code Extraction SFT Experiment Report

**Last updated**: 2026-03-12

## Goal

Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B on code-heavy web content from Common Crawl, then evaluate on HumanEval. Compare two data processing methods:

1. **Resiliparse**: Standard HTML-to-text extraction (DCLM-style). No LLM involved.
2. **8B Extraction**: LLM-based extraction using a Qwen3-8B rephraser to reformat HTML into structured source code files with comments.

Both branches use plain text SFT (no chat template). The question is whether LLM-restructured code data improves code generation over raw text from the same sources.

## Model

- **Architecture**: Qwen3-0.6B (hidden=896, layers=24, heads=14, kv_heads=2, intermediate=4864)
- **Tokenizer**: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` (151,936 vocab)
- **RoPE**: theta=1,000,000, factor=1.0
- **Max sequence length**: 4,096
- **Training**: 1-epoch SFT, batch=64, seq_len=4096, AdamConfig lr=2e-5, cosine schedule

## Data Sources

45 URL patterns across 4 categories, queried against the 10 most recent Common Crawl indices (2024-2026):

**Stack Exchange / Q&A (20 sites)**:
stackoverflow.com, codereview.stackexchange.com, codegolf.stackexchange.com, cs.stackexchange.com, cstheory.stackexchange.com, math.stackexchange.com, stats.stackexchange.com, physics.stackexchange.com, unix.stackexchange.com, askubuntu.com, softwareengineering.stackexchange.com, dsp.stackexchange.com, ai.stackexchange.com, datascience.stackexchange.com, electronics.stackexchange.com, crypto.stackexchange.com, security.stackexchange.com, tex.stackexchange.com, mathematica.stackexchange.com, mathoverflow.net

**Language documentation (11 sites)**:
docs.python.org, doc.rust-lang.org, pkg.go.dev, en.cppreference.com, kotlinlang.org/docs, docs.scala-lang.org, docs.julialang.org, hexdocs.pm, www.php.net/manual, ruby-doc.org, docs.rs

**Tutorials (5 sites)**:
rosettacode.org, www.geeksforgeeks.org, realpython.com, www.w3schools.com, www.tutorialspoint.com

**Framework / API docs (11 sites)**:
developer.mozilla.org, www.tensorflow.org, api.flutter.dev, doc.qt.io, huggingface.co/docs, llvm.org/docs, gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs, www.boost.org/doc, www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook, readthedocs.io (domain match), devdocs.io

**Common Crawl indices**: CC-MAIN-2026-08, CC-MAIN-2026-04, CC-MAIN-2025-51, CC-MAIN-2025-47, CC-MAIN-2025-43, CC-MAIN-2025-38, CC-MAIN-2025-33, CC-MAIN-2025-30, CC-MAIN-2024-51, CC-MAIN-2024-46

### Pipeline Data Flow

| Stage | Shards | Description |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| CDX query (3 match types) | — | domain, host, prefix queries across 10 crawl indices |
| WARC download (per type) | 500 each | 3 download steps combined |
| Combined HTML | 1,500 | Merged across all 3 match types |
| Filtered HTML | 1,343 | Deduplication and quality filtering |
| LLM extraction | 921 | Qwen3-8B extraction (pages with `[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]` or <50 chars filtered) |
| Resiliparse text | 1,500 | Standard HTML-to-text |

### Token Counts

| Branch | Tokens |
|--------|--------|
| Extraction (8B-extracted) | 177.5M |
| Resiliparse (plain text) | 792.5M |

The extraction branch has ~4.5x fewer tokens because the LLM filters out pages without code content (`[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]`) and removes boilerplate/navigation. The resiliparse branch retains all text from all pages.

### Extraction prompt

```
Extract the content from this HTML page and reformat it as a source code file with comments.

Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply:
- Page contains no code blocks or programming examples (inline code references do not count)
- Question listing, search results, or index page without actual content
- Login, signup, paywall, error page, or empty page
- Not primarily in English

If the page has code, reformat it following these rules:

Format — clearly separate code from text:
- Write all explanatory text inside /* */ block comments. Group related paragraphs together.
- Use // for short inline notes only.
- Put all code examples inside code fences.
- Start with a /* */ block summarizing the page topic.
- Use /* */ blocks as section separators between code examples.
- Do not use **bold**, ## headings, [links](url), or other markdown besides code fences.

Content — include everything from the page:
- Include every paragraph and code example. Do not shorten or omit content.
- Preserve all code exactly as written. Do not fix or improve it.
- Do not include any raw HTML tags or entities. Decode & < > " to their characters.
```

## Training

| | Extraction SFT | Resiliparse SFT |
|---|---|---|
| **Tokens** | 177.5M | 792.5M |
| **Training steps** | 677 | 3,023 |
| **Checkpoint** | `code-extract-general-qwen3-0.6b-sft-b2603e` (step-677) | `code-resiliparse-qwen3-0.6b-sft-c97c7a` (step-3023) |
| **Format** | Plain text (TextLmDatasetFormat) | Plain text (TextLmDatasetFormat) |

## Evaluation

**Benchmark**: HumanEval — 164 Python function completion problems. The model receives a function signature + docstring and must generate a correct implementation. Evaluated with `pass@1` (greedy, single attempt).

**Settings**: 0-shot only. HumanEval hardcodes `num_fewshot: 0` in its lm-eval-harness task YAML. When a task sets `num_fewshot: 0`, lm-eval silently ignores any override. The 4-shot eval results are identical duplicates of 0-shot.

## Results

| Model | pass@1 | vs. Baseline |
|-------|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline** (Qwen3-0.6B, no SFT) | 19.5% | — |
| **Resiliparse SFT** (step-3023) | **24.4%** | **+4.9pp** |
| **Extraction SFT** (step-677) | 12.2% | -7.3pp |

## Analysis

### Resiliparse wins (+4.9pp)

Continued pretraining on 792.5M tokens of raw code-heavy web text improved HumanEval by 4.9 percentage points (19.5% -> 24.4%). This is a meaningful gain from a simple pipeline: standard HTML extraction, no LLM involvement, just exposure to more code.

### LLM extraction hurts (-7.3pp)

The 8B extraction branch significantly degraded performance (19.5% -> 12.2%). Several factors likely contribute:

1. **Much less data**: The extraction branch has only 177.5M tokens vs 792.5M for resiliparse (4.5x less). The LLM filters aggressively — pages without code blocks are mapped to `[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]` and discarded. This may filter too much useful context.

2. **Format mismatch**: The extraction prompt reformats code into a `/* comment */ + code fence` structure. HumanEval expects raw Python function completions. Training on commented/fenced code may teach the model a completion style that doesn't match the eval format.

3. **Fewer training steps**: Only 677 steps vs 3,023 for resiliparse. With a single epoch, the smaller dataset means fewer gradient updates.

### Takeaways

- **Raw text wins for code**: Unlike the math domain where structured extraction might help with reasoning chains, code generation benefits more from volume of raw code exposure.
- **Aggressive filtering can backfire**: The extraction prompt's `[NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]` filter removed ~77% of the data. For a domain where the model needs broad code exposure, this is too aggressive.
- **Format matters**: Training data format should match evaluation format. Reformatting code into `/* */` comment blocks doesn't align with HumanEval's raw function completion format.

## Raw Eval Traces

### Resiliparse SFT (24.4% pass@1)

40/164 problems passed. The model handles straightforward algorithmic tasks well but struggles with multi-token string parsing and problems requiring careful case handling.

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/0 (PASSED) — close elements check**

Prompt:
```python
from typing import List

def has_close_elements(numbers: List[float], threshold: float) -> bool:
    """ Check if in given list of numbers, are any two numbers closer to each other than
    given threshold.
    >>> has_close_elements([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], 0.5)
    False
    >>> has_close_elements([1.0, 2.8, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 2.0], 0.3)
    True
    """
```

Generated:
```python
    for i in range(1, len(numbers)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(numbers)):
            if abs(numbers[i] - numbers[j]) < threshold:
                return True
    return False
```

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/25 (PASSED) — prime factorization**

Prompt:
```python
from typing import List

def factorize(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """ Return list of prime factors of given integer in the order from smallest to largest.
    Each of the factors should be listed number of times corresponding to how many times it appeares in factorization.
    Input number should be equal to the product of all factors
    >>> factorize(8)
    [2, 2, 2]
    >>> factorize(25)
    [5, 5]
    >>> factorize(70)
    [2, 5, 7]
    """
```

Generated:
```python
    factors = []
    while n % 2 == 0:
        factors.append(2)
        n = n // 2
    i = 3
    while i * i <= n:
        while n % i == 0:
            factors.append(i)
            n = n // i
        i += 2
    if n > 2:
        factors.append(n)
    return factors
```

Correct trial division algorithm — this is a non-trivial problem that the model handles cleanly.

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/4 (PASSED) — mean absolute deviation**

Generated: `sum(abs(x - mean) for x in numbers) / len(numbers)` — correct one-liner.

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/17 (FAILED) — parse music notation**

Generated iterates character-by-character instead of splitting on spaces — multi-character tokens like `o|` can never match a single `c`.

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/18 (FAILED) — count overlapping substrings**

Generated `string.count(substring)` which doesn't count overlapping occurrences.

**Resiliparse SFT — HumanEval/16 (FAILED) — count distinct characters (case-insensitive)**

Generated `len(set(string))` — misses the "regardless of case" requirement.

### Extraction SFT (12.2% pass@1)

20/164 problems passed. Three distinct failure modes:

1. **Format contamination**: Correct code followed by trailing code fences or `/* */` comment blocks from the extraction training format, causing syntax errors at execution time.
2. **Comment-only output**: Model writes comments describing an approach but generates `pass` or no implementation.
3. **Degenerate generation**: Long repetitive if-chains or comment loops instead of algorithmic solutions.

**Extraction SFT — HumanEval/0 (PASSED) — close elements check**

Generated correct O(n^2) pairwise comparison.

**Extraction SFT — HumanEval/31 (PASSED) — primality check**

## Base versus Instruct Qwen training

I came to an important realization in my SFT experiments (for MATH and CODE) that I was running on `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` which has already undergone post-training as opposed to `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base` which has not.  I reran experiments with this realization.

---

<details>
<summary>Results</summary>

### Math

#### GSM8K CoT 8-shot

| Condition | Base | Instruct |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline (no SFT)** | **60.65%** | 48.07% |
| LLM Extract (post-processed into GSM8k format) | 53.90% (-6.75pp) | **50.72%** (+2.65pp) |
| LLM Extract (original) | 55.12% (-5.53pp) | 47.46% (-0.61pp) |
| Resiliparse SFT | 48.60% (-12.05pp) | 41.39% (-6.68pp) |

#### MATH 4-shot

| Condition | Base | Instruct |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline (no SFT)** | 11.25% | 7.63% |
| LLM Extract (post-processed into GSM8k format) | 8.68% (-2.57pp) | 9.85% (+2.22pp) |
| **LLM Extract (original)** | **12.37%** (+1.12pp) | **10.41%** (+2.78pp) |
| Resiliparse SFT | 11.06% (-0.19pp) | 10.07% (+2.44pp) |

### Code

#### HumanEval pass@1

| Condition | Base | Instruct |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline (no SFT)** | **30.5%** | 19.5% |
| LLM Extraction SFT | 28.7% (-1.8pp) | 23.2% (+3.7pp) |
| Resiliparse SFT | 26.2% (-4.3pp) | **24.4%** (+4.9pp) |


### The Takeaway

A lot of the gains we were seeing was from the instruction model having lower scores on these tasks in part because the prompting-style of these tasks is not suited for instruction tuned models.  I want to keep iterating on top of the base models to get better performance on these tasks.  It seems that the gains we were seeing are in part due to this error, although the gains on MATH seem more real.

**Why?** I think that the Question/Reasoning/Answer format really does matter, but the data source is a better match for the MATH dataset than GSM8k.  The types of content covered on that forum are just more related to the MATH dataset than GSM8k.  For Code I think we aren't seeing serious improvements yet, so I think I need to keep iterating on the prompt.  I also might try updating the MATH prompt to encourage showing more arithmetic steps which will probably boost GSM8k performance but could lead to a "distillation effect" where a bigger rephraser imparts some capabilities to smaller models.

</details>

# Progress this week (3/16-3/20)

**Key Takeaways**:
- **Data filtering is extremely aggressive**. The full pipeline compresses raw HTML by ~400x, and DCLM pushes that to ~25,000x. The rephraser keeps only 10% of extracted text.
- **Code extraction SFT delivers real gains on Qwen3-14B-Base**. +23pp HumanEval from 260M tokens of web-extracted data, MBPP-neutral. Most of the improvement is formatting (clean output vs. markdown junk), but even the pure algorithmic gain is +6pp — significant for unsupervised web data. V3 extraction beats resiliparse at both model scales (14B and 0.6B), and gains scale with model size.
- **Math and medical are in progress**. ~70 math sources (extraction ~60% done), ~50 medical sources (not started). SFT experiments pending for both.
- **Project framing needs sharpening**. Three options: domain-specific data mixing for midtraining, full-scale pretraining comparison against other pipelines, or controllable pretraining with tagged/rewritten content.
- **Yejin's feedback points toward measuring/reducing extraction hallucinations and Quark-style reward token conditioning for steerability**.

---

<summary>Data Filtering Exploration</summary>

### Token Count Analysis: 150 WARC Files → Rephraser Cooldown Sweep

| Stage                  | Tokens           | % of Raw HTML | % of Resiliparse Text | Compression vs Raw |
|------------------------|------------------|---------------|------------------------|--------------------|

| DCLM-filtered          | 5,671,922        | 0.004%        | 0.16%                  | ~25,000x           |

  - 97.5% of raw HTML tokens are boilerplate (tags, scripts, CSS, navigation, ads) — resiliparse strips 144B tokens down to 3.6B
  - The rephraser keeps 10% of the extracted text (362M of 3.6B), selecting only high-quality, informative content

<details>
<summary>Code Experiment Findings</summary>

# Code Extraction SFT: 14B Hyperparameter Sweep Results

## Results

**Data:** 260M tokens from 45 URL patterns (Stack Overflow, Stack Exchange sites, language docs, tutorials, framework docs) across 10 Common Crawl indices, extracted with Qwen3-8B rephraser using V3 commented extraction prompt. Resiliparse comparison uses 793M tokens of plain text from the same HTML.

<details>
<summary>Mostly Basic Python Problems (MBPP) Validation Set</summary>
**MBPP 3-shot pass@1** (primary HP selection metric == validation set):

| Model | Extraction | MBPP 3-shot | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3-14B-Base** | none (baseline) | **74.0%** | — |
| Qwen3-14B-Base | V3 extraction | 73.8% | -0.2pp |
| Qwen3-14B-Base | Resiliparse | 73.2% | -0.8pp |
| **Qwen3-0.6B-Base** | none (baseline) | **39.8%** | — |
| Qwen3-0.6B-Base | V3 extraction | 39.4% | -0.4pp |
| Qwen3-0.6B-Base | Resiliparse | 38.2% | -1.6pp |

</details>

**HumanEval 0-shot pass@1** (test set):

| Model | Extraction | HumanEval 0-shot | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3-14B-Base** | none (baseline) | 54.3% | — |
| Qwen3-14B-Base | V3 extraction | **77.4%** | **+23.1pp** |
| Qwen3-14B-Base | Resiliparse | 59.1% | +4.8pp |
| **Qwen3-0.6B-Base** | none (baseline) | 30.5% | — |
| Qwen3-0.6B-Base | V3 extraction | **33.5%** | **+3.0pp** |
| Qwen3-0.6B-Base | Resiliparse | 31.1% | +0.6pp |


V3 extraction SFT is MBPP-neutral while dramatically improving HumanEval. The effect scales with model size (+23pp for 14B vs +3pp for 0.6B). V3 consistently outperforms resiliparse at both scales. All hyperparameter decisions (LR, BS, WD, warmup) were made using MBPP 3-shot as the primary metric; HumanEval was evaluated but not used for selection.

## What the SFT Actually Teaches

Analysis of all 164 HumanEval problems for 14B:

| Category | Count | % of fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Format/stopping fixes (correct code + trailing markdown junk) | 35 | 78% |
| Genuine algorithm improvements (wrong code → correct code) | 10 | 22% |
| Regressions (baseline passes, SFT fails) | 7 | — |

The base model already solves most problems but appends markdown fences that break the test harness. Stripping the format effect, real coding improvement is +6pp. The remaining +17pp is output formatting.

MBPP isn't affected because 3-shot prompting already teaches the base model correct output format, eliminating the SFT's formatting advantage.

---

<details>
<summary>14B HumanEval Output Samples</summary>

#### Example 1: Format Fix (HumanEval/18)

```python
def how_many_times(string: str, substring: str) -> int:
    """ Find how many times a given substring can be found in the original string. Count overlaping cases.
    >>> how_many_times('', 'a')
    0
    >>> how_many_times('aaa', 'a')
    3
    >>> how_many_times('aaaa', 'aa')
    3
    """
```

Both models generate identical, correct code. The baseline fails only because it appends a trailing markdown fence that the test harness interprets as part of the output.

**Baseline (FAIL):**
```
    count = 0
    for i in range(len(string) - len(substring) + 1):
        if string[i:i+len(substring)] == substring:
            count += 1
    return count
~~~
```
(The `~~~` above represents a trailing triple-backtick fence the baseline appends after the code.)

**V3 SFT (PASS):** Identical code, stops cleanly after `return count`.

---

#### Example 2: Genuine Algorithm Improvement (HumanEval/1)

```python
from typing import List

def separate_paren_groups(paren_string: str) -> List[str]:
    """ Input to this function is a string containing multiple groups of nested parentheses. Your goal is to
    separate those group into separate strings and return the list of those.
    Separate groups are balanced (each open brace is properly closed) and not nested within each other
    Ignore any spaces in the input string.
    >>> separate_paren_groups('( ) (( )) (( )( ))')
    ['()', '(())', '(()())']
    """
```

**Baseline (FAIL):** Uses a stack but doesn't track the actual characters — returns empty strings:
```python
    for char in paren_string:
        if char == '(':
            stack.append(char)
        elif char == ')':
            if len(stack) == 0:
                result.append('')     # always appends empty string
            else:
                stack.pop()
                if len(stack) == 0:
                    result.append('')  # never captures the group content
    return result
```

**V3 SFT (PASS):** Tracks `current_group` to build up each parenthesis group:
```python
    for char in paren_string:
        if char == "(":
            stack.append(char)
            current_group += char
        elif char == ")":
            if stack:
                stack.pop()
                current_group += char
                if not stack:
                    result.append(current_group)
                    current_group = ""
    return result
```

---

#### Example 3: Prose Contamination (HumanEval/17)

```python
from typing import List

def parse_music(music_string: str) -> List[int]:
    """ Input to this function is a string representing musical notes in a special ASCII format.
    Your task is to parse this string and return list of integers corresponding to how many beats does each
    not last.

    Here is a legend:
    'o' - whole note, lasts four beats
    'o|' - half note, lasts two beats
    '.|' - quater note, lasts one beat

    >>> parse_music('o o| .| o| o| .| .| .| .| o o')
    [4, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 4, 4]
    """
```

**Baseline (FAIL):** Outputs a natural language explanation instead of code:
```
To solve this problem, we need to parse a string of musical notes represented
in a special ASCII format and convert it into a list of integers indicating
the duration of each note in beats. Here's a step-by-step approach...
```

**V3 SFT (PASS):** Just writes the function body:
```python
    notes = music_string.split()
    beats = []
    for note in notes:
        if note == 'o':
            beats.append(4)
        elif note == 'o|':
            beats.append(2)
        elif note == '.|':
            beats.append(1)
    return beats
```

</details>

Reproduce the clinical reasoning, differential diagnoses, treatment recommendations, and explanations from the replies. When a reply explains a mechanism, treatment rationale, or diagnostic approach, include the full explanation. If the thread ends without resolving the question, state only what was established.
   - **Answer**: The final answer or clinical recommendation, only if present in the thread. If no clear answer was reached, omit the ## Answer section entirely.
   - If the thread contains multiple distinct questions, use separate ## Question, ## Discussion, ## Answer blocks for each.

5. For reference pages (medical encyclopedias, drug databases, clinical guidelines, educational content):
   Output the text in reading order. Keep all explanatory content, definitions, mechanisms of action, indications, contraindications, dosages, side effects, and clinical pearls. For drug pages, preserve the structured format (indications, dosage, interactions, etc.). For disease pages, preserve etiology, pathophysiology, symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment sections.

6. Do not add information that is not on the page. Every claim, drug interaction, dosage, or clinical recommendation in your output must come from the source HTML.
```

</details>

### Law (Exploratory)

Domain sources identified but not prioritized. ~25 legal Q&A sites (avvo.com, justia.com, law.cornell.edu, etc.) with domain-adapted extraction prompt preserving case citations and legal terminology.

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>Potential Framings/Regimes</summary>

I would like to think more about how this project is impactful both in encouraging the wider community to use the tool we've built and also how this is directly useful to the Marin project.

One thing that is clear: the place this wins is infinite compute world because it is very compute-intensive.

**Framing 1:** By prompt engineering the extractor model we can get purpose built datasets for downstream domains.  This data can be useful for midtraining or mixing into pretraining (see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.16177)

<img width="702" height="389" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d0b5ba7-a89c-4687-8eb6-c779cb5261e6" />

They mix in about 300M tokens of domain specific data during pretraining and it makes these domains easier to learn during SFT.  My code dataset is 262M tokens and Math + Medical are shaping up to be slightly larger so maybe there is potential for this to be the regime we are targeting.

**Framing 2:** Intelligent Pretraining Data selection for infinite compute.  Try to run the pipeline at pretraining scale with a few prompts and see if we get better performance.  Forget about filtering and try to extract as much data as possible from the internet.  Perhaps compare a training run versus other pipelines on the same amount of data.  E.G. maybe we take 3000 WARC files which is about 8B tokens and train a 400M parameter model on this, versus same 3000 WARC files and train on DCLM filtered data which would yield 120M tokens.  This is somewhat ridiculous but it would showcase how we can extract way more juice from the internet.

**Framing 3:** Controllable Pretraining.  Now that we have a model that can rewrite the web content we can steer pretraining in interesting directions.  For instance we can tag data with toxicity tags, or rewrite documents to change the outcomes.  Maybe this is the most interesting part of this tool, so I can select some ways that people would meaningfully want to improve models at the pretraining stage (value alignment, personality, etc.) and see if we can bake any of this into the pretraining.

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>Yejin’s Feedback</summary>

Yejin said that this is a cool tool.  She gave me a few projects she would be interested in working on.  If I were to continue working on this project she had two directions that were most interesting to her:

1. How can we reduce hallucinations in the text copying task?  Measure hallucinations better in my benchmark of the model copying from html to text.  Then we can make it a strong priority to reduce hallucinations.  We can study conditions where the hallucinations arise and ways to prevent the hallucinations when we do the distillation to the smaller model.
2. Similar to [Quark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13636) where they added reward tokens to the model to make it clear during pretraining which content was toxic, then downstream it was easier to reduce toxicity from the model by conditioning on the non-toxic token.  We could do this for things like value alignment, etc. by prompting the extractor model to add tags to the start of each document classifying things like toxicity, values, etc. and then later the model should be more steerable.
 
</details>

---

Flop Accounting We compute inference FLOPs per document by decomposing each forward pass into position-independent (MLP, projections, LM head) and position-dependent (attention) terms. For a request with $P$ input tokens and $O$ output tokens: $$\text{FLOPs} = \underset{\text{prefill}}{\left(C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot P + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2\right)} + \underset{\text{decode}}{\left(C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot O + C_{\text{attn}}\left(O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2}\right)\right)}$$ where $C_{\text{non-attn}}$ and $C_{\text{attn}}$ are constants derived from the model architecture (Qwen3-8B, 36 layers, $d=4096$, GQA with 32/8 heads). **Projection**: $6.60 \times 10^{22}$ total inference FLOPs (95% CI: $\pm 2.0%$). ---
Derivation ### Derivation of Inference FLOP Accounting **Starting point.** Levanter's `lm_flops_per_token` ([`flop_utils.py`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/utils/flop_utils.py)) computes FLOPs per token for a forward pass at a given sequence length $S$. We decompose it into position-independent and position-dependent terms for inference. **Step 1: Identify per-token components.** Each forward pass through one layer computes: | Component | FLOPs per token | Source | |---|---|---| | MLP (SwiGLU: gate, up, down) | $2 \cdot 3 \cdot h \cdot d_{\text{ff}}$ | `2 * 3 * hidden_dim * intermediate_dim` | | QKV projection (GQA) | $2h(n_h d_h + 2 n_{kv} d_h)$ | `2 * hidden_dim * (num_heads * head_dim + 2 * num_kv_heads * head_dim)` | | Output projection | $2h^2$ | `2 * hidden_dim * hidden_dim` | where $h$ is hidden dim, $d_{\text{ff}}$ is intermediate dim, $n_h$ is query heads, $n_{kv}$ is KV heads, and $d_h = h / n_h$ is head dim. These are **constant per token** regardless of position. The LM head adds $2hV$ FLOPs per token (applied once, not per-layer). Combining, the **position-independent cost** per token is: $$C_{\text{non-attn}} = L \cdot (6 h \cdot d_{\text{ff}} + 2h(n_h d_h + 2 n_{kv} d_h) + 2h^2) + 2hV$$ where $L$ is the number of layers. **Step 2: Identify the attention term.** The function computes attention FLOPs over the full sequence then divides by $S$: $$F_{\text{seq}} = S^2 (2 n_h d_h + 3 n_h + 2 d_h n_h) = S^2 (4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h)$$ This accounts for: - Key-query logits: $2 S^2 n_h d_h$ (matmul of $[S, d_h]$ queries against $[d_h, S]$ keys, per head) - Masking + softmax: $3 S^2 n_h$ (comparison, subtract max, exponentiate — 3 ops per element) - Value aggregation: $2 S^2 d_h n_h$ (matmul of $[S, S]$ attention weights against $[S, d_h]$ values) Per token (dividing by $S$), per layer: $$\text{attn per token} = S \cdot (4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h)$$ Defining the **attention cost per unit of context length**, per layer: $$c_{\text{attn}} = 4 n_h d_h + 3 n_h$$ The full attention constant across all layers: $$C_{\text{attn}} = L \cdot c_{\text{attn}}$$ **Step 3: Verify decomposition.** The original function returns: $$f(S) = C_{\text{non-attn}} + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot S$$ which is **affine in $S$** — this is the key structural property. **Step 4: Apply to inference.** Inference has two phases: *Prefill* ($P$ prompt tokens processed in parallel): Each token attends to all $P$ tokens (full-attention assumption from the original function). Total prefill FLOPs: $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{prefill}} = P \cdot f(P) = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot P + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2$$ *Decode* ($O$ output tokens generated sequentially): At decode step $i$ $(i = 0, \ldots, O-1)$, one token attends to a context of length $P + i$. Its FLOPs are $f(P + i) = C_{\text{non-attn}} + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot (P + i)$. Summing: $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{decode}} = \sum_{i=0}^{O-1} f(P+i) = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot O + C_{\text{attn}} \sum_{i=0}^{O-1}(P+i)$$ The sum is an arithmetic series: $$\sum_{i=0}^{O-1}(P+i) = O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2}$$ **Step 5: Combine.** $$\text{FLOPs}\_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{non-attn}} \cdot (P + O) + C_{\text{attn}} \cdot P^2 + C_{\text{attn}} (O \cdot P + \frac{O(O-1)}{2})$$ **Step 6: Plug in Qwen3-8B values.** With $h=4096$, $d_{\text{ff}}=12288$, $L=36$, $n_h=32$, $n_{kv}=8$, $d_h=128$, $V=151936$: $$C_{\text{non-attn}} = 36 \cdot (6 \cdot 4096 \cdot 12288 + 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot (32 \cdot 128 + 2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128) + 2 \cdot 4096^2) + 2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 151936$$ $$C_{\text{attn}} = 36 \cdot (4 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 + 3 \cdot 32) = 36 \cdot 16480 = 593280$$ This closed-form runs in $O(1)$ per document. We evaluate it for each record using exact token counts ($P$ from prompt reconstruction, $O$ = thinking + response tokens from `generated_text`), then sum across all records per batch and project via bootstrap.
---
---
Two Main Experiment Designs (and preliminary results) Everything is based on Delphi Scaling Laws: ---
Delphi Sweeps 78 candidates across 7 compute budgets. | Budget (FLOPs) | Tokens | Parameters | |---------------:|-------:|-----------:| | **3e+18** | 4.3B | 157M | | | 3.0B | 210M | | | 2.2B | 273M | | | 1.6B | 358M | | | 1.2B | 447M | | **9e+18** | 12.9B | 157M | | | 9.1B | 210M | | | 6.7B | 273M | | | 4.7B | 358M | | | 3.7B | 447M | | | 2.9B | 550M | | | 2.3B | 669M | | | 1.8B | 837M | | | 1.5B | 998M | | | 1.3B | 1.18B | | **2e+19** | 25.8B | 157M | | | 18.2B | 210M | | | 13.4B | 273M | | | 9.5B | 358M | | | 7.3B | 447M | | | 5.8B | 550M | | | 4.7B | 669M | | | 3.6B | 837M | | | 3.0B | 998M | | | 2.5B | 1.18B | | | 2.1B | 1.38B | | | 1.8B | 1.61B | | | 1.5B | 1.93B | | | 1.3B | 2.23B | | | 1.1B | 2.54B | | **3e+19** | 22.3B | 273M | | | 12.2B | 447M | | | 7.8B | 669M | | | 5.0B | 998M | | | 3.5B | 1.38B | | | 2.5B | 1.93B | | | 1.9B | 2.54B | | | 1.4B | 3.38B | | | 1.1B | 4.28B | | **9e+19** | 66.8B | 273M | | | 36.7B | 447M | | | 23.4B | 669M | | | 14.9B | 998M | | | 10.6B | 1.38B | | | 7.4B | 1.93B | | | 5.6B | 2.54B | | | 4.2B | 3.38B | | | 3.3B | 4.28B | | | 2.6B | 5.32B | | | 2.1B | 6.70B | | | 1.7B | 8.11B | | | 1.4B | 9.71B | | | 1.2B | 11.79B | | **2e+20** | 73.4B | 447M | | | 46.7B | 669M | | | 29.9B | 998M | | | 21.1B | 1.38B | | | 14.8B | 1.93B | | | 11.2B | 2.54B | | | 8.3B | 3.38B | | | 6.6B | 4.28B | | | 5.3B | 5.32B | | | 4.2B | 6.70B | | | 3.5B | 8.11B | | | 2.9B | 9.71B | | | 2.4B | 11.79B | | **3e+20** | 77.9B | 669M | | | 49.8B | 998M | | | 35.2B | 1.38B | | | 24.7B | 1.93B | | | 18.6B | 2.54B | | | 13.9B | 3.38B | | | 11.0B | 4.28B | | | 8.8B | 5.32B | | | 7.0B | 6.70B | | | 5.8B | 8.11B | | | 4.8B | 9.71B | | | 4.0B | 11.79B |
---
Experiment Version A: Use all data we have We just hit the token budgets for the Delphi sweeps by using every token at our disposal and epoch only as needed. This is just nemotron without any of the rephrases, but even with the rephrases my initial findings are that at small scale DCLM yields better loss on Paloma.
---
Experiment Version B: Simulated Epoching with Set Target (20T) | Pipeline | D_obs | D_proj | Epochs at T=20T | Epochs at T=200T | | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Raw HTML | 3.6T | 9,590T | 0.00 | 0.02 | | Resiliparse | 142.7B | 377T | 0.05 | 0.53 | | LLM Extraction (Qwen3-8B) | 58.9B | 155.5T | 0.13 | 1.29 | | DCLM | 2.7B | 7.0T | 2.85 | 28.5 | | Nemotron-CC | 2.7B | 7.1T | 2.80 | 28.0 | | Nemotron-CC (no rephrase) | 1.9B | 5.1T | 3.94 | 39.4 | | FineWeb-Edu | 817M | 2.2T | 9.27 | 92.7 |
Math Behind Projection Based Simulated Epochs ## Setup We sample 3,000 of ~7.9M Common Crawl WARCs and run each curation method on them: - **D_obs**: tokens in our sample (e.g. 2.66B for DCLM) - **s** = total_warcs / sampled_warcs ≈ 2,642 - **D_proj** = D_obs × s (projected full-CC token count, e.g. ~7.0T) ## Experiment B (simulated full-scale) Simulate training on D_proj tokens at target compute T_target by matching the **epoch count** of the full-scale regime. At full scale, epoch count = `T_target / D_proj`. We match this by training T_exp tokens on a slice: ``` slice = T_exp × D_proj / T_target ``` Verify: `T_exp / slice = T_target / D_proj` ✓ **Ceiling**: slice can't exceed D_obs, so: ``` T_exp ≤ T_target / s ``` Candidates above this ceiling are excluded from Experiment B. ## Example (DCLM, T_target = 20T, budget 3e18, d512 model) ``` slice = 4.3B × 7.0T / 20T ≈ 1.5B unique tokens epochs = 4.3B / 1.5B ≈ 2.87 (matches 20T / 7.0T ≈ 2.86 ✓) ```
--- **I ran the experiment with a 20T token target after discussing with Will (I kinda wanted 200T but Will brought up a good point that it might be too "sci-fi")** **DCLM:** **Nemotron (no synthetic):** **Comparison makes more sense here**: **Compute projections are a bit weirder but still seem directionally okay** ---
**THE PROBLEM:** The token cliff Sampling 3,000 of 7.9M WARCs gives a scale factor s ≈ 2,642, which caps Experiment B at T_exp ≤ T_target / s ≈ 7.6B tokens — excluding our largest compute candidates regardless of curation method. ### Solution 1: Increase Target Token Budget
Solution 1 This solution is to tackle the `T_target` part of the hard cap. We could raise to 200T tokens instead of 20T. **Pros:** Super simple. Probably also makes our method look insanely good because DCLM has to epoch 28x and we only need to epoch 1.2x **Cons:** Somewhat "sci-fi" and not as directly applicable to marin. Also epoxying some datasets 20-90x might ruin the scaling curves anyway.
### Solution 2: Increase Number of WARC files (with clever hack)
Solution 2 This solution is to tackle the `s` part of the hard cap. We could raise to 1000 WARC files instead of 3000. **Pros:** This is easier to justify and probably a more fair comparison. 10k WARCs is the minimum size DCLM releases for comparison. It also allows us to stay within the realm of "useful to marin". More extraction is free from all sources besides LLM extraction because I am just mapping from the data releases. **Cons:** LLM extraction is really expensive. This involves 3x scale up.... except there is a hack. **The Hack:**. Since we are simulated epoching at 0.13 epochs we actually only use a fraction of the data we extracted. We extracted ~60B tokens, and the hard cap would become 25.2B tokens. We can pretend we got these from 10k WARCs when we really got them from 3k. In fact we could push this as far as 20k WARCs, although at some point it really feels like we are punishing our method for over-extracting data.
---
---
---
Additional Ideas What are the possible ways that people might want to use our extractor? **Intelligent Filter** --> We show we get way more data out of the internet. **Controllable Extractor** --> We show we can get math, code, medical content and format it in useful ways **Synthetic Data** --> what is the experiment for this? One idea. Take the huggingface best practices for synthetic data (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13977) Show that Raw2Synthetic leads to better data than rephrasing already extracted web pages (will this be true?). We can take 250 WARC files and 4 prompts and process in 3-4 days. Only problem is the "token cliff" issue will be really bad so we may need to do spot checks instead of scaling laws...
---

---

# Progress this week (5/1-5/8) Mostly been working on the Neurips draft, but scaling results make me think maybe EMNLP will be a better venue for us. [https://www.overleaf.com/read/fztvgncptymj#15e2d5](https://www.overleaf.com/read/fztvgncptymj#15e2d5) **Abstract:** ``` Modern pretraining data curation pipelines are built by composing many independent stages such as URL filtering, text extraction, heuristic rules, deduplication, quality classification, and increasingly synthetic rewriting. Each carries its own thresholds and classifiers, with the pipeline's intent distributed across many artifacts. We propose replacing these complex pipelines with a single LLM call per html document, conditioned on a natural-language spec that jointly filters, extracts, and rewrites. The spec becomes the one human-readable, optimizable, and version-controllable artifact that captures curation intent. To make this practical at web scale, we distill GPT-OSS-120B into a Qwen3-8B extractor that runs over hundreds of millions of pages at roughly half the cost of the teacher. We demonstrate the approach in two settings: We find that by throwing away less web content our LLM extracted data can outperform existing curation pipelines when the data pool is held fixed. In a domain-specific case study with specs targeting math, code, and medical content our llm extractor yields gains over a resiliparse-only baseline by up to 18 percentage points on domain specific benchmarks through continued pretraining of Qwen3 base models. We release the distilled extractor publicly to encourage adoption of spec-driven web extraction for data curation. ``` ---
Paper Updates **Figure 1:** **Figure 2:** I polished up the distillation results from prior weeks: I also revisited the results for the domain specific extraction. Decided to switch to logprobs for MMLU (reason for the one missing result) and added 8B model, but overall things are looking good there too. One thing is I split the med data into val and test and apparently the test set makes 14B look worse, but overall results in most settings look reasonable. Last thing to discuss for what looks good is the 3000 WARC fixed pool (no scaling) looks good! Haven't polished the plot for this yet but the results themselves are strong:
---
The Scaling Results The original promising finding: Looks like we always win at high compute budget! But how high? That is the **problem** :( Plotted the cross over compute at each WARC budget: The cross over point is scaling super-linearly which is bad news for us, suggests that the compute cross-over point scales quadratically versus data source pool. Makes running no quality filtering extremely impractical. Another view without it being the optimal per WARC (just show all data): With just this regression we get the following predictions -- With the internet having 8M WARC files this puts us at a compute crossover of: 5.2 × 10²⁸ FLOPs Training a 1T parameter model this puts us at a compute crossover of: 6.2 × 10²⁶ FLOPs If frontier labs are training at 10^26 flops this puts us at beyond what the frontier is doing. Needs a discussion
--- **Discussion:** Experiment Pivots - Possibly extracting to different quality levels (add metadata tag) -- ideally we can be Pareto optimal at any compute budget, AND it allows for data mixing potentially - Alignment pretraining: https://x.com/rosinality/status/2051575415345390027?s=46 ---

# Progress this week (5/10-5/15) ---
New Extraction Prompts **Three levels of quality filtering**: ---
Low Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Follow all rules below. 1. Extract the full page content in reading order. Keep all explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 2. Remove boilerplate: navigation bars, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and user interface elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 3. Preserve all technical content exactly as written: code, math notation, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve the original line breaks and structure of code blocks. 4. Decode all HTML entities to their plain characters (e.g. & to &, < to <, > to >, ’ to ', – to –). Remove any raw HTML tags. 5. Every sentence in your output must come from the source page. Do not add, invent, or embellish content. 6. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what. Include usernames or speaker labels so contributions remain distinguishable. 7. If the text contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option and output clean text. If the majority of the page is spinner templates, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] instead. 8. Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply:    - Login, signup, paywall, registration wall, or "you must sign up to view" page    - Error page, empty page, or cookie/captcha wall    - Terms of use, privacy policy, or legal boilerplate page    - User profile page with no substantive content    - Page whose content has been removed, moved, or is no longer available    - Image gallery, photo album listing, or media archive without articles    - The text is incoherent gibberish or garbled encoding throughout    - The page has under ~50 words of substantive content after removing boilerplate    However, for index pages or directory listings, only filter if they contain nothing but links and titles. If an index page includes real text like discussion snippets or descriptions, extract it. ```
---
Medium Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below. 1. **Quality bar.** The page must be real written content — coherent prose that conveys information, ideas, narrative, or experience. Acceptable: articles, explanations, analyses, reviews with substantive commentary, tutorials, manuals, reference entries, documentation, and substantive forum or comment discussions. If the page does not pass, output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].    **Walk through each bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any bullet applies, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.    - **Navigation or aggregation** — exists to point elsewhere (forum indexes, category pages, tag clouds, search results, sitemaps, archive-by-date pages, contributor lists, topic-aggregation pages of one-line summaries). A tag archive showing one truncated post excerpt still fails — the page must contain at least one full post.    - **Site machinery** — login, signup, paywall, cookie banner, captcha, error page, "page not found", redirect notice, terms of service, privacy policy, subscription/notification form ("send to a friend", email signup), or instructions for using the site itself. Pages whose main content is hidden behind a login wall fail even when the page shows a "you must be logged in" prompt.    - **Fragments** — Tumblr-style image-reblog streams, social timelines, photo-blog feeds, lists of one-liner microposts, image gallery captions, personal "about me" pages, and repost stubs that consist of a brief excerpt plus a "Read on:", "Go to Source", "View original", or affiliate link to elsewhere. Pages of fragments and metadata rather than coherent passages.    - **Wrapper around non-textual media** — a video, audio, slideshow, photo, or interactive widget where the page exists to host the media rather than be read. Includes image-only social posts (Blingee/Pinterest-style), single-photo pages with a one-line caption, video-player pages with only a title/byline around the video, and blog posts whose body is a short reaction (a sentence or two) around an embedded video, image, or share.    - **Commerce or product page** — pages with prices, availability, "Add to Cart", or shipping/stock indicators. Vendor-written descriptions, specs, ingredients, and care instructions are commerce metadata, not content — they do not save the page. Keep only if the page contains an extended editorial passage about the product (a third-party review, comparison, or analysis), not vendor sales copy. Also includes **employer or company profile pages** ("Quick Look", "Company Overview") that are mostly company name, industry, size, and a bullet list of services or job categories.    - **Raw data dump** — structured data without surrounding narrative. This includes both rows of data (rosters, statistics tables, file indexes, contact directories, database exports) **and single-record entries** (museum specimen cards, IP whois / BGP route lookups, dictionary entries that are only a definition line, badge / user-profile / member pages). An article that uses tables to support its prose is fine.    - **Too short** — count the substantive sentences on the page after removing boilerplate, navigation, ads, comments, links, dates, and reposted excerpts. **If the remaining substantive prose is fewer than 5 complete sentences, the page fails.** Apply this strictly: a 1-paragraph news brief, a 2-sentence "X just opened in Y" announcement, a single-event calendar entry, "this section has moved" notice, "no results found" / "no products matching" / "click here to proceed" placeholder — all fail, regardless of how grammatical or informative-looking the few sentences are.    - **Incoherent** — gibberish, garbled encoding, machine-translated nonsense, or spinner templates throughout. First determine if the page clears the quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content. 2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks. 5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags. 6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page. 7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels. 8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. ```
---
High Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below. 1. **EXTREME quality bar — keep almost nothing.** This filter is designed to retain only the very best educational and informative content; only about 1 in 10 pages should pass. The **default is to output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]**.    **HARD GATES — check first, in order. If any gate fails, immediately output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop.**    - **Gate A — Language.** Is the body of the page written primarily in English? If the main prose is in any other language (French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Russian, etc.), output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. Quoted phrases, names, citations, or short snippets in another language are fine; a page whose main prose is non-English is not — even if the topic looks substantive.    - **Gate B — Prose depth.** Are there roughly 300 or more words of real *prose* — flowing sentences and paragraphs that explain, argue, or teach? Table cells, formula tokens, code-only listings, navigation labels, whois fields, stat lines, and metadata do NOT count toward the word budget. A page that hits 300 "words" only by counting structured-data fields fails this gate.    A page that clears both gates is kept ONLY if all four of these are also true:    - **Teaches the reader.** The page explains a concept, mechanism, method, or topic; develops an argument with evidence and examples; reports original analysis; or delivers substantive technical or instructional material. It must convey real knowledge of the world, not just headlines, facts, or summaries.    - **Carefully written.** Clear, structured, professional or academic-quality prose. Not casual, not fragmentary, not marketing copy, not auto-generated, not template-filled.    - **Self-contained value.** A reader who lands here learns meaningfully from this page alone — not from clicking through to something else.    - **Not matched by any FAILS bullet below.**    **Walk through each FAILS bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any matches, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.    Categories that typically qualify (still subject to all criteria above):    - Long-form journalism with original reporting and analysis — including editorial tech journalism or product reporting that includes quotes, context, history, or analysis (even when the subject is a company's product launch)    - Educational or explanatory articles (science, math, history, engineering, medicine, philosophy, economics, etc.)    - Tutorials, how-tos, and documentation with real teaching — instructions plus the reasoning behind them    - Encyclopedia and reference entries written with substantive prose    - **Substantive technical forum, mailing-list, or Q&A threads** — e.g., a Stack Overflow question with a thorough accepted answer, a numpy/scipy mailing-list discussion working through a real problem, a developer forum thread that reaches a meaningful technical conclusion. The "casual forum threads" FAILS bullet does NOT apply when the discussion is technical and develops the topic.    - Research papers, white papers, technical writeups    - Essays and analyses that develop an argument with evidence — including substantive opinion or commentary on a personal blog or social platform like Tumblr/Medium/Substack    - Code accompanied by genuine teaching, not just a snippet    - Technical blogs sharing real domain expertise    - Institutional or organizational descriptions with substantive prose (academic program pages with curriculum and outcomes, organizational reports, conference or event summaries with real narrative)    - Religious or scriptural texts presenting substantive narrative or doctrine (e.g., a Bible chapter, Quran sura, philosophical canon — numbered-verse format is fine)    Categories that FAIL — filter even if the writing is fine:    - **News briefs, sports recaps, and transaction roundups** — "X happened, said Y" reporting without analysis, depth, or context. Includes local sports recaps ("West Side beat Cumberland 14-4"), team transaction logs ("Signed pitcher X to a minor-league contract"), and short news items even when several are stitched together on one page.    - **Personal lifestyle or diary blogging** — daily-life updates, travelogues, opinion pieces without intellectual substance. (A personal blog with substantive analysis or argument is fine — judge by content, not platform.)    - **Light reviews — including aggregator pages of light reviews** — "I tried it, it's good" without genuine analysis or comparison. A page that strings together several short product blurbs is still light reviews, not substantive content.    - **Reference stubs and structured-data dumps** — one-paragraph wiki entries, definitions, factoid lists, player stat cards, whois/BGP/DNS records, raw lookup results, single-formula pages. If the page is mostly a table, a record, or one isolated fact, it fails — fastText-style classifiers may rate this content highly because it "looks structured," but it is not teaching prose.    - **Casual forum threads** — chit-chat, brief Q&A without resolution, social exchanges that don't reach a meaningful conclusion. Technical mailing-list or Q&A threads that DO develop the topic are covered by the qualifying bullet above and are NOT this.    - **Vendor sales copy or purely promotional material** — product descriptions, ad copy, "buy now" pages. (Institutional descriptions of academic programs, mission statements with real content, organizational reports, or editorial journalism about a product launch are NOT this; judge by whether the page sells a product or describes/teaches.)    - **Mostly un-decoded HTML / escape soup** — pages where the visible text is dominated by raw HTML entities (` `, `<`, `&`, `&#NNN;`), escape sequences, or malformed markup that survived the page render. Even if the underlying content might be code or text, a page presented this way is junk for training.    - **"No results" / search-empty pages** — "your search returned no results", "no items match", "0 records found" — even when they list related links or alternative searches alongside.    - **Anything that fails a normal quality filter** — commerce pages, navigation or aggregation surfaces, login walls or other site machinery, fragments and microposts, wrappers around non-textual media, raw data dumps, empty placeholders, incoherent text    **When in doubt, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].** Reject borderline pages aggressively; only clear winners pass. First determine if the page clears the EXTREME quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content. 2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks. 5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags. 6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page. 7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels. 8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. ```
--- Using these prompts I have gotten the following distributions of tokens: Looks even better than DCLM **and** with more tokens: Unfortunately higher budget jobs have been queued for a little while. ---
How did I settle on these prompts? Only works if hosted: [http://localhost:8090/?show_token=dclm%3Adclm_full&show_token=dclm%3Av15_then_dclm_full&show_token=curator%3Acurator_general_v15&show_token=curator%3Acurator_quality_v8&show_token=curator%3Acurator_extreme_v5&url=&sort=record_index&reverse=0&state.dclm=&state.dclm_full=&state.v15_then_dclm_full=&state.curator_general_v15=&state.curator_quality_v8=&state.curator_extreme_v5=](http://localhost:8090/?show_token=dclm%3Adclm_full&show_token=dclm%3Av15_then_dclm_full&show_token=curator%3Acurator_general_v15&show_token=curator%3Acurator_quality_v8&show_token=curator%3Acurator_extreme_v5&url=&sort=record_index&reverse=0&state.dclm=&state.dclm_full=&state.v15_then_dclm_full=&state.curator_general_v15=&state.curator_quality_v8=&state.curator_extreme_v5=) Observing how random sample of 1k documents was extracted by each.
--- Not too long before I finish scaling up the high quality prompt: This has also been slightly problematic for cluster contention so we are redesigning the distributed inference stack: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1UEnIabqLPrjfYfSDGqQVad252nLETi8L9MeBvh81YoY/edit?tab=t.xe6eofm9ervd#heading=h.46dj0uyi8n53 ---
---
Deduplication Deduplication ended up being pretty important! Now all my experiments with resiliparse and llm_extracted are using deduplication: ``` Exact dedup runs inside marin.datakit.normalize.normalize_step with DedupMode.EXACT — it drops byte-identical documents by xxh3_128 hash of the text field (one hex id per record). Fuzzy dedup then runs MinHash-LSH connected-components on top with 286 permutations / 26 bands / 5-char ngrams / seed 42 / ~0.75 Jaccard threshold, keeping one canonical doc per cluster (see experiments/baseline_collection/dedup_extracted.py:380-419). ``` Dedupe was even important for the **high_quality** filter because of sites like this: And there are sometimes articles are posted multiple times: [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/clusters_high_quality_100.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/clusters_high_quality_100.html)
---
Scaling Plan Once I have this plot for **low_quality**, **med_quality** (maybe), and **high_quality**. [http://localhost:8091/plots/eval_lima_loss/grid_compressed_x_tokens_all_epochs.html](http://localhost:8091/plots/eval_lima_loss/grid_compressed_x_tokens_all_epochs.html) Then I will use the [Meunninghoff et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.16264) scaling laws to figure out how we should expect each data source to scale with epoching. Where N' and D' are the discounted tokens and parameters from epoching or training excess parameters. Then I get a relationship where I can predict loss from a given parameter and compute budget and can make a plot like this: **NOTE I don't think I've fit this quite right yet, so don't trust this exact plot but this is meant to serve as an example:** My plan would be to show the tradeoff between high_quality, med_quality, and low_quality perhaps both at the literal compute budget we train at AND if you were to scale up to training trillion parameter models. The argument would be this is something you could do at small scales to predict what dataset you should use when you scale up.
---
Next Steps - Finish Extracting **High_Quality** spec docs (1-2 days) - Train Scaling Ladder for High_Quality spec (3 days) - Run CORE evals on the lowest loss config with every dataset (ensuring that val loss was a predictive measure) (hours) - (Optional) Run Extraction on **Med_quality** spec (6-7 days) - Plot the tradeoff of parameters and compute versus what dataset you should use. (bottlenecked by me figuring this out)
---
Beyond the Paper I think one particularly promising idea would be if we truly are getting higher quality data than DCLM at 4x the tokens, this would be worth making a case for trying to scale up to actually run this closer to internet scale. One potential path: - If we end up locking in a specific spec we could distill an even smaller model on just that spec. We actually have a ton of data now to do this and might even be possible to train a model from scratch! - We would need to secure more compute for this... Right now extracting 3k WARCs takes 6 days (optimistically). Extracting 8 million WARCs would thus take (8M / 3k = 2666 * 6 days = 16,000 days / 365 = ~43.84 years) about 44 years. I think by distilling a smaller model we can dramatically reduce that but probably would be a combination of that plus more compute. - The other question is if this is worth the squeeze versus just generating synthetic data or something else.

# Progress this week (6/1-6/5) Paper draft is looking good :) Main points for discussion today: - Is my approach for fixing the sampling issue satisfactory? - Planning the scale up timeline and strategy. - Plan for scientific paper versus bigger pretraining data project. ---
Paper is done! Overleaf: [https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4) We evaluate models on RealToxicityPrompts \cite{gehman-etal-2020-realtoxicityprompts} judged by Detoxity \cite{Detoxify} and find 2.9B models trained on our **High-Quality extraction only produce toxic completions on 3.3\% of prompts compared to 5.1\% with DCLM**. One thing that is missing is Decontamination. I still need to run Decontamination.
---
The sampling issue There are three ways to resolve the sampling issue. I think one makes more sense for the paper and the other we will get for free as we start to scale up. **Option A: ** Extract the 10,364 WARC files that make up the DCLM 400m-1x pool with our high quality Spec. This is a RANDOM sample of WARC files but it is limited to 2013-2022 (Nemotron-CC goes until 2024). For our scaling experiments we leave the biased sample and make that clear (don't re-extract "low-quality" and "medium-quality" spec). Pros: Directly comparable to DCLM. In fact we will get to upload to the DCLM leaderboard. Any sampling bias can be attributed to DCLM's choices. Also gives us more useful extracted data than rerunning all specs at all scales. Cons: Still somewhat biased against Nemotron-CC. Still takes 2 weeks to run. The biased sample was provably harmful for nemotron: I think ultimately we can do a completely unbiased sample versus nemotron once I start to scale up to the whole common crawl with my more efficient method (more on this later), but perhaps this is good for the "scientific" writeup? **Option B: ** Re-extract a completely random sample with all extractors for fair comparison to Nemotron-CC. This means we cannot compare to DCLM (cutoff 2022). About the same 2 week timeline (maybe 2.5 weeks) **Option C: ** Just extract random 3k sample from the DCLM range with all methods. Same timeline, but not really new useful data and we still know we are biased against nemotron by missing 2022-2024.
---
Distilling the full "Spec-Driven Extraction Pipeline" Two Main things I need to achieve: 1. Distill the CONTENT FILTERING decision into a single fastText classifier. 2. Distill a Single-Spec into a much smaller LLM given that we no longer care about swapping the spec. 3. Reduce the size of the input prompts to the LLM extractor stage ### Single Filter FastText Classifier Pretty good success so far! Training a fastText classifier on about 13M documents that our Spec-Driven curator made decisions on yields a model that can retain 95% of useful content while dropping 79% of junk content! This will hopefully lead to an 80% cost reduction with only a slight quality reduction. ### Distill a Single Spec Model Less progress here so far. Kicked off some Qwen3-0.6B runs based on data from 2930 WARC extractions with the High Quality spec. ALSO trying to remove reasoning now that we are doing single spec and a lot of the reasoning had to do with whether or not we extract the content. Reasoning was accounting for **3x as many tokens as extraction** (this includes on filtered rows though which explains part of the problem. Benchmarking GPT-OSS versus our 8B extractor in the single spec setting. This is where I will compare Qwen3-0.6b when SFT is done. ### Reduce the size of the inputs to the Model I realized that I was running the extractor on the FULL HTML which is great for the paper (super clean story) but bad for throughput. Now I am stripping to just the body tag and removing script tags which we showed worked earlier but I accidentally didn't do for our production runs. This leads to a median 21% reduction in the size of the input that gets to the model. ### Speedup Assuming: - 80% time reduction from FastText - 20% time reduction from input size reduction - 40% time reduction from dropping reasoning and smaller model (pretty much a guess) New pipeline should take 9.6% of the time to process, but I still need to benchmark. This isn't good enough.... that brings us from 42 years down to 4.2 Years. I need to be 563 times faster to bring things from 42 years down to 1 month.
---
Todo Items Hopefully can achieve these milestones by middle of June as a target. **For Scientific Report**: - Compare with FineWeb - Extract DCLM-scale 10k WARC comparison - Train DCLM model on their training scripts so we could release to their leaderboard (not a priority) - Run Decontamination on the 10k Extraction **For Major Extraction Run** - Achieve 563x speedup - Ensure that quality exceeds Nemotron at truly random sample - Ensure Long Context is not a serious bottleneck.

# Progress this week (6/15-6/19) --- Key Question: **How should I fairly run DCLM COREv2 Evals on these models when there is token count/quality mismatch?**
Random WARC Extraction Took the full DCLM 400M-1x Data Pool. We now have a competition ready compatible submission for DCLM **Old results**: **New results**:
---
Decontamination [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/decon_inspect_n15.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/decon_inspect_n15.html) A document was removed if it contained even a single 15-word-gram that also appears in a DCLM CORE v2 eval item — provided that 15-gram is distinctive (appears in ≤10 eval-source docs).
--- Key Question: **What signs of life should I prioritize on the fast data curation pipeline to be sure this is working well at scale?**
Pipeline Improvements ---
Rule Based Heuristics Expressed each DCLM and custom HTML rule as a tunable threshold on a single feature, then greedily assembled them under a hard recall ≥ 0.99 constraint: at each step we add the threshold that discards the most no_useful documents per unit of useful lost, stopping once the ~1% recall budget is spent.
---
FastText + ModernBERT Usefulness Classifier Cascade **fastText (stage 1)**: Trained as a binary "useful vs [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]" classifier on ~2.46M raw body_strip HTML docs (189k useful + 2.27M non-useful, the 12:1 deployment ratio) from 80 WARCs across 24 CC snapshots, using the hand-set DCLM bigram recipe (epoch 5, lr 0.1, dim 100, wordNgrams 2, softmax). Pruning with --min count 500 shrank it to a sub-GB model (0.96 GB) at full quality (F1 0.594). **ModernBERT (stage 2)**: Fine-tuned answerdotai/ModernBERT-base (8192 ctx) on the same target but over 1M docs sampled only from the fastText survivor pool, on TPU v6e-4 with PyTorch + torch_xla in bf16 (effective batch 256, lr 5e-5, 1 epoch). Training on the survivor residual specialized it for exactly the deployment distribution, lifting standalone F1 to 0.705 and giving the best high-recall operating point in the cascade.
---
jusText Custom Extractor Fork AutoResearched it! Each cycle, we sampled the worst-scoring documents on the dev set, found a recurring fixable artifact (forum/comment/FAQ structure, code/URL/encoding mangling, list/dash formatting), fixed it in justext/core.py, and re-measured against the baseline across all five datasets — shipping only changes with no real regression and logging each in research_log/. On top of ~70 such structural fixes we layered a learned paragraph classifier (RandomForest stacked with a fastText keep-probability model), and validated the whole thing once on the held-out test split at the end to confirm we generalized rather than overfit. [https://github.com/XenonMolecule/jusText](https://github.com/XenonMolecule/jusText) [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/jusText/benchmark/runs/current-cmarker/general/dev.report.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/jusText/benchmark/runs/current-cmarker/general/dev.report.html) [dev.report.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29150650/dev.report.html)
---
FastText Router The jusText-extractability router is a fastText classifier that predicts, from a raw doc, whether a cheap jusText extraction will land within 0.85 normalized Levenshtein similarity of the gold LLM extraction (i.e. ≥85% character-identical) — labeling such docs "extractable" (→ jusText) and everything else, including all [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] abstentions, as "needs LLM" (→ 1.7B/gpt-oss-120b). Because only ~5.5% of docs naturally clear that strict bar, at its F1-optimal threshold the router sends just ~8% of survivors (3,381 of 41,245 ≈ 1.9% of all raw docs) to jusText and leaves the remaining ~92% (37,864 docs) on the expensive model path, offloading less than a tenth of the extraction workload.

If you look to LIMA loss it is less clear that we are better than DCLM anymore (we used to be at 3k scale): Maybe I need to add in some domain specific and more benchmark relevant val loss sets to compare with when building my spec?
--- 4. Perhaps our dataset is better at some domains and worse at others? -- **plausible**
Experiments This part of the analysis is admittedly a bit claude driven where the rest was under my direct supervision, so take some of these insights with a grain of salt. [corev2_worse_on_examples.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29647720/corev2_worse_on_examples.html) [corev2_better_on_examples.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29647739/corev2_better_on_examples.html) Our worst Gap: LAMBADA Our Best Gap: BoolQ Heatmap for OLMES Benchmark: Overall it seems plausible that we are better at reasoning from context and doing mathematical manipulations/physical reasoning, but worse at recalling factual information. This could be consistent with broader factual information in our pretraining mix so the stuff tested on is less prevalent however the stuff tested on is pretty important...
--- What to do about it? 1. I could run decontamination on the other baselines (might help a bit but probably doesn't solve our complete problem) 2. We should figure out what evals and behaviors we trust and care about 3. We should figure out what validation losses actually correlate with performance on those benchmarks. 4. I will need to revise my spec to get better validation losses with small scale extraction runs 5. I can rerun a bigger extraction once we are more confident the spec is locked in for also improving benchmark scores 6. Then I can redistill the fast pipeline on top of our re-optimized pipeline. The good news is in parallel I can keep optimizing our fast pipeline and I think it is looking good. **If we have ideas that don't involve basically redoing the extraction I am super open to them haha since this is non-trivial (might add a month of work that we didn't otherwise plan for.**
---
(Seemingly Pretty Positive Result) New Pipelines Found a pipeline that is time scale reasonable and decent at filtering: **"ModernBERT Recall 0.9 - 100% acceptance"** Then tested 5 variants by just reducing the modernBERT acceptance rate from there. **80%** **60%** **40%** **20%** Despite the stuff above (in the DCLM negative result section), if we can still trust val loss the results are promising: And all of this completed in less than a day! Much faster than the ~1 month it took before to do this extraction at this scale:
**TLDR (since we probably won't get to it today)**; Distilled pipeline can run in 1.2 months and seems just as good as the original if not better (since we fix some long-context issues etc.). AND I still have more experiments ongoing on how to make it even better. ---
Extraction Exploration Related Methods that I must compare to (was my plan for yesterday before all of the negative results came in): - https://usefeyn.com/blog/pulpie-pareto-optimal-models-for-cleaning-the-web/ - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.16397 I will run these on my benchmarks, but I will also run my stuff on their benchmarks. It might be possible to fine-tune Pulpie to do better paragraph selection for keep/delete based on what my LLM extractor deems relevant.

The main thing is I didn't realize **we were still relying on scale to win**. We were **not Pareto dominant at DCLM evals even at the 3k scale** and this was hidden by evaluating only on the points that had minimum val loss on uncheatable eval. Compute matched we were losing.

Where are the gaps/successes in our data? ### uncheatable eval: **AO3 (Fanfiction)** **BBC News** **Github Python** **Wikipedia (English)** **Github C++** **arXiv CS** **arXiv Physics** ### Olmo: **QA_bpb** **Code_bpb** **Math_bpb** ### Full Dashboard: Locally: file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/plots/subcomponents_10k/subcomponents_dashboard.html Unfortunately too big to host this html on GitHub :( ### Takeaways: We are better at code, and pretty on par with others at math/wikipedia language modeling. New Devset (and ways of measuring spec quality) **Labelled a Devset of 935 docs so far (999 to go, but seeing if claude can help)** Labelled it for keep, weak keep, weak drop, or drop. Also marked some for top quality (we really MUST keep), and some that are tricky edge cases to test the extraction. ---
How the docs were selected **Document selection.** The core of the dev set is a *disagreement-and-topicality* sample from a 10,000-WARC CommonCrawl pool: for each held-out eval example that `high_quality` scored worse on than DCLM/Nemotron, we built a keyword fingerprint and selected corpus documents containing ≥3 and ≥80% of that example's keywords, then joined each to a membership table recording every pipeline's keep/drop decision (hq, DCLM, Nemotron-CC, FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb-CC) and stratified the draw by (register × cross-pipeline agreement × hq's own decision) so both kept and dropped documents appear in every register. We then supplemented this with an unbiased uniform sample from a 2013–2026 CommonCrawl timeline, targeted raw-HTML scans that recover code/table pages (via `
`/``/`` and
syntax-highlighter signatures that extraction destroys), diverse general-forum threads, mined
hard-negatives, and the highest-confidence documents DCLM keeps but hq drops.

**Register identification.** Registers were first assigned by domain — each URL reduced to its
registered domain (eTLD+1) and matched against a hand-curated, priority-ordered list of
domain-substring patterns per register — but because that mis-binned platform domains (e.g. a
chemistry article on `geeksforgeeks`, a novel e-text on `gradesaver`), every document was subsequently
re-classified by *content*, with an LLM reading the extracted text and assigning the register it
actually belongs to.

I did do some preliminary experiments to explore if the data mix was the core driver of the problems we are seeing.  I don't think it is, however I didn't do this experiment super carefully (see below):

---



Data Mix and Epoching Tests

hq is the most *permissive* extractor (keeps the most URLs) but the most *diluted* corpus
(85.7% generic "other" vs DCLM's ~72%; knowledge char-share 1.69% vs DCLM 2.77%). Two
mechanisms could explain the gap at fixed compute:

| # | hypothesis | variant | what it changes | holds fixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | **density/composition** | `hq_reweight` | mixes full hq (w=0.856) + a knowledge-dense `hq_dense` cache (w=0.144) -> dense char-share **12.3%->25%** (= DCLM) | token budget |
| B | **epochs/repetition** | `hq_epoch` | uniform 34.4% subsample -> **7.33B tokens** (= DCLM's count), so more epochs per token | composition |



Did not work when we unweighted or epoched but we did this in a super naive way...

---



How we defined knowledge-dense

How the `hq_dense` reweight bucket was defined in the Phase-2 dilution ablation
(`experiments/baseline_collection/build_hq_variants.py`).

A doc was counted as **dense** iff its **registered domain** contained one of the substring
patterns below — i.e. `categorize(url) in {reference_wiki, academic, blog, news, qa_help}`.
This is a **domain-only heuristic** (never reads page text); patterns are **priority-ordered**,
first match wins, else `other`. Source of truth: `CATEGORY_PATTERNS` in
`experiments/baseline_collection/provenance_audit_10k.py`.

The five "fact-bearing expository" registers were chosen to mirror what DCLM over-represents
(knowledge-gap decomposition: reference_wiki 2.4×, blog 2.6×, academic 1.7× char-share vs hq).
This subset was ~12% of hq tokens; mixed back at weight 0.144 it lifted the dense char-share
~12% → 25% (matching DCLM) at a fixed token budget.

## reference_wiki (11 patterns)

```
wikipedia, wikia, fandom, wiktionary, wikihow, wikimedia, wikinews, wikibooks, britannica, wikidot, wikispaces
```

## academic (22 patterns)

```
arxiv, biorxiv, ssrn, researchgate, academia.edu, jstor, sciencedirect, springer, ncbi.nlm.nih, plos, pubmed, semanticscholar, citeseerx, iopscience, ieee, acm.org, aps.org, mdpi, tandfonline, wiley, oup.com, sagepub
```

## blog (12 patterns)

```
blogspot, wordpress, tumblr, typepad, medium.com, livejournal, blogs., blog., ghost.io, substack, wixsite, weebly
```

## news (29 patterns)

```
bbc., cnn., nytimes, theguardian, reuters, washingtonpost, forbes, bloomberg, huffpost, huffingtonpost, npr.org, apnews, aljazeera, telegraph, dailymail, foxnews, nbcnews, cbsnews, usatoday, wsj., economist, theatlantic, politico, news, tribune, gazette, herald, chron., latimes
```

## qa_help (6 patterns)

```
answers., ask., support., help., faq, howto
```

## Caveats

- **Plain substring match on the domain** — over- and under-catches. Generic `news` grabs any
  domain containing "news"; `faq` / `howto` are bare substrings that can match mid-domain;
  `blog` is really the *platform* (blogspot/wordpress), whose content is heterogeneous.
- **Domain-only, no text** — "academic" is genuinely journal/preprint domains, but expository
  *quality* within blog/news is unresolved. So the reweight concentrated these **registers by
  domain**, not fact-dense text — a coarse proxy, and part of why the reweight moved nothing.

<details>
<summary>Current Specs I am trying out</summary>

There are now two types of systems I am operating with.  **Multi-Stage** and **Single Stage**.  The Multi-Stage system has a first spec which is just for filtering (reasoning on) and the second stage is extraction from html for pages that are kept.  Single Stage does both and must keep reasoning on for both.  As a result, **multi-stage is approximately 3x faster to run**.

| Spec | Stage | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **high_quality** | Single stage | One-prompt extraction with hard gates (English, ≥300 prose words) + positive criteria; deliberately strict, keeps ~1 in 10 pages. |
| **med_quality** | Single stage | One-prompt extraction with a looser-than-HQ quality bar that still filters nav/boilerplate, fragments, commerce, and incoherent pages. |
| **high_quality_v2** | Multi stage | Basically high_quality but two-stage (filter/quality-gate call, then a separate extraction call); better on fiction and QA/forum content. |
| **llm_pipeline_v1** | Multi stage | Two-stage: a filter/voting gate call, then a separate head + continuation extraction call. |
| **llm_simple_v1** | Single stage | The one-call variant — judging and extraction merged into a single call (plus a continuation call only for long docs). |

If the main prose is in any other language (French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Russian, etc.), output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. Quoted phrases, names, citations, or short snippets in another language are fine; a page whose main prose is non-English is not — even if the topic looks substantive.
