# Weekly Sync 7/27-7/31 ---
New Extraction Spec Last week I noticed that my extractor was making subtle mistakes that Levenstein distance was forgiving of, but would hurt us downstream, such as dropping parts of code (e.g. if the site had execution outputs it might leave those lines out). I spent a lot of time iterating on our extractor over the weekend and got to something I was pretty happy with. I also switched back to **markdown** format following our discussion and rule that throwing away information seems like a bad tradeoff to make just for lower loss or benchmark scores. ---
Old Spec ``` Extract this web page's content as clean plain text. You are given a MIDDLE OR END SECTION of a long page whose beginning was already processed and judged worth keeping. This section can begin or end mid-sentence; that is expected. Extract what is in front of you, in the order it appears. Extract only what this page is about: its article, its story, its thread, its question and the answers to it. Around that, pages show pointers to other pages — "related" or "popular" link lists, teasers and headlines of other articles, archives of past posts, lists of other questions. Those are pointers, not content: leave them out. KEEP the content a reader came to this page for: articles, news stories, blog posts, essays, fiction and stories, explanations, tutorials, reference material, the question and its answers, the thread's posts and comments, code with its explanation, mathematics (keep LaTeX), data tables and statistics, product reviews, and scientific, medical, legal, historical, or educational writing. REMOVE page furniture: navigation menus, headers, footers, sidebars, search boxes, forms, ads, cookie banners, newsletter prompts, share buttons, related-link lists, breadcrumbs, and repeated boilerplate. Begin your output directly with the content. If this section is entirely page furniture with no content in it, output nothing at all. ```
---
New Spec ``` Extract this web page's content as clean markdown. You may be given the whole page, or one section of a long page; a section can begin or end mid-sentence. Extract what is in front of you, in the order it appears. Think of it as retyping the page's own writing in markdown. The page's HTML tells you the marks to use:

–

→ #, 
/code → \`\`\` fences,  → | rows, LaTeX/MathML → $…$. Nothing else gets a mark, and nothing gets invented — no added headings, numbering, bold labels, inline code, link targets, or HTML tags.

What gets retyped: the article, story, or thread; the question, every answer, and the comments under them; code, math, and tables character for character; repeating items (cards, entries, definitions) down to the last one. Rough, pasted, or repetitive writing is still the page's writing.

What does not: menus, sidebars, footers, ads, forms, share buttons, breadcrumbs, cookie banners; teasers and "related" lists; tag, topic, category, and archive indexes, however long; shop-by filters, product rails, trending strips; text with template placeholders. A related question whose full answer is printed here is content, not a pointer.

Where to stop: at the end of the page's own piece. Author bios, "latest posts by", and feeds of other articles come after that ending, and are not part of it.

Attribution: every post in a thread, Q&A, or comment section starts with **Author — date** and keeps that shape in every section of the page. The profile furniture around a post is not part of it: member rank, registration date, post count, location, and the signature line repeated under every post by the same author all stay out.

Begin directly with the content. Write nothing about the extraction itself. If this section holds only furniture, output nothing at all.
```



---

The vibes with the spec are pretty good: 



https://claude.ai/code/artifact/344c5a6c-2da1-44ef-87c7-2b4e978f154f 

**Benchmark numbers are promising but don't paint this as a slam dunk:**



Custom Metrics

Three numbers for "did the extraction keep the page's content, and nothing else."
Everything is computed on **normalized** text, so markdown, emphasis, quotes,
dashes, whitespace and rendered-vs-LaTeX math (`κ` = `\kappa`) never count as a
difference.

Let $G$ be the gold text and $P$ the prediction.

- $S(x)$ = the **set of 5-grams** of $\text{normalize}(x)$
- $U(G)$ = the **sentences of $G$** with at least 8 words

## KEPT — recall

Fraction of gold's sentences that survive. A sentence counts as kept if at least
half of its 5-grams appear anywhere in the prediction:

$$\text{KEPT} = \frac{1}{|U(G)|}\sum_{u \in U(G)} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\frac{|S(u) \cap S(P)|}{|S(u)|} \ge 0.5\right]$$

Sentences shorter than 5 words can't form a 5-gram, so they're matched by direct
substring containment instead.

## CLEAN — precision

Fraction of what we emitted that actually exists in gold:

$$\text{CLEAN} = \frac{|S(P) \cap S(G)|}{|S(P)|}$$

## FIDELITY — the headline

F-score of the two, with **recall weighted twice as heavily** as precision
($\beta^2 = 2$), because dropping content is worse than keeping extra:

$$\text{FIDELITY} = \frac{(1+\beta^2)\cdot \text{CLEAN} \cdot \text{KEPT}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}} = \frac{3\cdot \text{CLEAN}\cdot \text{KEPT}}{2\cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}}$$

The same construction gives **CODE**, **MATH**, **TABLE** and **WHO** — identical
to KEPT, but with $U(G)$ replaced by gold's code lines, math expressions, table
cells, or speaker names.




Overall I think our new spec is better but it wasn't as easy to hill climb this as I had hoped.

# Weekly Sync 8/3 - 8/7 ---
Extraction Unit Tests Ran some other benchmarks: Pretty universally it seems like we get way higher recall but lose on precision. HOWEVER I looked into these benchmarks and they reward things like removing titles, authors, copyright info, and comments sections which are all things I deliberately chose to KEEP in the document, so we can either remove copyrightten documents or include interesting discussion about articles. This is not to say that we don't incidentally extract some stuff that is genuine garbage. Sometimes author bios for articles end up being advertisements for something that person wants to sell you, sometimes related articles are not that useful (however sometimes related questions end up being a nice QA style chunk of questions AND their answers so it is an edge case). On our own unit tests we look pretty good. The unit tests are comprised of domain specific evals. 13 code, 10 math, 9 tables, 29 prose, 12 attribution, 5 structure, 24 negative. ---

The Problem with DCLM Core DCLM Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/dc5f1cf5-eb62-4c99-9e2f-70472b28797e OLMO Disaggregated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ce4e61f6-f3e9-433b-ae76-805a12015ee5 DCLM Core is super noisy. Some are higher signal (basically hellaswag), and with mixing we can improve over Hellaswag: But many **many** are just noise, and no sense of trying to win on them at this scale: In contrast OLMO bpb seems to be pretty high signal: Although there are some that are still noisy here too: My thought: **maybe we forget about DCLM Core and showcase wins on OLMO Base Easy instead at least for spec-driven project at smaller scale** This is where we already win, no new specs, no mixing needed!

Plan **Experiment Idea**: Scale everything down by 20x. So instead of a 100B model we are training a 5B, and instead of nemotron producing 7T tokes we sample 350B tokens. And instead of a 2T token target or similar we have a 200B token target. Once I extract 5% of the internet I will have about 3-4T tokens or so. We would be comparing 350B tokens of nemotron to 2T tokens of my data, on a 200B token target for a 5B model. We can do whatever data mixing we choose but at the end of the day we need to find the best 200B tokens to train that 5B model. # Weekly Sync 8/31-9/4 ---
"Hero" Data Curation Run Progress We currently have about 10T tokens of pre-dedupe data processed! This will be significantly lower after dedupe, but dedupe alone now takes many hours (days?) to run, so I don't have timely feedback about how much data we have post-dedupe. **Updated this morning:**
> [!TIP] > The run is about 15% of the way through and will finish in the next 2 weeks if I don't steal my compute for other experiments. ---
More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.
> [!TIP] > The distilled pipeline is projected to take about 5e21 flops to run on the full 8M WARC files. > The previous 8B model running on all of the internet was projected to take between 3e25 and 1.8e26 flops depending on if I used the pipeline version or the single call spec. > The fact that it is taking a month is likely somewhat due to poor MFU ---
Updated Main Results from Mixing
> [!TIP] > Finally showing signs of how the "more data" really helps at scale (100B+ tokens) ---
Beta Paper Outline Old Paper: https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4 New Paper (extremely preliminary for now, will auto-update here): https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 **Introduction:** Something about how we should spend way more compute on data curation but it doesn't need to be more complicated. **Background**: Current data curation pipelines including data mixing **Method**: Spec-Driven Curation, as well as the distillation into FastText, Pooled Transformer, and Ettin68 (modernBERT) **Swapping the spec enables control of the data distribution**: We show different specs lead to expected changes in data downstream
Plots
We then argue that because of the mixing and the growing demand for tokens we opt to use the coverage spec. **Spec-Driven Curation Yields Bigger and Better Data**: We show that by using our high coverage spec distilled pipeline we get more data and can mix it to be better at many domains.
Plots **Bigger**: Everything else bends upwards, but we can train on 100B+ tokens from just 10k WARCs. If we 800x (which is a bad way to do this bc no accounting for dedup), then we should be able to train on 80T tokens without issue. **Better Coverage**: We can mix for several downstream target capabilities.
**Ablations**: When we remove parts of the system how much does it impact performance. All ablations will be done on the olmo base easy eval set.
Plots **THESE ARE JUST STAND IN PLOTS, I HAVE TO RUN THESE EXPERIMENTS:** **Original Resiliparse vs Our "AutoResearch" Resiliparse**: **Spec for Quality ("High Quality") vs Spec for Coverage ("High Coverage")**: **Distilled Pipeline into Classifiers vs Original**: **Mixing vs No Mixing**:
**Discussion**: Scaling this up to the full internet **Conclusion**: Invest more flops into the pretraining data curation.
> [!TIP] > I tore apart the old paper but tried to keep the focus around the spec-driven idea. Interested to discuss if this is the right framing :) ---

Rescraper on GPU ### Hallucination | Method | Pages | Major ↓ | Med ↓ | Minor ↓ | Spacing Errors | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | **Rule-Based Extraction** | | | | | | | Trafilatura | 1,000 | 0.0% | 1.3% | 0.7% | 11.5% | | Resiliparse | 1,000 | 0.0% | 1.9% | 1.9% | 13.6% | | GC Cascade | 1,000 | 0.1% | 3.1% | 1.7% | 17.8% | | **LLM-Based Extraction** | | | | | | | Qwen3-8B Distill | 1,000 | 1.6% | 5.4% | 8.5% | 4.0% | | GPT-OSS-120B | 1,000 | 2.0% | 7.1% | 7.3% | 5.4% | | GLM-5.3 | 1,000 | 0.3% | 2.9% | 2.2% | 1.9% | | **LLM-Based Scraping and Cleaning** | | | | | | | ReScraper (Qwen3-0.6B), full | 1,000 | 2.4% | 4.3% | 3.7% | 5.2% | | ReScraper, non-rewrite pages (`` + ``) | 874 | 0.3% | 1.9% | 1.7% | 5.8% | | ReScraper, rewrite pages (``) | 34 | 61.8% | 76.5% | 64.7% | 2.9% | Comparison: https://claude.ai/artifact/3LqZrupWBLkCw2dVtQ1pkv Hallucinations: https://claude.ai/artifact/BuQKeKP5s31kSD89cSfy9U ### Diversity | Method | SRS on ReScraper's 906 kept pages | |---|---:| | Trafilatura | 2.40 ± 0.20 (n=905) | | Resiliparse | 3.04 ± 0.18 (n=906) | | GC Cascade | 2.74 ± 0.20 (n=906) | | Qwen3-8B SFT | 2.64 ± 0.20 (n=906) | | GPT-OSS-120B | 2.50 ± 0.20 (n=906) | | GLM-5.3 | 2.65 ± 0.20 (n=905) | | ReScraper (Qwen3-0.6B) | 2.28 ± 0.21 (n=906) |
> [!TIP] > Turns out most of the atrocious performance we were seeing is attributed to the vllm-tpu bug (discussed below) but `rewrite` pages do have a high rate of hallucination still. ---
Why do TPU and GPU differ? RoPE bug in vllm-tpu version :( Our TPU inference stack (vLLM + Google's `tpu-inference`) has two ways to run a model: a JAX re-implementation of each architecture (the default for dense Qwen3, Qwen2, Llama) and a path that runs vLLM's PyTorch model definition through torchax. The JAX Qwen3 implementation reads the model's RoPE settings from the Hugging Face config like this: ```python self.rope_scaling = getattr(config, "rope_scaling", None) ... if rope_scaling: # truthy dict -> apply Llama-3 long-context scaling timescale = apply_rope_scaling(timescale, rope_scaling) ``` With transformers 4.x, a model that uses no RoPE scaling (Qwen3's `config.json` says `"rope_scaling": null`) returned `None` here, and nothing happened. transformers 5 changed the API: `config.rope_scaling` is now an alias of `rope_parameters` and returns `{"rope_type": "default", "rope_theta": 1000000}`. That dict is truthy, so the JAX port started applying `apply_rope_scaling`, which never checks `rope_type` and uses hard-coded Llama-3 defaults (scale 8, cutoffs at 2k and 8k tokens). Result: 37 of Qwen3's 64 RoPE frequency bands were rewritten, the lowest divided by 8. The model's sense of position was wrong at every token, and worse the farther apart two tokens were, so long documents suffered most. ### Timeline - **2026-06-12** tpu-inference cuts `releases/v0.23.0`; the bug is latent (it needs transformers 5). - **2026-06-26** Google fixes it on `main` (PR #2838, "Get the right rope_scaling values from config"); the fix ships in v0.24.0 and later, never in v0.23.0. - **2026-06-29** Marin `main` migrates to transformers 5 (#6735) while every tpu-inference pin from 06-17 to 08-13 is v0.23.0-based, so `main` is broken for every dense model on the default JAX path. - **2026-08-13 11:39 PT** `main` auto-refreshes the stack to v0.26.0 (#8207) and is fixed, by accident. - **My checkout** tracked `main` as of 05-06 (transformers 4.57.5, tpu-inference 0.18.0 fork) until the parity sync on **2026-08-13 13:54 ET**, which landed 11 commits before #8207. With transformers 4 the config reports `rope_scaling = None` and the scaling branch never runs, so the lpv11 10k extraction (late July to ~Aug 20), the 3,000-WARC llm_pipeline_v1 run and all distillation data gathered by Aug 12 were produced on a correct model. Being behind `main` skipped the broken window entirely. - **after the sync, from the same checkout** (transformers 5.12.1 + the v0.23.0-based `e8809d49` pin): the lpv11 gap-fill (12 re-extracted WARCs, 09-01 to 09-04), WebMainBench 7,809 (09-19), the devset "lpv11 direct" reruns, classifier logprob scoring, and all ReScraper TPU runs (late Sept to 10-12): broken port. Any 10k-extraction worker relaunched after 08-13 13:54 ET would also have picked up the new lock; the tail of that run (~Aug 13-20) should be checked against the job logs. - **2026-10-13** root-caused and confirmed. Reruns on the correct path are in progress. ### Something nice we know (more easily) because of this GitHub issue log **FROM AUGUST 12th THE DAY BEFORE** So 7k WARC files were processed properly. The last 3k may be corrupted by this. All of our distillation data for the cascade came from an uncorrupted version. **I AM RUNNING SOME EXPERIMENTS NOW AND TRYING TO DETERMINE HOW SERIOUSLY THIS IMPACTS RESULTS**
> [!TIP] > A bug impacted RoPE embeddings on vllm-tpu. This only impacted us after August 13th so the damage is somewhat contained. Doing a deeper analysis of what this fully impacts. ---
Updated Ablation Plots
> [!TIP] > Better presentation of our filter and extractor ablations. ---
Investigating Filter Disagreements Artifact: https://claude.ai/artifact/6dJ1HuoXNyofFeJhbXwdbM My general sense: Although I prompted the LLM against keeping docs like this (and on average it drops them) there are edge cases where long lists make it through, and these are not high quality training docs: **ONLY LLM KEEPS** **ONLY CASCADE KEEPS** The cascade has a few of these too: Clear that the LLM noise drops some good docs that the cascade keeps: === Extraction Differences === Less clear why the rule based is better for extraction... If anything I like a lot of the LLM extractions better. Might be the hallucination problem especially for the last 3000 WARC files with the tpu-inference bug. Extractions Viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/DvebZUJJy3w3647QzArytD
> [!TIP] > Investigated qualitatively why the cascade is better. Some clear cut cases for the filtering, but the LLM extraction really does seem better, so it is a bit odd that the cascade extraction seems so much better on downstream benchmarks after you train the model. ---

## Weekly Sync 10/19 - 10/23 **Agenda:** - Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data - Deduplication details - Decontamination plan - Release Plan ---
Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data Last week's worry: the last ~3k WARCs of the lpv11 10k extraction might have run with the vllm-tpu RoPE bug. **They did not. No LLM data we use was affected.** **Why:** the bug lives in tpu-inference's JAX re-implementation of Qwen3. Our Qwen3-8B extractor loads from a `gs://` checkpoint through the runai streamer, and the JAX Qwen3 port has no streaming weight loader, so vLLM's `auto` setting resolves to the PyTorch-via-torchax path, which is correct. **Only models loaded from the HF cache or local disk took the JAX path. In our work that was only ReScraper.** **Verified three ways:** - Code path and old job logs: every Qwen3-8B run used the torchax path (lpv11 10k extraction, gap-fill, WebMainBench 7,809, devset, classifier scoring). - Reruns with the implementation pinned to torchax: devset 99.8% decision agreement; WebMainBench shard 00 F1 .6400 vs .6422; 1k lpv11 pages 626/975 byte-identical, median similarity 0.994 on the rest. - Quality unchanged on the 1k rerun: major hallucinations 1.1% vs 1.6%, within judge noise (51 vs 52 flagged on identical pages); SRS 2.64 vs 2.66. **The 8M hero data runs no LLM at inference time:** it is resiliparse-rs extraction, then a fastText gate, then a ModernBERT classifier. The LLM only produced the distillation labels, and those came from the correct path.
> [!TIP] > False alarm for our data: only ReScraper (loaded from local disk) hit the bug. Every Qwen3-8B extraction ran on the correct path, which logs and reruns confirm. ---
Deduplication details | Stage | Docs | Characters | Tokens (llama3) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Extracted (8,582,115 WARCs) | 61.21B | 341.8T | ≈80.6T | | After exact dedup | 21.84B | 133.9T | ≈31.6T | | After fuzzy dedup (hero cluster method, c075) | **9.95B** | **72.7T** | **17.15T** | Characters are exact at every stage. The final token count is measured; the first two use the final corpus's 4.239 chars/token. - **17.15T llama3 tokens** (72.7T chars, 26.5 TB). The refit after the 2M run projected 16.9T (15.7–18.9T); the projections made at 500k (21.8–25.0T) were too high. - 64% of extracted records were exact duplicates, confirmed to be the same pages recrawled across crawls. - By source: **CC-MAIN 16.68T**, **CC-NEWS 0.21T** (tagged `CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM`, so it can be mixed separately), **CC-SUPPLEMENTAL 7.8B**. - Random-sample viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/9Wp8sdhFwC7xmRqz74ddpx
> [!TIP] > Dedup is done: **17.15T tokens** from 8.58M WARCs, in line with the post-2M projection. The hero run used ~25T. ---
Decontamination plan Full walkthrough with examples: https://claude.ai/artifact/FPrunN93nfrApC6j4hcgSN **How Marin's decon works.** Take the test questions and answers from every benchmark we report (the 9 Artificial Analysis benchmarks plus the lm-eval tasks in Marin's eval suite). Split each training doc into paragraphs. If at least half of a paragraph's 13-word runs also appear in the eval text, the doc is removed. Phrases that are common all over the web are ignored, so boilerplate can't trigger a removal. The version the hero run used (v3) adds one more check for short paragraphs (3–12 words), which are too short to contain a 13-word run: a short paragraph that exactly matches a short line from the evals also removes the doc. That check is meant to catch short eval answers, but it also matches ordinary lines like "2 years ago" or "Lana Del Rey". Marin changed this after the hero run (v4, PR #8327, Sept 24): a paragraph now needs at least two different eval phrases in it to count, so a single short line can't remove a doc by itself. **Where we are.** Every doc in the pool has been checked. Picking a rule now just means one ~3 h filter run, then an ~18 h re-tokenize. **Tokens each rule would remove** (estimated from a 24k-doc audit sample): | Rule | Eval set | Docs removed | Tokens removed | |---|---|---:|---:| | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's + 118 tasks the hero failed to load | ~11M | ~87B (0.5%) | | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's | ~5M | ~40B (0.23%) | | v4 (Marin `main` today) | hero's + 118 tasks | ~0.46M | ~8B (0.05%) | The two v3 numbers will drop somewhat: I'm re-running the boilerplate count with the hero's sample size (1M docs per crawl; my first pass used ~80k). **Problems with the hero run's decon:** 1. **gsm8k was probably never checked.** 118 of the lm-eval tasks, including gsm8k, truthfulqa, winogrande, boolq and triviaqa, failed to load in the hero's eval set because their old dataset names break with the `datasets` version the hero branch uses. The pipeline skips tasks that fail to load instead of stopping. This is based on the eval set's manifest in us-central2. **Not yet checked against the CoreWeave copy that production actually used.** 2. **The short-line check mostly removes harmless pages.** On our data, ~95% of v3 removals come from a single short line like "2 years ago" or "Mechanism of Action", and none of the 40 I read by hand were contamination. Our extracted text has lots of standalone short lines (96% of docs have one, against 25–77% in Nemotron-CC), so this hits us harder than it hit the hero data. v4 fixes the second problem. On the audit sample it still caught every real overlap we found (SQuAD passages, wikiHow/HellaSwag, MATH problems, paper abstracts) and only let through stray short phrases and two generic LSAT question stems. **Decisions:** 1. **Eval set:** add the 118 tasks the hero missed? 2. **Rule:** v3 (~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages) or v4 (~8B tokens, same real catches)? 3. **ACTION ITEM:** Check with Will about the potential GSM8K gap in decontamination
> [!TIP] > Every doc has been checked against the evals. The hero run's rule (v3) would remove ~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages; Marin's current rule (v4) removes ~8B with the same real catches. The hero run also perhaps checked 117 fewer tasks. ---
Release Plan **Need to run the embedding and scaling ladder**: Reached out to Will to discuss this. I have all my data in `us-central2` ready to run a scaling ladder! Just want to figure out pointers on what to run and if I need to do control against Nemotron or if that has already been run somewhere. **Otherwise after decontamination the data is ready to go!**
> [!TIP] > After decontamination we are ready to release! ---

## Weekly Sync 10/26 - 10/30 **Agenda:** - Decontamination Conclusion - Discussions with CCF - Release Timeline ---
Decontamination Conclusion Artifact Viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/35vPM8xar7mPgConPqKtkY Our investigation turned up that it seems several datasets were not fully decontaminated in the marin data. In our direct message discussions we determined that we should decontaminate against: **lm_eval, AAII, Paloma, Uncheatable Eval, and LIMA**. Last week I reported that decontamination with Marin's Rules would remove 8B tokens. Actually running it for benchmarks only removed 3B tokens. Adding in Paloma, Uncheatable and LIMA originally brought this up to 20B tokens. (Note these datasets are just 66M tokens - mostly Paloma). **REMINDER:** The Marin Decontamination rule put simply - **A document is removed when any blank-line-separated paragraph has at least half of its 13-gram phrases** (every overlapping 13-gram window, excluding common _**boilerplate phrases**_ and phrases with no letters) **found in an eval set, with at least two different phrases matching**, or when the whole document is a single matching 3–12-word line, or has only one usable phrase and it matches. **What counts as boilerplate?** a phrase counted as boilerplate (and was ignored in matching) if it appeared in at least 0.5% of the first 5,000 docs of any single crawl, or in at least 50 docs across at least 3 crawls within a sample of the first 1M docs per crawl. I noticed some problems with decontaminating against document-level based evals which we weren't seeing from the benchmark evals: Code is really impacted by this!! TWO REASONS: - Comments - Imports Comments vary from language to language. People paste license text into files, but the comment style matches the language that they are writing the code in. So sometimes this license text is not marked as boilerplate simply because of a few comment characters that break the count. Imports are fairly ubiquitous in a given language HOWEVER, the order of imports is not something consistent. Since there is exponentially many orderings to reasonably import your files certain import orders are never marked as boilerplate. **We were discarding a lot of useful code data!** To fix this I did something simple. I am not super satisfied with this but feels like this is a reasonable action given we don't want to launch a whole new project on just fixing decontamination right now. **New rule for boilerplate:** A phrase counts as boilerplate (and is ignored in matching) if it appears in at least 0.5% of the first 5,000 docs of any single crawl, in at least 50 docs across at least 3 crawls within a sample of the first 1M docs per crawl, in at least 1,000 docs across at least 3 crawls in the full pool, **or in at least 100 files of StarCoderData.** Starcoder data is just programming data in 86 languages. My hope was that this would at least cover more of the license files and import orders even if this isn't a _complete_ solution. Ultimately with these rules we ended up removing 12B tokens. Note still most of this comes from the validation datasets (since the benchmarks removed 3B tokens) **I ran this updated version and have the data ready for upload to the Common Crawl Foundation.**
---
Discussions with Common Crawl Foundation The CCF gave me a small bucket to test sharing the data with them, and all seems to work, so just waiting to hear back from them about a larger bucket and if the file format is good. ``` Atlantic CC release format (as agreed with CCF; part/row-group sizes pending their final OK) Location: s3://commoncrawl/projects//v1.0/parquet/crawl=/part-NNNNN-of-MMMMM.parquet plus v1.0/_manifest.json (record and part counts per crawl) Versioning: v1.0 = this release; appending new crawls = v1.1; changing the pipeline/algorithm = v2.0 Crawls: one prefix per crawl (249: CC-MAIN-YYYY-WW, CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM, CC-SUPPLEMENTAL). Dedup is global, so each doc appears once, under the crawl its kept copy came from. Format: Parquet, zstd level 9, ~300 MB parts, 10k-row row groups. No JSONL. Size: 9,950,417,677 records, 87,203 parts, 22.75 TB Fields: record_id string WARC-Record-ID (UUID) of the source record url string source page URL crawl string crawl the WARC belongs to (e.g. CC-MAIN-2025-08, CC-NEWS-2016-08) warc_hash string first 12 hex chars of sha256(WARC file path) text string extracted main text (resiliparse-rs, light markdown) fasttext_score float quality stage 1 (fastText imitating the LLM filter's keep/drop decision) pooled_prob float quality stage 2 (90M pooled-transformer classifier) modernbert_prob float? quality stage 3 (Ettin-68M classifier); null if stage 2 kept the doc outright exact_copies int docs in the pre-dedup pool with identical text (1 = unique) fuzzy_cluster_size int size of the doc's near-duplicate component (~4.56B = the one giant chained component) Processing: extraction -> 3-stage quality cascade -> exact + fuzzy dedup (c075) -> decontamination (Marin v4 rule, eval set = benchmarks + Paloma + Uncheatable + LIMA; 1.35M docs / ~12B tokens removed) ```
---
Release Timeline/Ideas If I hear back from CCF folks soon I think we should **release next Monday**! I have some ideas for the release: - Twitter Thread - Website (http://atlantic-cc.org/) - Arxiv (Add ReScraper results and update Figure 2 - some spacing improvements) - Marin Blog? What would need to be done for that to be possible? Should I just do my own blog? (Perhaps this can be done in a week or two when we have the scaling ladder, this would be more Marin-specific) The blog would be more about showing data samples and intuitively explaining the data. Other interesting ideas: - Maybe we should release subsets (DCLM-400M-1x, DCLM-1B-1x, etc.) for all the people who may want to compare against our data on academic compute scales. - Release a small sample viewer anyone can view like 100 docs (maybe extra data check for legal)
---

issues.title: Spec-Driven Large-Scale Pretraining Data Curation from Common Crawl

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
Snapshot updated **27 October 2026**. Measurements span 23 September–23 October and apply to their recorded revisions. Expand sections below for configs, run IDs and evidence; comments retain the experiment history.

## At a glance

- **4K RL:** With captured-route replay, Hero passed the recorded gate and gained **+4.6 / +5.5 GSM8K percentage points** on H100 / GB200 after 64 updates. Optimizer restore and continuation passed on both. See C1.
- **65K training:** Full Hero completed updates on **192 H100s with MuonH/AdamH/Adam**, and **64 GB200s with AdamW**. Workloads and layouts differ. See P1/C2.
- **Long-context serving:** Requests reached **256K on 64 H100s or 16 GB200s**, with one- or 64-token outputs. Sustained long-response throughput remains unmeasured. See P4.
- **Numerical limits:** Batch-dependent learner scores and gradients remain. PP48/EP4/CP4 replay reduced measured order sensitivity at **5.3% median scoring-plus-update cost**. Serving–trainer differences persist. See P5.

## Serving: supplied 4K workload

BF16, TP1, non-eager batch-invariant vLLM, continuously supplied by replacement clients. Mean lengths are **149 prompt tokens / 767 generated tokens**, with a **4,096-token combined cap**. Rates count generated tokens while prefill shares the GPUs. See P2.

| Model | Hardware | GPUs | Clients | Generated tok/s | Tok/s/GPU | KV preemptions |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 32 | 1,280 | **5,243** | 164 | 120 |
| Hero | GB200 | 16 | 3,072 | **9,142** | 571 | 0 |
| Snowball | H100 | 8 | 4,096 | 32,967 | 4,121 | 0 |
| Snowball | GB200 | 16 | 4,096 | 29,354 | 1,835 | 0 |

Engine limits and sharding differ. **36.6K tok/s per 64-GB200 rack is a linear projection**, not a rack measurement.

## Whole asynchronous RL: 4K GSM8K

Rates count **accepted, loss-masked response tokens** over warm cycles, including wait, scoring, updates and publication; evaluation/checkpoints are excluded. Batches and responses differ. See P3.

| Model | Hardware | Learner GPUs | Serving GPUs | Staleness limit | Accepted tok/s |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 128 | 32 | 1 | **2,266** |
| Hero | H100 | 192 | 32 | 1 | **1,981** |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 8 | 1 | **75.5** |
| Hero, expert-block publication diagnostic | GB200 | 48 | 8 | 2 | **153.1** |
| Snowball | H100 | 32 | 8 | 1 | 5,743 |

Staleness two is outside the original qualification. H100 timing includes diagnostic weight-readback overhead. These are observed system rates, not model-only speed ratios.

## Remaining limits

- **Long responses:** Sustained long-response serving, >4K RL correctness and post-cooldown/SFT coding remain unmeasured.
- **Sizing:** Minimum/optimal fleets and a universal Snowball→Hero multiplier remain unproved. Exact 192+64 H100 online execution was not measured.
- **Integration:** Later PR ports and current `main` require their own qualification. FP8 is out of scope.

<details>
<summary>C1 — 4K correctness, learning and restore evidence</summary>

The accepted 4K rule requires at least 50,000 independent response tokens per platform, fewer than 0.1% of same-token trainer/serving probability ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]` at fixed weights, and actual PPO clipping below 1% per normal update. It is an empirical acceptance rule, not exact equality or a bound for every future batch.

| Hardware | Ratio outliers / tokens | GSM8K correct, version 0 → 64 | Step-32 restore → 64 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H100 | 6 / 50,059 | 563 → 610 / 1,024 | Passed |
| GB200 | 5 / 54,090 | 569 → 625 / 1,024 | Passed |

The H100 numerical point is from a separate integrated run, not its learning continuation. Both learning runs used the permanent step-144000 BF16 export, eight responses per group, at most 4,096 combined tokens, non-eager batch-invariant vLLM, captured-route replay, fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam at `1e-6`, frozen query-balancing bias and staleness at most one. Resuming restored the RL optimizer state. One training seed per accelerator was tested.

The paired 95% question-bootstrap intervals for held-out gains are **+2.54 to +6.64 points** on H100 and **+3.61 to +7.32** on GB200. They exclude training-seed variation. Strict `#### number` rewards were independently recomputed from 12,288 retained evaluation responses; the parser can reject correct answers in other formats. Repeated same-checkpoint evaluations changed three answers per platform.

- [Numerical decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299979623); [complete step-64 learning and restore audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299981395).
- H100 learning: `/romain/hero-learning-h100-01a0dca4-a6`, 128 learners + 24 servers, TP1/PP16/EP8/CP2, SkyRL `ff03e83baa0624144cdeb9944b72f96813468045`.
- GB200 learning: `/romain/hero-learning-gb200-01a0dca4-a3`, 48 learners + 16 servers, TP1/PP12/EP4/CP4, SkyRL `d9c9997ea13c314fd2ddd2c698b8d2d50320e2a0`.
- vLLM source for both: `25f0fc1aae71cccb6da65046cff13145512a6946`.
- H100 reward manifest: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/analysis/h100-step64-rewards-20260927/manifest.json`.
- GB200 reward manifest: `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-learning-01a0dca4/analysis/gb200-final64-20260927/manifest.json`.

Later P5 tests address additional batch/gradient sensitivity. They do not expand these historical 4K gates to 65K, every batch shape, another task or current `main`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P1 — learner-only measurements, 65K fit and later performance fixes</summary>

**Short fixed bank.** Each update uses 128 sequences containing 19,327 prompt plus 97,024 response tokens: 116,351 nonpadding tokens, maximum combined length 4,041. Bank SHA256 `6d97026e4235babacdfe1d04d4e53d9e7deef4c68e1c96a6be73a12ced09c896`. Rates exclude scoring, serving and checkpointing. Hero uses fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam; Snowball uses AdamW.

| Model | Hardware | Learner GPUs | PP / EP / CP | Seconds/update | Sequence tok/s/GPU |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 96 | 24 / 4 / 1 | 19.97 | 60.7 |
| Hero | H100 | 128 | 16 / 8 / 2 | 18.54 | 49.0 |
| Snowball | H100 | 32 | 2 / 8 / 1 | 5.57 | 653 |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 12 / 4 / 4 | 60.36 | 40.2 |
| Hero | GB200 | 64 | 16 / 4 / 4 | 52.13 | 34.9 |
| Snowball | GB200 | 16 | 2 / 8 / 1 | 10.45 | 696 |
| Snowball | GB200 | 32 | — | 6.16 | 590 |

These are efficient tested points, not physical minima. Increasing Hero GB200 learners 48→64 cuts update time 13.6% but adds 15.1% GPU-seconds/update. Same-bank learner GPU-time ratios are **10.76× for Hero96/Snowball32 H100s** and **17.32× for Hero48/Snowball16 GB200s**; optimizer and layout differences are included.

H100 jobs: `/romain/hero-learner-h100-96g-01a0dca4-a2` and `/romain/snowball-learner-h100-32g-01a0dca4-a1`, sources `80907a6d` and `fa705954`. GB200 source `ca91727c`; jobs `/romain/hero-gb200-learner-48g-01a0e406-a1` and `/romain/gb200-snowball-learner-16g-01a0e406-a1`. [Hero GB200 comparison][gb-learner]; [Snowball GB200 comparison][snow-learner]. The short-bank active-FLOP estimates exclude recomputation/optimizer/communication; they are not measured device utilization.

**65K fit on 192 H100s.** The October 1 run used fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam, TP1/PP24/EP8/CP4, dense DP2, microbatch one and batch = mini-batch = 32. Each update processed 2,097,152 nonpadding sequence tokens with 8,072 loss positions. Muon momentum was offloaded to CPU, with FP32 masters/gradients and full recomputation.

- Warm update median **59.94 s**; scoring median **19.06 s**. Peak warm CUDA allocation/reservation **72.54/74.57 GiB per GPU**; lifetime host cgroup peak **217.97 GiB/node**.
- Save **998.42 s**, restore **595.93 s**, normal post-restore update **63.84 s**. A diagnostic reloaded identical full model/buffer and optimizer/master hashes on all ranks. Subsequent updates were finite but **not byte-identical**; their discrepancy was not quantified by that run.
- Jobs `/romain/hero-h100-65k-192-01a0f44c-a3` and `/romain/hero-h100-restore-192-01a0f44c-a1`, producers `1cdd283f` and `d5352c14`. [Timing/memory analysis][h100-fit]; [restore analysis][h100-restore]; [source/config provenance][h100-provenance].

**Later full-token comparison, October 14–15.** At batch 96 on 192 H100s, Megatron shared dispatch took **93.77 s/update** versus **118.12 s** for Levanter, or 26.0% more nonpadding tokens/s. All 65,535 valid next-token predictions per row carry loss. Megatron batch 384 reached **89,371 sequence tok/s**, with **8.31% estimated common MFU**. These use fresh states, native routing, no replay and different viable layouts. They are separate from the response-masked RL-shaped timings above. [Full comparison, common MFU formula, raw evidence and precision limits](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/1009).

**Later RL-shaped tuning, October 17–23.** All rows below are 192-H100 learner measurements. Each sequence has 65,536 nonpadding tokens and a short loss window. Rows from different studies are not one controlled speedup chain.

| Paired change | Observed result | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Training NCCL cap 1 → 8, batch 32 | Update **50.74 → 29.08 s**; scoring **16.05 → 11.16 s** | Same fresh workload; training update time −42.7%. Broadcast publication keeps its serving settings. |
| Batch 32/device saves → batch 64/pinned CPU saves | Update **29.87 → 45.00 s**, twice the sequence tokens; **365.7 → 485.5 sequence tok/s/GPU (+32.8%)** | Ten warm samples per arm; fresh-weight throughput. Trained memory confirmation retained 4.60 GiB sampled GPU headroom; trained throughput was not benchmarked. |
| PP24/EP8 replay → PP48/EP4 replay, 256 sequence rows | Scoring + update **177.90 → 187.39 s (+5.3%)** | Three synthetic input families; traded some learner performance for lower measured order sensitivity. See P5. |

Eight-channel sampled whole-device memory rose from 71.00 to 74.40 GiB in the first pair. Automatic channel selection later OOMed on update two; its eight-channel control completed eight updates, with six warm samples at **29.29 s/update**. No warmed automatic result exists.

The eight-channel option is qualified with broadcast publication. The separate `expert_block` transport requires the inherited channel setting or a cap of one; its combination with the override has not been qualified. PP, EP and CP denote pipeline, expert and context parallelism.

- [Channel timing and exact config][nccl-timing]; [trained one/eight comparison][nccl-numerics]; [automatic-selection report][nccl-auto]. Related port: [Marin #10368](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10368).
- [Batch-64 evidence archive][batch64-archive], including `HERO65K-BATCH64-FINDINGS-ADDENDUM.txt`, `HERO65K-BATCH64-RECIPE.json` and the paired analyses. Archive SHA256 `06e75f212ae122e43aedf7d3a6f0793376d23dcafaa4253c87ff63a91b325f94`. It records exact copies, producer revisions, timings and numerical limits. Related port: [Marin #10376](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10376).
- [October 23 numerical findings and PP48 recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6379516756).

No whole-RL speedup or new learning curve is established by these learner-only tuning studies.

</details>

<details>
<summary>C2 — earlier 32K/65K AdamW capacity and checkpoint baseline</summary>

Full Hero at the step-108000 BF16 export completed repeated synthetic AdamW updates, checkpoint save/restore and a bitwise-matching next update. Both layouts used context parallelism four, activation recomputation and CPU optimizer offload. These are historical AdamW results; the later 192-H100 MuonH result is in P1.

| Hardware | GPUs / hosts | 32K → 65K peak PyTorch allocation, GiB/GPU | 65K warm updates, s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H100 | 256 / 32 | 38.34 → 63.15 | 42.46 / 41.78 |
| GB200 | 64 / 16 | 138.26 → 154.02 | 22.65 / 22.74 |

Different sharding and optimizer-offload fractions prevent a controlled hardware comparison. PyTorch peaks omit other CUDA allocations. Neither run used vLLM or established long-context RL quality.

H100 job `/romain/hero-megatron-full-h100-01a0bca4-a10`, source `d386f521`; GB200 job `/romain/hero-megatron-full-gb200-01a0bca4-a6`, source `7dc88a2b`. [Original report and exact configurations](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/e3f5fff039f9b965d3f014584f8abd34164c0381/docs/grug-megatron-training.md#full-hero-capacity). Raw reports remain under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-megatron-01a0bca4/full-h100-a10/report.json` and `.../full-gb200-a6/report.json`.

Experimental checkpoint objects from these capacity runs were later retired. Reports preserve the measurements; exact resume requires a retained checkpoint or rerunning the producer.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P2 — serving load curves, cache pressure and hardware comparison</summary>

The 1,024-row forced-length GSM8K bank has SHA256 `b15aeac7c3eb714fe45fc6b8e274342ad26f00970d84f2b7985b42c422b4e905`. Each selected point runs at least four client waves. Rates come from native token-counter deltas during a supplied window before final drain; they are neither pure decode-kernel capacity nor whole-bank completion rates. The engines use BF16, TP1, batch-invariant non-eager vLLM `25f0fc1a`, a 4,096-position cap, `max_num_batched_tokens=512` and prefix caching off. Hero H100 uses DP/EP32; Hero GB200 uses DP/EP16, with PP1.

| Hero layout | Clients | Max sequences/engine | Supplied generated tok/s | KV preemptions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 H100 | 768 | 64 | 3,558 | 0 |
| 32 H100 | 1,024 | 64 | 4,558 | 10 |
| 32 H100 | 1,280 | 64 | 5,243 | 120 |
| 32 H100 | 1,536 | 64 | 5,690 | 448 |
| 16 GB200, earlier setting | 1,024 | 64 | 3,492 | 0 |
| 16 GB200 | 3,072 | 256 | 9,142 | 0 |
| 16 GB200 | 4,096 | 256 | 9,960 | 218 |

The H100 1,280→1,536 step improved whole-bank rate only 1.7%, despite higher supplied decode. GB200 at 3,072 clients peaked at 88.4% sampled KV use; 4,096 reached 100%. These curves do not establish global hardware maxima. The 3.5× difference in quoted Hero tok/s/GPU includes different concurrency, caps and expert groups. At 1,024 clients and cap 64 on both fleets, the observed ratio is about 1.53× per GPU, still with different clients/GPU and sharding.

Snowball GB20016 delivered 15,879 / 22,309 / 29,354 supplied tok/s at 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,096 clients; its curve was still rising, with no preemptions at those points. Its cap was 512. The earlier Snowball H1008 point used cap 1,024. A single hardware-independent Snowball→Hero serving factor does not follow.

**Prefill and decode are recorded separately.** At the two Hero points in the opening table, the retained native histograms give:

| Mean elapsed seconds/request | 32 H100s, 1,280 clients | 16 GB200s, 3,072 clients |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Prefill | 1.17 | 0.91 |
| Decode | 166.11 | 245.30 |
| Queue | 1.57 | 3.56 |
| Time to first token | 2.95 | 4.74 |

These latency means cover the full completed banks: 5,120 H100 requests and 12,288 GB200 requests. The quoted throughput uses the earlier supplied windows. Requests overlap, and phase durations include time while other requests are served; their sums do not measure each phase's share of GPU time. Different concurrency also prevents treating these latencies as a chip-speed comparison.

The short prompts and longer answers emphasize decode; single-turn requests still require both phases. P4's long-prompt, one-token-output banks focus on prefill. Pure phase GPU time or FLOPs would require profiling.

- [Hero H100 curve][h100-serve]: `/romain/hero-h100-serve-32g-knee-01a0e406-a1`, producer `9ffb4919`, raw report SHA256 `3093ac5959d84e2f2be00fd0e5d657481e184bd53b9b392e8e364f997d159dab`.
- [Hero GB200 curve][gb-serve]: `/romain/hero-gb200-serve-16g-cap256-01a0e406-a1`, producer `dfdc80be`, raw report SHA256 `04b728f72b5dd8a67b19efb4b4c884d5c525da531685e3bcc2f4cd47012c289a`.
- [Snowball GB200 curve][snow-serve]: `/romain/gb200-snowball-serve-16g-01a0e406-a1`, producer `9ffb4919`, raw report SHA256 `f9b73d0d02244dbc07ea27aa36b6d7b1a2c7a1c0cc41212da5206fea1df0fe40`.
- Raw run prefixes: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-serve-32g-knee-a1/` and `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/` for the GB200 runs.
- [Prefix-cache comparison][prefix]: short repeated prompts produced 30–34% input-token hits, but after-pause whole-bank rates were 755.78 OFF versus 755.51 ON response tok/s. This provides no general recommendation to disable prefix caching for long or multi-turn workloads.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P3 — async supply, publication and server-count experiments</summary>

Eight completions form one group. Generation overlaps training. A learner still needs a complete eligible batch, and group tails, staleness limits and publication pauses can leave GPUs waiting. More standalone serving capacity does not guarantee more accepted training tokens.

**H100, October 1.** Hold 192 learners fixed and vary serving GPUs. Each update consumes 512 prompt groups × eight responses; staleness one, 512 group leases, a 1,024 untrained-group cap and four warm cycles (updates 2–5).

| Serving GPUs | Total GPUs | Accepted response tok/s | Total warm response wait, s | GPU-seconds/accepted token |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 24 | 216 | 1,357 | 2,064 | 0.1591 |
| 32 | 224 | 1,981 | 377 | 0.1131 |
| 48 | 240 | 1,937 | 525 | 0.1239 |

Twenty-four servers had heavy KV pressure (20,115 KV preemptions). At 32, 99 stable training/publication snapshots had empty engine queues and a complete future batch: the admission cap had removed available inference work. Forty-eight did not improve the observed rate. Responses were sampled independently; this does not prove that adding servers intrinsically slows serving.

A 192+32 staleness-two control increased the untrained-group cap 1,024→1,536: warm wait fell **376.61→2.73 s**, and accepted rate rose **1,981→2,195 tok/s**. Longer learning behavior was untested. The nearby 128+32 staleness-one run reached **2,265.78 tok/s**; its 65K learner fit was not tested.

Publication timing includes roughly 128–140 seconds of diagnostic readback per cycle. A readback-free production rate is unmeasured. [Matched 24/32/48 comparison][h100-online]; [128+32 window][h100-online128]; [staleness-two window][h100-stale2]; [provenance and exact Iris IDs][h100-provenance]. Producers `5fcaaa3f`, `9f481a0e`; vLLM `25f0fc1a`. The exact 192+64 job did not execute because its 32-node request exceeded the then-schedulable East capacity.

**GB200, September 27–29.** The original 48+16 run spent **57.9%** of ordinary warm time waiting for response groups and **28.3%** in publication. This was an online admission/group-tail problem at low engine load, not evidence of a saturated decode kernel.

| 48 learners + 8 servers | Staleness limit | Accepted tokens | Warm wall time, s | Accepted tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Broadcast control | 1 | 161,495 | 2,140.12 | 75.46 |
| Larger admission window + broadcast | 2 | 161,621 | 1,804.63 | 89.56 |
| Larger admission window + expert-block publication | 2 | 170,418 | 1,113.45 | 153.05 |

The first change also increases workers and the completed-group buffer, so its +18.7% result does not isolate staleness. The expert-block comparison holds config fixed except transport and run identity: four-step publication fell **737.93→117.27 s**. Different sampled responses yielded 5.44% more accepted tokens, so the observed +70.9% end-to-end rate is not a pure transport speedup. Publication includes alignment/drain work as well as byte transfer. The larger admission window and expert-block path were not combined with the later H100 NCCL/offload recipes.

[Transport comparison][gb-publication]; [separate full receiver-byte/replica replay][gb-full-replay]. Trial producer `e2695759`, final report SHA256 `d3eab5bdde398985bb49f5c1775c8c096debd71d25fd10e9bb2c1e776884d346`. The separate replay succeeded at `97bae9fb`, report SHA256 `ca5c3022ecf6bf777a6b0bf66dc3db402e0428bd57350a84337b9f6921fdf65e`. Exact jobs: `/romain/hero-gb200-expert-block-48p8s-s2-01a0e406-a4` and `/romain/hero-gb200-expert-block-verify-48p8s-s2-01a0e406-a6`; consult the linked records for their retained report identities.

The Snowball H10032+8 row is the earlier two-update control, with 256 groups/update: `/romain/snowball-integrated-h100-01a0dca4-a3`. Its task/batch/response differences prevent a matched whole-RL model ratio.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P4 — measured long-context serving and conditional training estimates</summary>

Disposable serving configs raised HF, vLLM and rotary limits together. The permanent step-144000 export and qualified RL path retain their 4,096-position bound. Current weights were used only as a performance workload, with repeated GSM8K prompt text. There is no long-context answer-quality claim.

The table uses **one-token outputs** and includes prefill plus request overhead. Most banks use one concurrent client per serving GPU. Separate 64-token continuations passed at the displayed longer lengths; they do not measure sustained aggregate long-response decode.

| Combined length | H100 GPUs | H100 prompt tok/s/GPU | GB200 GPUs | GB200 prompt tok/s/GPU |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4K | 32 | 294 | 16 | 538 |
| 8K | 32 | 302 | 16 | 547 |
| 16K | 32 | 334 | 16 | 445 |
| 32K | 32 | 293 | 16 | 442 |
| 64K | 32 | 329 | 16 | 530 |
| 128K | 32 | 268 | 16 | 506 |
| 256K | 64, PP2 | 159 | 16 | 371 |

The 32-H100 layout had about 208K KV slots/engine, insufficient for a 256K request; 64 H100s with PP2 passed. Sixteen GB200s had about 1.13M slots/engine. At 256K, increasing GB200 clients 16→32 raised its one-token prompt rate **371→586 tok/s/GPU**, without preemptions. These finite banks are not demonstrated throughput ceilings.

Long-context decode adds attention over a growing cache. The short-output probes cannot justify a single context multiplier for 32K generated coding traces. Training also retains backward activations and uses context parallelism/recomputation; inference KV scaling cannot be applied to training memory.

For the **older fixed AdamW layouts in C2**, two measured 32K/65K points gave these conditional same-layout extrapolations:

| Fixed layout | 128K update-time scenario | 128K allocated-memory scenario | 256K update-time scenario | 256K allocated-memory scenario |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 H100 | 74–105 s | 113 GiB/GPU | 137–358 s | 212 GiB/GPU |
| 64 GB200 | 41–59 s | 186 GiB/GPU | 76–202 s | 249 GiB/GPU |

These are arithmetic scenarios with unchanged sharding/offload, not runnable configurations. Their memory projections exceed hardware HBM. They do not describe the later MuonH/offload recipes or prove minimum GPU counts at 128K/256K.

- [H100 64K/128K][h100-long]: `/romain/hero-h100-long-32g-128k-01a0e406-a1`, source `1e0f0571`, raw SHA256 `4d98a3c024438dc84a2dc971fd4fede729ece41d2097d0a272b03aba4a505788`.
- [H100 256K PP2][h100-256]: `/romain/hero-h100-long-64g-256k-pp2-01a0e406-a2`, source `78489524`, raw SHA256 `f66944e7c639c95f20c094a62acbc3116e07edd98fa2f2a56e973f0741104e92`.
- [GB200 64K–256K][gb-long]: `/romain/hero-gb200-long-16g-256k-01a0e406-a1`, source `0e4aacd8`, raw SHA256 `fcedf2cc1aa6dacf9eefec047f555b5e4d6c67cc58e91aec848efc80268ced5c`. [Higher-client 256K bank][gb-long32].
- Raw prefixes: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/h100-long-32g-128k-a1/`, `.../h100-long-64g-256k-pp2-a2/`, and `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/users/romain/hero-perf-01a0e406/gb200-long-16g-256k-a1/`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>P5 — numerical alignment versus performance: measured choices and gaps</summary>

Training–inference mismatch (TIM) compares learner and serving scores for the same tokens and weights. Batch invariance asks a different question: whether changing the other examples or execution shape changes a token's score. The batch-invariant switch alone did not establish exact learner invariance in later trained-model tests.

| Choice | Numerical observation | Measured cost or benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 recorded-route path instead of native routing | Ratio outliers **114→5 / 50,962 tokens** | **+24.1% scoring time** for the replay path including controller overhead; whole-RL cost unmeasured. |
| GB200 recorded routes instead of native routes, replay controller retained | Outliers **145→5 / 51,326** | Scoring **20.10→20.25 s**; this excludes the controller-removal saving. |
| H100 learner batch-invariant mode OFF, replay retained | Outliers **5→4 / 50,962** on the fixed short bank | Update **18.538→18.473 s**; no online learning/quality comparison. |
| GB200 learner fused → flash attention, replay retained | Outliers **5→4 / 51,326**, similar mean/tail gaps | Update **63.30→61.18 s (−3.4%)**; no paired online result. |
| GB200 NCCL publication flag bundle ON | No paired score-gap benefit was measured | Learner **59.75→63.73 s (+6.7%)**. OFF was learner-only; publication safety was not established. |
| H100 training channel cap 1 → 8 | Exact scores and expert sets in eight fixed-shape trained cases | Fresh update **50.74→29.08 s**. Both settings retained baseline cross-batch sensitivity. |
| PP24/EP8 → PP48/EP4, recorded-route replay | Reordering delta **71.96%→1.37%** in the unit-importance-coefficient gradient control | Median scoring + update **177.90→187.39 s (+5.3%)**; sampled GPU headroom **4.73→9.27 GiB**. |

The first H100 replay timing compares the complete native/no-controller path to the replay path. Holding the controller present while changing routes gives **5.251 s native versus 5.147 s replay**, so 24.1% cannot be assigned to expert selection alone. [Original controlled H100 comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299980536). [GB200 route/attention pair][gb-tim]; [GB200 NCCL pair][gb-nccl]. Disabling the complete NCCL bundle OOMed the tested 96- and 128-H100 layouts, so those arms supply no warmed OFF rate.

The later [trained one/eight channel investigation][nccl-numerics] found maximum same-prefix log-probability changes of 4.2972 at 65K when batch geometry changed, at both channel caps. Changing the cap did not fix or worsen that measured baseline. [Automatic selection][nccl-auto] OOMed on the second full-model update. Keep training communicator tuning distinct from the tested publication communicator settings; no single NCCL flag was isolated as the cause of the original publication failure.

The [October 23 PP48 study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6379516756) uses 256 graded 4K responses (64 prompt groups × four samples) with real advantages for its numerical controls, plus separate synthetic 65K timing banks. Its order statistic is **100 × `||g_shuffled − g_original||₂ / ||g_original||₂`**, over all trainable parameters, with importance coefficients held at one. The 1.37% result is near its **1.28–1.48% same-order repeat variation**; it is not ground-truth gradient accuracy or an approved learning-error threshold.

The actual configured-loss gradient differs by **7.7–7.9% relative L2** from the same-order unit-coefficient reference: `||g_actual − g_unit||₂ / ||g_unit||₂`. That reference is diagnostic. TIS was off. This study establishes neither a new learning curve nor universal batch invariance, and serving–trainer differences remain.

Batch-64 testing likewise found larger trained-model score drift than fresh-weight probes. Recorded routes reduced it but did not remove it. Keep old-score computation and training geometry aligned; do not treat trainer self-match as proof of serving alignment. The batch-64 report and PP48 recipe record their exact scopes.

Serving batch-invariance OFF and eager alternatives lack a valid same-token online performance/safety pair. [vLLM #81](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/issues/81) retains the FA4 batch-invariance/performance follow-up; no Hero FA4 speedup is established here.

</details>

🤖 **Hero 4K Megatron update (2026-09-23).** At the pinned step-108000 BF16 export, full Hero scored four prespecified H100 GSM8K captures on the same token IDs, positions, masks, and captured 48-layer routes: **15,831 response tokens**. Full-prefix `abs(log p_Megatron − log p_vLLM)` was mean **0.010696**, p99 **0.060486**, max **0.528999**. The importance ratio had **2/15,831 below 0.8**, none above 1.2; actual PPO clipping was zero under the probe’s *synthetic alternating* advantage signs. Real advantages and learning quality are unproven because all 32 saved GSM8K continuations hit the 4K cap without an exact final-answer line.

The 128-H100 retry succeeded 16/16. On one 4K backward/update, captured-route hit and executed-set match were both **1.0**, native ordered/set mismatch **0.318/0.100**, router gradient norm **0.135**, and update time **118.9 s**. All per-token Megatron scores in three route modes reproduced exactly across two independent runs. The zero trainer log ratio compares Megatron with its own rescored old-action values; it is not serving parity. No causal SkyRL defect or code fix was identified. The two largest rank-0 outliers are response indices **1,532/2,672** (prediction positions **1,661/2,801**) for the serving-path trace.

Report, raw per-token scores, resolved config, and exact producer scripts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-megatron-4k-01a0bca4/h100-128-a2/` (`report.json` SHA256 `8e17cdac1348d2ce997e0a6eec3f17df26ed3537d971575c1ef1f7bedd0a4320`). The 64-GB200 transfer check was deferred: only 48 GB200 were free cluster-wide at the final check. The larger correctness sample and sustained end-to-end RL timing in this issue remain open.

🤖 **Hero BF16 4K update (September 23).** Explicit `<|eot_id|>` stopping in the diagnostic H100 vLLM producer ended 29/32 GSM8K responses before the 4K cap; 3 still hit it. All 32 matched the earlier run token-for-token until the new stop. Eight had the required final `####` line, and five were correct. The earlier “32/32 length-capped” result came from a producer with no effective EOS (`skip_tokenizer_init=True`); it does not establish production SkyRL stopping behavior.

At the pinned step-108000 BF16 export, 128 H100s scored all 32 saved trajectories with full-prefix captured routes. The table covers **29 stopped responses, 3,334 distinct response tokens**. Gaps are absolute selected-token log-probability differences at fixed weights; the ratio count is outside `[0.8, 1.2]`.

| Same-token comparison | Mean gap | p99 | Max | Ratio count |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Megatron route replay vs sampled vLLM | 0.004997 | 0.050673 | 0.120830 | 0 |
| vLLM full-prefix prefill vs sampled vLLM | 0.011993 | 0.133770 | 0.339922 | 9 |

The three length-capped responses contributed 11,751 more tokens and two Megatron/sampled-vLLM ratios above 1.2. Same-input serving prefill changed the top token at 19/3,334 stopped positions. This is a serving execution-shape effect at the same weights, not evidence that Megatron alone causes the residual.

A focused 619-token, four-response learner probe used exact-final-line rewards `[1, 0, 1, 0]`. One `behavior_clip` update took 115.9 s; captured-route hit and executed-set match were 1.0, PPO clipping was zero, full-model hashes changed on all 128 ranks, router gradients were nonzero, and frozen query-bias hashes stayed equal. Batch shape alone changed pre-update Megatron scores by up to 0.0721, so the earlier mixed-shape readback was not a clean update measure; the focused run measured before and after on the *same batch*. This proves an observable reward-derived update, not learning quality or sustained RL throughput. It used one response from each of four different prompts, so it does not exercise grouped GRPO, weight publication, or staleness. The older zero log-ratio checks remain Megatron self-consistency checks, not vLLM agreement.

**Decision:** H100 is **NO-GO for current-checkpoint RL qualification**: the matched numerical sample uses step 108000, and a normal grouped update, weight-version sync, and sustained iteration timing remain untested. GB200 is **NO-GO / untested**: the known 64-GB200 layout cannot safely place on the spare rack while another 64-GPU job is scheduling-gated. The inspected current Hero checkpoint line reaches permanent step 144000, but no matching BF16 serving export was found in the inspected roots. Next: export the current permanent checkpoint to BF16 serving weights; run matched tokens, weights, and executed routes plus a grouped 32×4 update with publication/readback and sustained timing on H100, then repeat on GB200 when the spare rack is safely available. Propose an RL acceptance rule for Romain's approval before any GO; the old Levanter gate remains unchanged.

**Candidate RL gate for Romain's approval:** on each accelerator at a matched current BF16 export, use production-shape 32×4 grouped rollouts; require full captured-route hit and executed-set match, and at most 0.1% sampled-vLLM-versus-Megatron fixed-weight ratios outside the behavior-clip band `[0.8,1.2]` across *all trained response tokens*, with stopped, capped, and reward-valid subsets reported separately. Then verify a finite grouped update, frozen query bias, router-weight change, weight-version publication/readback, and at least ten end-to-end iterations at configured sync/staleness, reporting latency and peak memory. The H100 diagnostic's 2/15,085 out-of-band ratios motivate the proposed band, but do not satisfy the remaining conditions or constitute approval.

- The opt-in final-line GSM8K reward rule is in [draft PR marin-community/MarinSkyRL#751](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/751); default scoring remains unchanged.

🤖 **Hero BF16 4K RL: GO on H100 and GB200 under the accepted RL rule.** This decision covers the complete permanent step-144000 export, non-agentic GSM8K, at most 4,096 total tokens, and normal grouped asynchronous PPO/GRPO. The old Levanter gate is unchanged.

Romain accepted at least 50,000 independent fixed-weight response tokens per platform with under 0.1% of ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]`, then four normal grouped updates with exact routes and weight versions, admitted staleness at most one, finite rewards and router gradients, and under 1% actual PPO clipping per update.

The independent fixed-weight comparison uses 64 natural responses per platform and identical token IDs with captured response routes. The gap is mean/max `abs(log p_Megatron − log p_sampled-vLLM)` over response tokens; outliers count importance ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]`. Online clipping is the *actual PPO-clipped token fraction*, not that fixed-weight outlier rate.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| H100 | 57,039 | 0.008291 / 0.2910 | 4 (0.0070%) | 4 | 0.2065% | 4,211 s |
| GB200 | 60,694 | 0.009345 / 0.2921 | 2 (0.0033%) | 4 | 0.0353% | 3,454 s |

Each platform completed four reward-derived grouped updates and five exact selected-weight/all-48-router-bias readbacks. Captured routes were executed exactly; router weights changed, query biases stayed frozen, and rewards and router gradients were finite. No admitted group was more than one version stale; one stale group was rejected on each platform's fourth update. The B200 run trained 99,860 aligned response tokens across its four updates. Its 48-trainer/16-serving placement avoids the host/GPU OOM seen in earlier 32-trainer attempts. In a traced H100 case, the first different model tensor was the layer-0 FA3 local-window attention output just past position 2,048; a matched FA2 control removed the sampled-vLLM versus full-prefill discrepancy. This trace does not prove an instruction-level kernel defect or set a full-Hero error bound. The old 16-layer investigation likewise sets no full-Hero bound. The accepted RL measurements support this bounded GO decision, not bitwise serving/training parity, learning quality, 8K, FP8, or general throughput. Step-time totals have different token counts and placements, so they are not a matched H100/GB200 speed comparison. 🤖 **Hero MuonH/non-eager BF16 4K: GO on H100 and GB200 under the accepted numerical rule (September 25).** Both used the same permanent step-144000 BF16 export, 16 fixed non-agentic GSM8K prompts, a 4,096-token combined cap, and batch-invariant vLLM. The old Levanter gate stays unchanged.

| Platform | Fixed-weight independent responses / tokens | Megatron versus sampled-vLLM mean / max absolute log-probability gap | Ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]` | Normal grouped updates | Maximum actual PPO clipping |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| H100 | 96 / 100,803 | 0.008866 / 0.419475 | 14 (0.01389%) | 4 at 128 learner + 24 serving | 0.00548% |
| GB200 48 + 8 | 96 / 92,113 | 0.007997 / 0.287569 | 6 (0.00651%) | 4 | 0.01864% |
| GB200 48 + 16 | 96 / 97,563 | 0.008153 / 0.335155 | 4 (0.00410%) | 4 | 0.01261% |

All 16 prompts produced six distinct seeded responses on each platform. The fixed-weight comparison rescored identical response tokens with their captured response routes, after exact selected-weight and all-48-router-bias readback. Each normal MuonH grouped run checked exact executed routes and five weight-version readbacks, finite rewards and router gradients, maximum admitted staleness of one version, and actual PPO clipping below 1% **in every update**. The zero training log ratio compares Megatron with its own rescored values; it is not the serving comparison in the table. The 48 + 8 GB200 layout measured 43.68 warm aligned tokens/s aggregate (0.780 per allocated GPU), versus 32.16/s (0.502/GPU) at 48 + 16 on different sampled responses. Its fixed-weight report completed all 96 scores; Iris lost one pod after saving that report, and the pending retry was canceled.

The result is a bounded numerical GO, not a learning-quality or longer-context claim. A 16-layer numerical investigation does not bound full Hero. Same-input vLLM sampled decoding versus full prefill had 120/100,803 H100, 194/92,113 GB200 48 + 8, and 239/97,563 GB200 48 + 16 out-of-band ratios; those are a separate execution-shape diagnostic, not the accepted Megatron-versus-sampled-vLLM gate. Eager/non-eager causality still needs a same-token, same-route control. An actual 8K H100 probe hit a compiled vLLM position-index bound of 4,096, so this pinned export/runtime does not support 8K. Its completed actual-4K serving cases were saved. Dedicated actual-4K one-request-per-serving-GPU probes are complete on both platforms. H100 measured 519.06 prompt tokens/s/GPU for a 4,095-token prompt and 7.904 response tokens/s/GPU for a 3,072-prompt + 1,024-response case including prefill; GB200 measured 896.62 and 4.070 respectively. Their engine counts and configured maxima differed, so these are layout rates, not an isolated accelerator speed ratio. H100 128 + 24 and GB200 48 + 8 / 48 + 16 each completed eight grouped updates, a 4.88-TiB MuonH checkpoint at step six, and two post-save updates. Warm steps 2–8 including that save measured 46.30 / 29.11 / 24.88 aligned response tokens/s aggregate (0.305 / 0.520 / 0.389 per allocated GPU), on samples of 231,971 / 194,375 / 171,925 aligned tokens. Different response lengths limit causal comparison. Step-six saves took 1,158.74 / 1,058.65 / 1,077.66 seconds. A fresh full-size H100 restore took 703.63 seconds and its next grouped update passed. GB200 fresh restore and continuation remain unproven: a 48 + 16 trial OOM-killed at 928 GiB; a 48 + 8 one-reader retry reached an NCCL broadcast timeout after long sequential DCP reads. A first two-reader 48 + 8 attempt exhausted four Iris preemptions before checkpoint loading. A fresh attempt reached the first large-shard wave with sampled policy-node memory below 740 GiB, then was preempted mid-load; its restart was preempted during setup and canceled. No GB200 restore or step-nine update is established. A 980 GiB/node request could not schedule and was canceled before GPU work. The focused production work is in draft PRs [#766](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/766), [#767](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/767), [#770](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/770), and [#771](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/771).
