spillover_issues.author: ayush1298
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Related to the evals wish-list in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7090 (item 12). Proposing a procedurally generated, difficulty-parameterized proxy for SciCode. This issue is a design proposal only. I'd like agreement on scope and on the questions at the bottom before writing the generator.

Of the four proxy items (10–13), SciCode is the only one that is (a) graded programmatically with no judge model, (b) amenable to procedural instance generation with provably correct gold answers, and (c) validatable end-to-end on modest compute.

Briefly, why not the others yet:

- **GDPval-AA v2 (10)** — needs expert/LLM grading of open-ended deliverables plus an agentic shell+browse scaffold.
- **𝜏³-Banking (11)** — needs a user-simulator LLM per episode; sub-8B models floor on multi-turn tool use, so there is no rank signal at the scales we can cheaply validate against.
- **AA-Omniscience (13)** — its index rewards abstention, but small instruct models essentially never abstain, so the index degenerates to `2·accuracy − 1` and the calibration axis (the point of the benchmark) disappears during validation.

## The problem with SciCode as-is

SciCode is 338 subproblems from 80 main problems. At publication, the best model solved ~4.6% of main problems in the most realistic setting. A benchmark where the frontier scores single-digit and near-zero pass rates also mean near-zero information per item, so distinguishing two checkpoints needs an impractical number of samples.

The proxy's job is therefore not "SciCode but easier." It is:

> One generator and one difficulty dial such that a ~300M model sits in the sensitive band at low difficulty, a frontier model sits in the sensitive band at high difficulty, and **model ordering is preserved along the whole dial**.

## Design

### Three response modes

Same underlying item, three regimes — so one dataset serves in-loop pretraining evals *and* post-hoc generation evals:

| Mode | Format | Scoring path | Signal range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M** | multiple-choice over candidate implementations | logprob → runs **in-loop** via the Levanter harness | ~150M–1B |
| **F** | full function given, one line masked | short generation | ~1B–7B |
| **G** | write the function from the description (SciCode-native) | generation + unit tests | 7B–frontier |

### Difficulty as a vector, not a scalar

Independent axes so we can ablate which one actually drives ranking; scalar presets `D1…D5` are fixed combinations.

| Axis | Range |
|---|---|
| `d_chain` | 1 → 6 dependent subproblems |
| `d_scaffold` | L3 formula + shapes + worked example · L2 background prose · L1 terse signature (SciCode "no background") · L0 main problem only, model decomposes |
| `d_derive` | formula given / one step away / must be derived |
| `d_numeric` | benign inputs, `rtol=1e-3` → stiff, ill-conditioned, boundary-edge, `rtol=1e-8` |
| `d_libs` | scipy allowed → numpy only → pure Python |
| `d_noise` | irrelevant prior functions injected into context |

### Metrics

- SciCode-native: **subproblem pass rate** (gold prior steps injected) and **main-problem pass rate** (all-or-nothing, model's own prior steps).
- Proxy-native: **`D50`** — difficulty level at which pass rate crosses 50%, from a logistic fit to the pass-rate-vs-difficulty curve. Scale-free and immune to both floor and ceiling effects.
- Reported separately: **format-failure rate** (unparseable output), so we can tell a genuine capability signal from markdown compliance.

### v0 task families

Mirroring 4 SciCode's categories (numerical methods/simulation / scientific calculation):

- `numcalc` — quadrature, root finding, finite-difference derivatives, Richardson extrapolation
- `ode` — Euler / RK4 / velocity-Verlet / symplectic Euler on harmonic oscillator, damped-driven pendulum, Lotka–Volterra, SIR, Kepler two-body
- `numla` — Gram–Schmidt, power iteration, Jacobi/Gauss–Seidel, Thomas tridiagonal solver, Householder QR
- `quantum1d` — finite-difference Schrödinger: build D², build H, ground state, expectation values; box / harmonic / double-well / Pöschl–Teller potentials

Some other things as well, that we can use if we were not able to get good quality samples in v0: PDE finite-difference, thin-film transfer matrices, tight-binding band structure, Ising Metropolis, Needleman–Wunsch, DFT/PSD.

### Generation

Per family, not per instance: `sample_spec(rng, difficulty)` → `reference(spec)` → `render_prompt(spec, difficulty)` → `make_tests(spec, rng)`. Test outputs are produced by running the reference, so tests are correct by construction and instances are unlimited.

**Two-implementation gate.** No instance ships unless the reference agrees with an independent source to ≥2 orders of magnitude tighter than the test tolerance — RK4 vs `solve_ivp`, harmonic-well FD Schrödinger vs analytic `E0 = ½ħω`, Gram–Schmidt vs `np.linalg.qr`, Simpson vs `scipy.integrate.quad`. This replaces scientist annotation as the correctness guarantee.

**Determinism.** Explicit seeds; pinned shape/dtype/ordering/sign/units asserted before value comparison; no wall-clock, network, or ordering-dependent structures; 5s per-test timeout; `np.allclose` with both `rtol` and `atol`; CI runs every gold solution through the grader and requires 100% pass.

**Contamination.** Randomized identifiers and parameters mean no verbatim string exists upstream. Dataset carries a canary GUID. Memorization probe: check whether a strong model reproduces the reference verbatim on a canonicalized (non-randomized) variant; if so, that family needs more randomization.


### Difficulty analysis

Difficulty analysis across four layers, cheapest first.

#### (a) Empirical difficulty curves

Pass rate vs. each axis, per model. Fit a 2-parameter logistic and report **`D50`** (difficulty at 50% pass rate) and the **slope**. Slope matters as much as location — a flat curve means the knob does nothing and the axis should be dropped or redesigned.

#### (b) Item Response Theory (2PL)

Fit `P(correct | model m, item i) = σ(a_i (θ_m − b_i))` by marginal maximum likelihood over the full model × item matrix. Three outputs, each doing real work:

- **`b_i` — item difficulty** on a common latent scale, so items from different families become directly comparable. This is what lets us claim the scalar presets D1–D5 mean the same thing across `numcalc` and `quantum1d`.
- **`a_i` — item discrimination.** The screening tool. Low-`a` items fail to separate models regardless of how hard they are, and get cut from the frozen set. This is how we avoid shipping 600 items where 200 carry the signal.
- **`θ_m` — model ability**, the natural quantity to correlate against SciCode instead of a raw pass rate.

Fitting is seconds on CPU (`py-irt`, or EM in numpy) — the constraint is having **per-item** results, not compute.

#### (c) Axis attribution

Mixed-effects logistic regression on item-level outcomes:

```
correct ~ d_chain + d_scaffold + d_derive + d_numeric + d_libs + d_noise
          + (1 | model) + (1 | family) + (1 | problem)
```

Coefficients quantify how much each knob actually moves difficulty; random effects prevent one badly-calibrated family from driving the fit. Report standardized effect sizes so axes are comparable. This is also the check against the "proxy measures numpy fluency, not science" risk — we want `d_derive` and `d_scaffold` carrying weight, not `d_libs` alone.

#### (d) Validation of the dial

Three preregistered checks:

- **Monotonicity** — pass rate non-increasing in each axis, per model.
- **Ordering stability** — model ordering preserved across ≥3 consecutive difficulty levels (Kendall τ between adjacent levels).
- **No axis inverts** — no axis where increasing difficulty *helps* some model class, which would indicate the knob measures format compliance rather than capability.

#### (e) Decomposing knowledge vs. implementation

Two mechanisms, neither requiring a judge model, both falling out of owning the reference implementation.

**Dual grading.** Score each response twice: strictly (`np.allclose`), and again under a *declared* convention group — sign/phase, scalar unit factor, eigenvalue ordering, transpose, 0-vs-1 indexing. The gap between the two scores is the **implementation tax**. A model at 30% strict and 55% tolerant knew the science and lost 25 points to conventions.

**Automatic error taxonomy.** Failures classify themselves:

| Code | Failure | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| E0 | no parseable code | format |
| E1 | syntax / import error | format |
| E2 | runtime exception | implementation |
| E3 | wrong shape or dtype | implementation |
| E4 | right shape, values far off | **knowledge** — wrong algorithm |
| E5 | right shape, close but outside tolerance | **implementation** — convention, units, off-by-one, precision |

The **E4:E5 ratio** gives a knowledge-vs-implementation split per model and per difficulty level, at no extra cost.

**Factorial isolation.** The axes are manipulable independently, so:

- *Knowledge held out, implementation varied:* fix `d_derive = 0` (formula given verbatim), sweep `d_numeric` and convention strictness.
- *Implementation held trivial, knowledge varied:* one-line function body, no shape juggling, sweep `d_scaffold` L3 → L0 and `d_derive` 0 → 2.

Collapse in the first sweep implies implementation dominates; collapse in the second implies knowledge does. An interaction is the likely and most interesting outcome.

#### Reporting discipline

Format-failure rate (E0 + E1) is reported separately throughout, never folded into the headline. If it exceeds ~10% for a model, that model's scores are not interpretable and it is **excluded** from the correlation rather than quietly averaged in.

---

## Validation plan

We want to ensure that model rank correlation should hold w.r.t. original SciCode at substantially lower cost. Protocol:

1. **Preregister** model roster, difficulty presets, prompt template, and target metric in this issue before any correlation is computed.
2. **Dev / held-out split by family.** Tune presets on `numcalc` + `ode`; report final correlation on `numla` + `quantum1d` only.
3. **Measure the reference directly.** Run original SciCode on the roster (288 test-set subproblems, short outputs, CPU-only grading — tractable at these model sizes) rather than relying solely on published leaderboard numbers. Use published numbers as a secondary external anchor.
4. **Roster, two groups.**
   - *Scaling ladders (validity check — true order known a priori):* Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B→1.5B→3B→7B; Llama-3.2-1B→3.2-3B→3.1-8B
   - *Cross-family spread:* Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, SmolLM2-1.7B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-4B/8B, **Marin-8B-Instruct**
5. **Statistics.** Spearman ρ and Kendall τ_b, with bootstrap CIs resampled over models *and* over items. Plus **pairwise order agreement restricted to model pairs whose reference scores differ by more than their combined 95% CI** — correlating against noise otherwise inflates ρ.
6. **Acceptance targets:** held-out ρ ≥ 0.90; pairwise agreement ≥ 0.85; monotone recovery of both scaling ladders across ≥3 consecutive difficulty levels.
7. **Cost claim, quantified.** Report `n_80%` — items needed for 80% power to detect the observed gap at α=0.05 — for SciCode vs. the proxy at matched difficulty, alongside token counts, wall-clock, and per-item curation cost.

## Scope

**In scope for v0:** 4 families × 5 difficulty levels × ~30 instances (~600 items) plus Mode M variants; harness-agnostic generator + scorer; frozen JSONL snapshot; validation report.

**Out of scope for v0:** additional families, paper-derived "realism tier," multi-language support, RL/training use.

## Milestones

- [ ] Design agreed (this issue)
- [ ] Generator interface + `numcalc` end-to-end + sandboxed grader + CI gold-solution check
- [ ] Remaining three families, two-implementation gate applied, v0 snapshot frozen
- [ ] Reference SciCode measured across roster
- [ ] Proxy sweep, presets tuned on dev families only
- [ ] Held-out correlation + D50 curves + power analysis + memorization probes
- [ ] PR: generator, dataset, scorer, harness wiring, docs, validation report

## Some questions:

1. **What model scale must show signal?** Does this need to discriminate ~300M ablation checkpoints, or is 8B+ sufficient? This determines whether Mode M is essential or optional.
2. **Which harness should it land in** — evalchemy post-hoc, Harbor, or a custom evaluator under `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators`? I plan to keep the generator and scorer harness-agnostic either way.
3. **Is a code-execution sandbox available in the eval path** as Numerical tolerances depend on versions of different libraries like numpy/scipy.
4. Is cluster time available if I want to run > 8B models?

comments.body:
The multidimensional vector evaluation looks great. 

There are results from more recent models in 
[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/scicode) and [LLM Registry](https://llm-registry.com/benchmark/scicode?view=all&variants=0&range=all), are they in the same scale compared to the original set?

comments.author: ayush1298
comments.body:
@Nativeatom, below are answers to your questions as per my analysis: 

## 1. Same scale as the paper?

No. The paper's **4.6%** is **main-problem** accuracy — all-or-nothing over a chain, using the model's own prior steps. AA's ~60% is the **subproblem** metric over the 288 test-set subproblems. Different denominator and aggregation.

**LLM Registry isn't a second data point** as it lists AA as its source and the numbers match (Gemini 3.1 Pro 59.0% vs 58.9%). 

**The bigger issue is compression.** Median 44%, top three within 1.5 points. At n=288 the SE at p=0.6 is 2.9pp — and subproblems are nested in 80 main problems, so at ICC 0.2 effective n is ~190 and SE rises to ~3.6pp. Minimum detectable difference on unpaired aggregates is **~11pp**. The top of that leaderboard is one statistical tie.

Two consequences: run the reference ourselves for **per-item** results, since paired comparison is far more powerful than the above; and restrict the correlation target to model pairs actually separated in the reference, or ρ is attenuated and uninterpretable.

It also sharpens the motivation that SciCode has a **floor problem at small scale** *and* a **ceiling-compression problem at the frontier**, which is why the headline metric is `D50` rather than a raw pass rate.

## 2. Scientific Knowledge or snippet implementation?

**Both, binding at different scales.** Knowledge gates whether a small model attempts the right algorithm at all; implementation thoroughness is what's compressing the top.

The Ewald example on AA's own page: all four energy terms are given in full LaTeX, so barely any derivation remains. What's left is broadcasting bookkeeping (`(natoms, npairs, 1, 3)` against `(natoms, 1, ncells, 3)`), an exclusion rule stated purely as boundary conditions, and unit discipline (zJ / nm/ps / g·mol⁻¹, `kB = 0.0138064852 zJ/K`, a g/mol → kg/particle conversion). A model can know exactly what Ewald summation is and fail all of it.

On the contrary, EAIRA's SciCode analysis found significant gains from supplying scientific background, which reads as a real reasoning limit rather than a coding one.

So rather than assert a winner, the proposal now includes two mechanisms that measure the split directly, neither needing a judge model . **dual grading** (strict vs. convention-tolerant; the gap is the implementation tax) and an **automatic error taxonomy** separating "right shape, values far off" (knowledge — wrong algorithm) from "right shape, outside tolerance" (implementation — convention, units, off-by-one). That ratio gives the split per model and per difficulty level. My prediction is that it flips from knowledge- to implementation-dominated somewhere in the 3–7B range.

comments.body: @Nativeatom please follow up whenever you get a chance?

comments.author: rfgordan
comments.body:
There are a lot of cool ideas here. 

A couple thoughts on the goals of this work, related to your last question: 

> What model scale must show signal? Does this need to discriminate ~300M ablation checkpoints, or is 8B+ sufficient? This determines whether Mode M is essential or optional.

My understanding is that the critical piece here is discriminating the post-training checkpoints (I believe I've seen RL experiments down to 1B). I think the pretraining metrics can be deferred to future work. Also, in the validation plan here its called out that the eval should be "substantially lower cost". I think cost is a nice property but it's not highlighted as a primary goal in the Epic.

With that in mind, I would consider what the minimum viable version of this that still discriminates at lower scales would be. For example, Mode G + the first three difficulty vectors are quite intuitive as easier versions of SciCode, so require a little bit less faith in the statistical machinery proposed here. Worth testing how low you can go with just those. Relatedly, with something like the D50 metric, I'd be worried that there may be some reliance on properties of the underlying scaling curve that aren't guaranteed.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
The marin SFT launcher (`experiments/sft/`) has two latent bugs on the **GPU (CoreWeave H100)** path that block a full-parameter SFT of any non-trivial checkpoint. Both surfaced running a 25B dense SFT (`delphi-1e23`) on a single `8xH100` node, and both are specific to the GPU path — the recipe was previously validated only on TPU, where `ResourceConfig.with_tpu` sizes the host from the slice, so neither was ever exercised. The training child dies before completing a step in both cases. Suggested fixes below (the first is already applied in a working tree and can be upstreamed as-is).

## Bug 1 — GPU pod gets no host RAM, OOMs during `initialize_from_hf`

`experiments/sft/launcher.py::resources_from_accelerator` built the GPU `ResourceConfig` with `with_gpu(variant, count=..., regions=[ANY_REGION])` and **no `ram=`/`cpu=`/`disk=`**, so it inherited the `ResourceConfig` default of ~4 GB host RAM. `initialize_from_hf` buffers the entire HF state dict in **host RAM** before device placement (Levanter `_load_from_remote`); a 25B fp32 checkpoint is ~100 GB, so the child is `SIGKILL`ed reading the first ~2.8 GB shard. The failure is silent — no traceback, just an OOMKill — and Iris surfaces the last-flushed stdout line as a misleading "reason", so it reads like a checkpoint/IO error rather than host-RAM exhaustion.

**Suggested fix (applied, working):** size host cpu/ram/disk with the GPU count in the GPU branch, mirroring what `with_tpu` already does per slice. The node (`gd-8xh100ib-i128`) is 128 vCPU / 2 TB, so per-device 8 vCPU / 96 GB / 48 GB (→ `8xH100` = 64 vCPU / 768 GB / 384 GB) is comfortable headroom:

```python
_GPU_HOST_CPU_PER_DEVICE = 8
_GPU_HOST_RAM_GB_PER_DEVICE = 96
_GPU_HOST_DISK_GB_PER_DEVICE = 48

def resources_from_accelerator(accelerator: str) -> ResourceConfig:
    gpu = _GPU_ACCELERATOR.fullmatch(accelerator)
    if gpu is not None:
        count = int(gpu["count"])
        return ResourceConfig.with_gpu(
            gpu["variant"], count=count, regions=[ANY_REGION],
            cpu=_GPU_HOST_CPU_PER_DEVICE * count,
            ram=f"{_GPU_HOST_RAM_GB_PER_DEVICE * count}g",
            disk=f"{_GPU_HOST_DISK_GB_PER_DEVICE * count}g",
        )
    return ResourceConfig.with_tpu(accelerator)
```

(Resources are a runtime arg excluded from the step fingerprint, so this does not fork any cached artifact.)

## Bug 2 — tokenizer staging rejects `s3://`/`gs://` paths (`HFValidationError`)

When a `ModelSource` resolves the tokenizer path to an object-store dir (e.g. `PreparedModel`, whose `tokenizer_path = ctx.artifact_path(step)` is `s3://…` / `gs://…`), the SFT dies **before compile** with:

```
HFValidationError: Repo id must be in the form '.../...' … 's3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/checkpoints/delphi-1e23-prepared/2026.07.19'
```

The **weights** path handles URL-like ids: `compat/hf_checkpoints.py` routes `if "://" in id` through fsspec (`_load_state_dict` ~L752) and loads the HF config under `_patch_hf_hub_download()` (~L1599), whose `custom_validate_repo_id` bypasses `validate_repo_id` for `_is_url_like` ids (~L1306). But the **tokenizer** staging path does not: `levanter/tokenizers.py::load_tokenizer` (~L732) → `_stage_tokenizer` → `_stage_from_hf` (~L857) calls `huggingface_hub.snapshot_download(name_or_path, allow_patterns=…)` (~L868) **with no `_is_url_like` guard and outside `_patch_hf_hub_download()`**, so `validate_repo_id` rejects the object-store dir.

**Suggested fix:** in `levanter/tokenizers.py`, add a `_is_url_like` check so URL-like tokenizer paths are fetched via fsspec (download the tokenizer files from the `s3://`/`gs://` dir) instead of being handed raw to `snapshot_download`/`validate_repo_id` — or, minimally, wrap the `snapshot_download` in the same `_patch_hf_hub_download()` context the weights path uses so the URL bypass applies uniformly. Either makes the tokenizer path consistent with the already-URL-aware weights path.

**Current workaround** (does not need the fix): point the SFT `ModelSource` at an HF **repo id** rather than an object-store dir (the `HFModel(model_ref=<hf repo>)` path, which the proven `delphi_1e22` config uses). That is why `PreparedModel(step=…)` — designed to init from a prep-step's object-store output — is unusable on this path today.

## Impact / scope

- Bug 1 affects **every** GPU SFT of a checkpoint whose host-RAM state dict exceeds ~4 GB (i.e. anything past a small model), independent of dataset.
- Bug 2 affects any `ModelSource` that resolves the tokenizer to an `s3://`/`gs://` dir — notably `PreparedModel`, making the reproducible "prep-step → init-from-step-output" flow unusable on GPU/CoreWeave until fixed; the HF-repo staging workaround is the only path today.

Both are in the `experiments/sft/` + Levanter tokenizer-staging code and were confirmed by an end-to-end 25B `8xH100` run that, once both were addressed, compiles and trains cleanly (first step 30.9 s, ~4.3 s/it).

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
## What is present vs. missing (precise)

**Present — Grug MoE trains on both TPU and GPU today, but entirely through JAX (Levanter/Haliax):**
- TPU path (megablox Pallas GMM) drives the **67B-A2B run** on v4-2048 (#6044).
- GPU path is **validated end-to-end on H100**: Grug MoE ran on CoreWeave first-try (#3025), plus active MFU optimization (#4302, #6367 d2560 H100 MFU, #6493 Muon single-node GPU, #6492), enabled by the **Triton `ragged_dot`** fallback (PR #4297) and **DeepEP** dispatch (#6251); ring EP lowers + executes on GPU (#6532). Blackwell/B200 via QuACK is WIP (#7012, #6597).

**Present on the PyTorch side too:** MarinSkyRL **already trains MoE policies in PyTorch** — GRPO on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B / Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (#7052, #6335). So "MoE in PyTorch" is *not* missing.

**Missing:** there is **no PyTorch implementation of the Grug kernels**, and no bridge that lets MarinSkyRL inherit Grug's kernel performance or verify numerical parity against it. The boundary MarinSkyRL faces is **JAX→PyTorch (framework)** — orthogonal to, and harder than, the **TPU→GPU (hardware)** boundary, which is largely solved. Direct extraction of the JAX/Pallas kernels into PyTorch is not viable (megablox is a JAX `pallas_call`/Mosaic op with no standalone form; PyTorch interop was explicitly out of scope in the kernel epic #5328). The realistic path is **share the same *upstream* kernels** (SonicMoE/QuACK, DeepEP, vLLM/SGLang fused_moe — all PyTorch-native) behind a common `grouped_gemm(lhs, rhs, group_sizes)` + dispatch/combine interface, and use the **Grug JAX forward/backward as a numerical oracle**. The gaps below are what that requires.

---

## Gaps (isolated scope · criticality · definition of done · links)

> **MarinSkyRL status (2026-08-05):** the PyTorch Grug path landed in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#110 (canonical `grug_moe` model + FSDP2 RL, reference impl checked against the committed Levanter oracle). G5 and G6 are completed; G1/G2/G3/G4 ride on the grouped-EP work in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open) plus the merged parity/divergence tests below.

### G1 — Fast grouped-GEMM expert kernel in the MarinSkyRL trainer — 🚧 in progress
**MarinSkyRL:** marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open) adds native grouped MM for Grug with a 109.6× one-H100 benchmark; not yet merged.
**Scope:** Confirm what expert-GEMM the MarinSkyRL MoE training forward uses today (reference torch loop vs. a fused grouped-GEMM). If it's a reference path, back it with a PyTorch-native fast kernel (SonicMoE/QuACK CUTLASS, `grouped_gemm`, or vLLM `fused_moe`).
**Criticality: Medium** — throughput only; it *works* today, the upside is trainer step-time at 30B-A3B+. (RL is rollout-bound, so this is secondary to G3.)
**DoD:** trainer MoE layer calls a fused grouped-GEMM; measured step-time delta vs. the reference on the target 30B-A3B/35B-A3B; no regression in loss curve.
**Links:** #7012 (QuACK SM100), #5328 (SonicMoE epic — the JAX counterpart), #7052 (RL step-time feasibility).

### G2 — Backward-pass numerical parity for the fused expert GEMM — 🚧 partial
**MarinSkyRL:** marin-community/MarinSkyRL#110 (merged) keeps the reference PyTorch backward checkable against the Levanter oracle; marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open) adds the four-H100 raw-gradient/AdamW parity. The custom-vs-recompute decision and finite-difference gate ride on #276.
**Scope:** Any fused grouped-GEMM needs a hand-written PyTorch backward (`autograd.Function`). Verify it against a reference. Marin's JAX experience is the warning: every custom path needed a `custom_vjp`, and #5328's `unpack_bwd` study found the fancy Pallas backward bought ~2.8% e2e vs. +21.8% for plain forced-recompute — i.e. the custom backward frequently isn't worth it.
**Criticality: Critical** — a wrong backward silently biases gradients with no crash.
**DoD:** PyTorch backward matches finite-difference AND matches the Grug JAX gradient (via G5) within tolerance on a fixed (tokens, router-logits, weights) case; decision recorded on whether a custom backward beats plain recompute.
**Links:** #5328 (unpack_bwd decision log), PR #4297 (Triton custom_vjp).

### G3 — Train↔rollout routing-semantics parity — 🚧 partial
**MarinSkyRL:** marin-community/MarinSkyRL#110 (merged) synchronizes mixed BF16/FP32 routing state to vLLM; marin-community/MarinSkyRL#280 (merged) adds a policy-forward capture/replay harness that re-runs the trainer boundary without rollout/inference. The explicit trainer↔inference expert-assignment + gate-weight parity test rides on marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open).
**Scope:** top-k selection, token-sort order, and tie-breaking must be identical between the MarinSkyRL trainer forward and the rollout/inference engine (vLLM/SGLang) forward. Any divergence injects policy-gradient bias.
**Criticality: Critical** — this is the RL-specific trap: MarinSkyRL already runs TIS/R3 to correct train↔infer mismatch (#6335), and a routing mismatch compounds exactly what TIS is meant to fix. #6044 flagged the local token-sort for QB routing as hardware-dependent.
**DoD:** a parity test asserting identical expert assignments + gate weights between trainer and inference engine on a fixed batch; the tie-break rule is documented and enforced in both.
**Links:** #6335 (TIS/R3 on MarinSkyRL), #6044 (token-sort hw-dependence), #7052.

### G4 — EP dispatch/combine reduction parity (only if EP>1 in the trainer) — 🚧 in progress
**MarinSkyRL:** marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open) delivers torch all-to-all EP with averaged expert gradients + the mixed-EP lifecycle capstone (global expert-row gather, checkpoint continuation, multi-owner FP32 bias readback). Collective divergence is bounded by the merged marin-community/MarinSkyRL#288, #272, #271, #270, #269, #268 (EP4/FSDP4 mesh schedules).
**Scope:** If MarinSkyRL trains at expert-parallel degree >1, the dispatch/combine (DeepEP, which both stacks can share upstream; or all_gather+reduce_scatter) must be reduction-order-consistent with what produced the reference gradients.
**Criticality: Medium** — bites only at EP>1; the current 30B-A3B RL may run EP=1. Downgrade to Low if EP=1 is confirmed.
**DoD:** EP combine is reduction-consistent and validated at the EP degree MarinSkyRL actually uses; DeepEP wired as the shared transport if EP>1.
**Links:** PR #6251 (assigned-token DeepEP dispatch, closed) + the landed `_moe/ep_deepep.py` backend, #6532 (ring-EP-on-GPU + megablox `shard_map` lowering findings).

### G5 — Cross-framework parity harness (Grug JAX forward/backward as oracle) — ✅ completed
**MarinSkyRL:** marin-community/MarinSkyRL#110 (merged) keeps the reference PyTorch `grug_moe` forward/backward/routing/bias checkable against the committed Levanter oracle without adding JAX to the runtime; validation report linked in the PR. This is the runnable oracle harness the DoD asks for.
**Scope:** Build a harness that runs a fixed input (tokens + router logits + expert weights) through both the Grug JAX MoE layer and the MarinSkyRL PyTorch MoE layer, and diffs routing decisions, per-expert outputs, and gradients.
**Criticality: High** — it's the enabling infrastructure for G2/G3/G4; without it, "parity" is unfalsifiable.
**DoD:** a runnable harness + a committed tolerance report for the target model; wired into CI or a manual gate before MoE-kernel changes land in MarinSkyRL.
**Links:** #2828 (established the shared `(lhs, rhs, group_sizes)` API), #5328.

### G6 — MoE checkpoint / expert-weight-layout interop (only if weights cross frameworks) — ✅ completed (N/A)
**MarinSkyRL:** the gap is moot by the issue's own escape clause ("N/A if MarinSkyRL loads HF-format weights directly"): marin-community/MarinSkyRL#110 (merged) loads HF safetensors straight into the PyTorch `grug_moe` and synchronizes mixed BF16/FP32 state to vLLM, so no Levanter↔PyTorch expert-tensor converter is needed. EP-owner transfer readback is covered by marin-community/MarinSkyRL#276 (open).
**Scope:** If Grug-trained (Levanter/JAX) MoE checkpoints feed the PyTorch RL policy — or MOPD/distillation moves experts between them — the expert weight layout (gate/up/down packing, expert-major vs. token-major, sharded vs. dense) must be mapped and tested.
**Criticality: Medium** — only if checkpoints actually cross the JAX↔PyTorch boundary; N/A if MarinSkyRL loads HF-format weights directly.
**DoD:** a documented, round-trip-tested weight converter for MoE expert tensors between Levanter and the PyTorch model; parity of a forward pass on converted weights.
**Links:** — (new); relate to the hero-model MOPD path if/when specced.

---

## Suggested sequencing
G5 (oracle harness) first — it unblocks the two Critical correctness gaps. Then G3 (routing parity, the RL-specific trap) and G2 (backward parity) in parallel. G1 (perf) and G4/G6 (conditional) follow once correctness is proven. Confirm the open scoping questions early: (a) what expert-GEMM MarinSkyRL uses today, (b) its EP degree, (c) whether checkpoints cross the JAX↔PyTorch boundary — these set the criticality of G1/G4/G6.

## References
Runs/experiments: #6044 (67B-A2B TPU), #3025 (Grug MoE on CW GPU, first-try), #4302 / #6367 / #6493 / #6492 (H100 MFU), #7012 (B200 QuACK), #6597 (fused EP NVLink), #7052 (MarinSkyRL 30B/35B-A3B RL step-time), #6335 (TIS/R3 on MarinSkyRL).
Kernels/PRs: #2828 (GPU port + shared API), PR #4297 (Triton ragged_dot, merged), PR #5718 (sonic gather/combine, merged), PR #6251 (assigned-token DeepEP dispatch, closed), #5328 (SonicMoE epic), #6532 (zero-bubble PP for Grug-MoE — ring-EP-GPU + megablox `shard_map` findings), #3431 (abandoned fused TPU-EP).
Code: `lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py:18-23,335-360`; `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:184-217`; `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/{local.py:32,scatter.py,sonic.py,ep_ring.py,ep_deepep.py}`; `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/model.py:121,512`.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Fast-track addendum: the checkpoint→GPU path already exists (HF-native); the residual is *one* training modeling class.**

Digging into the recent GPU-serving work (#6869, PR #6966, PR #6891, marin-community/vllm#7) sharpens **G6** and collapses the "get RL running on Grug MoEs" critical path. What's already built, then the one concrete TODO.

## Already built (checkpoint interop is ~solved for *serving*)

1. **Export is HF-native.** `experiments/grug/moe/model.py` defines `GrugMoeHfConfig(HfConfig)` (L96) + architecture `"GrugMoeForCausalLM"` (L56); the Levanter checkpoint exports through the standard `HFCheckpointConverter` (`to_hf_config()`) → a plain HF checkpoint (`config.json` + safetensors).
2. **GPU rollout serving is done.** `marin-community/vllm` ships a native PyTorch `grugmoe.py` (`GrugMoeRouter` / `GrugMoeGatedNorm` / `GrugMoeMLP`) that `load_weights` the HF checkpoint and runs experts on vLLM **`FusedMoE`** + expert parallelism — preserving Levanter's router math incl. the `1e-9` combine-weight epsilon (marin-community/vllm#7). Parity-validated vs a JAX bf16 reference (PR #6966/#6891) on `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/moe_may_compute_opt_d512_ep1-05c39b/checkpoints/step-10980` (DP8/EP8 on one H100×8, TP=1); the 67B BF16 export was exercised DP8/EP8.

Note: GPU serving uses **vLLM FusedMoE, not the Grug JAX kernels** — the "share upstream kernels" pattern; the Grug JAX kernels never cross into the GPU rollout path.

## Fast-track TODO — the one thing actually missing

**→ Write a *training* `GrugMoeForCausalLM` PyTorch modeling class.** The config, the arch string, and an *inference* model (the vLLM fork) all exist; what's missing is a training-capable forward+backward. Concretely:
- reuse `GrugMoeHfConfig` and lift `GrugMoeRouter` (top-k + the `1e-9` epsilon) **verbatim** from the vLLM fork — that's what buys train↔rollout parity;
- replace vLLM's inference `FusedMoE` with a **training-capable expert forward**: start with a reference grouped-GEMM (dense/loop over experts) → autograd-correct, *no* custom backward; drop in SonicMoE/QuACK/`grouped_gemm` + a hand-written backward later (that's G1/G2, deferred);
- load the exported safetensors via the same weight-key mapping vLLM's `load_weights` uses.

**→ Load it into MarinSkyRL via `from_pretrained`** — the exact path #7052 used for Qwen-Coder-30B-A3B. Start on the parity-validated `moe_may_compute_opt_d512_ep1` step-10980 checkpoint, EP=1/8, **TIS on** (#6335) to absorb the expert-GEMM numeric residual.

Everything else in this issue (**G1** fast kernel, **G2** custom backward, **G3** routing parity, **G4** EP, **G5** parity harness) becomes the **parallel track** — gated behind TIS + the RL-parity checklist #6341, not blockers. The fast-track is ~one modeling file, not a kernel project.

## "How do you add a custom model to HF short of a PR?"

You don't need a `transformers` PR. Three options, easiest first:
- **(a) In-repo class in MarinSkyRL** — define `GrugMoeForCausalLM(PreTrainedModel)` in the RL repo, construct the policy from it directly, `load_state_dict` the safetensors. No HF Hub, no `Auto*` registration, no `trust_remote_code`. Simplest when the trainer is the only consumer.
- **(b) `trust_remote_code` custom-code-on-Hub — ✅ PREFERRED** — ship `configuration_grugmoe.py` + `modeling_grugmoe.py` next to the checkpoint (HF repo or local dir) with an `auto_map` in `config.json`; `from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True)` loads it anywhere (the MarinSkyRL trainer *and* any other consumer — eval, a second RL stack, a notebook) with one call, no per-repo model code and no upstream `transformers` PR. This is the right default: the *training* class lives with the checkpoint and is reused by everyone. *Caveat:* the HF mirror must include the `.py` files (our `mirror_hf_to_gcs.py` `INCLUDE_PATTERNS` needs `.py` for `auto_map` models, or they silently don't ride along).
- **(c) Upstream to `transformers`** — a real PR; only worth it for broad external reuse, not needed here.

The vLLM side effectively took a 4th route (a vendored model in a vLLM *fork*). **Go with (b)** — publish `modeling_grugmoe.py` + `auto_map` alongside the checkpoint so the training class is Hub-portable and any consumer loads it via `from_pretrained(trust_remote_code=True)`; keep (a) only as a throwaway in-repo stopgap if you need something running before the Hub files land.

**Bottom line:** because the export is already HF-format and the vLLM fork already proves the PyTorch router/attention/weight-mapping, "RL on Grug MoEs" fast-tracks to **write one training `GrugMoeForCausalLM` + `from_pretrained` it into MarinSkyRL** — with parity as the parallel track.
